10060-discourses-biological-geological-e:
Thomas H. Huxley's 1894 collection gathers his great popular lectures on biology and geology. It opens with On a Piece of Chalk, his 1868 lecture to Norwich working men, and moves to the problems of the deep sea and the results of the Challenger expedition.

Later essays treat yeast, the formation of coal, the lobster as a study in zoology, biogenesis and abiogenesis, and palaeontology and evolution. Huxley, Darwin's bulldog, writes with clarity and force. Readers get Victorian science at its most readable, from a chalk cliff to the origin of life.
10142-maezli-a-story-of-the-swiss-valley:
Johanna Spyri, author of Heidi and Cornelli, wrote Mäzli, a story of the Swiss valleys, translated by Elisabeth P. Stork in 1921. It opens in Nolla, with divers worries, Castle Wildenstein, and an unexpected apparition.

Oppressive air, new friends, and a mother's absence with its consequences follow, as Mäzli pays visits and enters the castle. Spyri writes with warmth about Swiss country life and a child's courage. Young readers get another Heidi-like heroine: lively, kind, and at home among mountains, castles, and neighbors. Spyri's mountain world feels as real as Heidi's.
10433-a-flock-of-girls-and-boys:
Nora Perry published this story collection in 1895, with pictures by Charlotte Tiffany Parker. Perry, author of Hope Benham and Lyrics and Legends, writes short tales of children at home, school, and holiday time. The tone is gentle, comic, and moral, in the style of late Victorian children's books.

That little Smith girl, the egg boy, Major Molly's Christmas promise, Polly's valentine, and Sibyl's slipper stand among the pieces. A boarding-school Samaritan, an April fool, and a Thanksgiving guest add variety. Readers get a sweet, old-fashioned flock of tales for young readers and their families.
10623-plays:
Susan Glaspell, a leading voice of the Provincetown Players, gathers four plays in this volume: Trifles, The Outside, The Verge, and Inheritors. Trifles was first staged at the Wharf Theatre in Provincetown in August 1916. It opens in a gloomy farmhouse kitchen, where a county attorney and a sheriff hunt for clues while two wives notice what the men miss.

The other plays widen her range, from a woman's inner life to questions of inheritance and belief. Glaspell writes plain, tense dialogue and trusts small details to carry meaning. Readers meet a founder of modern American drama, whose short plays still anchor courses and stages a century later.
10658-hilda-lessways:
Arnold Bennett published Hilda Lessways in 1911 as a novel about a young woman making her way in the English Midlands. Hilda starts life in a modest household, works as an editorial secretary, meets the Orgreave family, and travels to London. Later books of the novel follow her recovery, her burdens, her fall, and her punishment, in Bennett's plain chapter titles.

Bennett follows Hilda's choices, mistakes, and second chances with close attention to work, money, and feeling. The novel belongs to his Clayhanger series, and Edwin Clayhanger himself appears in its pages. Readers get a serious, detailed portrait of a woman seeking independence in Edwardian England.
10708-miscellaneous-essays:
Thomas De Quincey, author of Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, gathers some of his best-known short pieces in Miscellaneous Essays. The volume holds his famous essay on the knocking at the gate in Macbeth. It also holds his darkly comic "Murder, Considered as One of the Fine Arts" with a second paper, his portrait of Joan of Arc, and his mail-coach memoir.

De Quincey's style runs from boyhood puzzlement over Shakespeare to grand, dreamlike prose on travel and sudden death. The essays show a mind that turns small questions into wide meditations. Readers meet one of the great English essayists at his most inventive and personal.
10911-buried-alive-a-tale-of-these-days:
Arnold Bennett's Buried Alive, a tale of these days, opens on a London summer night in Selwood Terrace, South Kensington, where two lights burn in number ninety-one. Chapters follow a puce dressing-gown, a pail, a photograph, a scoop, Alice on hotels, a Putney morning, a confession, an invasion, a secret, and an escape. Bennett's comedy grows from modern life and its masks.

The tale turns on identity, fame, and the wish to vanish, as its hero slips the life the world expects of him. Bennett writes with wit and a keen eye for London manners. Readers get a clever, humane comedy from the author of the Clayhanger novels.
11020-angels-and-ministers-and-other-vic:
Laurence Housman collected short plays about Victorian and later public life in this volume. Part one, Angels and Ministers, shows Queen Victoria at Balmoral with John Brown, her Highland servant, in a garden tent, writing letters and ringing for a chair with a lean back. Other scenes explain political myths and stage a political finale.

Part two, Possession, offers a peep-show in paradise, while part three, Dethronements, moves from a king-maker at Brighton in 1891 to a man of business at Highbury in 1913. Housman writes with wit and a light satirical touch, imagining private moments behind public history. The plays suit readers of historical drama and of Victoria's reign.
11023-gems-of-poetry-for-girls-and-boys:
Short poems for children fill this 1850 illustrated collection, opening with a May-Day song of flowers, brooks, lambs, and bees. A child begs to laugh and play in May, and a mother answers that the maker of the blooming earth smiles on an infant's joy. Alexander Selkirk follows, monarch of all he surveys, lonely on his island and longing for society, friendship, and love.

Other poems include the old oaken bucket at a father's plantation well and two good-natured girls, Julia-Ann and Maria, who would rather give up a thing than quarrel over it. Pictures face the verses, including a view of Cincinnati and a cotton plant. The book gives young readers cheerful, moral verse in short, singable lines.
11026-literary-and-general-lectures-and-:
Charles Kingsley gathered literary and general essays in this volume, opening with The Stage as it was Once. Kingsley takes readers back 2,314 years to Athens in 440 BC, to a theatre hewn from rock on the Acropolis slope, with the Parthenon gleaming above and Salamis across the blue sea. There, he argues, reverence, heroism, and love of beauty joined in public enjoyment.

Other essays treat Shelley and Byron, Alexander Smith and Pope, Tennyson, Burns and his school, sacred and legendary art, English composition, and hours with the mystics. Kingsley writes as a preacher and critic, earnest about literature's moral power. The collection suits readers of Victorian criticism and of Kingsley's wide-ranging mind.
11675-vanishing-roads-and-other-essays:
Richard Le Gallienne's 1915 essays, Vanishing Roads and Other Essays, open with a dedication to Robert Hobart Davis, a fellow wayfarer on the vanishing road of the world. Le Gallienne recalls meeting Davis years before, and his early welcome to America, his promised land and final home.

Essays follow on vanishing roads, woman as a supernatural being, and the lack of imagination among millionaires. Later pages praise English footpaths winding over hill and dale, and the pheasant's gift to English woodland. The book is a reflective walk through landscape, friendship, and the changes of a new century.
12244-in-the-name-of-the-bodleian-and-ot:
Augustine Birrell published these essays in London in 1906, taking his title from a paper on the Bodleian Library at Oxford. Birrell, a lawyer, politician, and man of letters, wrote for readers who loved books as objects and as company.

Essays on bookworms, confirmed readers, first editions, and Charles Bradlaugh mix anecdote with literary judgment, and several first appeared in the Outlook, the Nineteenth Century, and the Speaker. Birrell praises miscellaneous writing itself, quoting Shaftesbury on the charitable author who invented it. The book is a companion for book lovers: witty, digressive, and content to wander from a library shelf to a life.
12591-tiger-and-tom-and-other-stories-fo:
Tiger and Tom and Other Stories for Boys, compiled from Sabbath Readings and illustrated in 1910, promises words fitly spoken, with a lesson in every story. Tiger and Tom stand faithfully in the market-place each morning, in the frontispiece illustration. Stories were gathered from church papers of the 1870s, Methodist, Lutheran, Presbyterian and others.

Contents add Those Scars, Coals of Fire, Lyman Dean's Testimonials, Bert's Thanksgiving, The Boy and His Spare Moments, Will Winslow, Only This Once, The Right Decision and The Use of spare time. Publishers call the tales a breath of fresh air for home reading. The book offers earnest, moral boys' stories, simple in style and strong in lesson.
12610-nan-sherwood-s-winter-holidays-or-:
Annie Roe Carr's 1916 Nan Sherwood's Winter Holidays, or Rescuing the Runaways, opens at Christmas time on Lake Huron's icy shore. Professor Krenner blows a silver bugle down Pendragon Hill, its strain echoing from the Isle of Hope, a wooded eminence half a mile offshore near Freeling. Winter holds Michigan in an iron grip, and Lakeview Hall girls enjoy winter sports.

A boathouse cove, once thought haunted, becomes a smooth skating pond, and the strait to the island freezes solid. Nan and friends, runaways and rescues follow, in a girls' school story of snow, skating and friendship. Carr writes in a warm, wholesome manner for young readers, mixing adventure with school life.
12651-the-humour-of-homer-and-other-essa:
Samuel Butler's essays, collected by R. A. Streatfeild, form the nucleus of the volume. The core collection, Essays on Life, Art and Science, first appeared under Grant Richards in 1904 and was reissued by Fifield in 1908. Streatfeild adds the title essay, The Humour of Homer, a biographical sketch by Henry Festing Jones, and a photogravure portrait from 1889.

The humour essay began as a lecture at the Working Men's College in Great Ormond Street. Butler's wit, scepticism and classical learning run through the volume, turning Homer, science and art into occasions for argument. The book offers Butler at his most readable, a Victorian freethinker in essay form.
1276-the-rhythm-of-life-and-other-essays:
Alice Meynell opens this 1893 volume with an essay on the rhythm of life, the quiet beat that runs beneath days and seasons. She follows it with short pieces on the sun, the flower, the railway side, and the writers she loved, from Holmes to Lowell.

Meynell's prose is brief, fine, and meditative, with a poet's care for small things. The essays ask for slow reading and reward it with calm. The book gives a gentle introduction to a master of the short essay, and it suits readers who like reflection over noise.
12797-the-log-of-a-cowboy-a-narrative-of:
Andy Adams wrote The Log of a Cowboy in 1903 from his own trail years, dedicating it to the cowmen of the old western trail. The log follows one herd north from Texas through the Atascosa, Colorado, Brazos, and Platte country to Dodge, Ogallala, and the Yellowstone. Stampedes, dry drives, boggy fords, and river crossings mark the road.

A mid-book council with Apache riders, talked through in Spanish, shows the trail's mix of danger and diplomacy. Adams writes with a drover's eye for cattle, horses, and men. The book stands as the classic first-hand account of the great cattle drives.
1288-dream-days:
Kenneth Grahame, author of The Wind in the Willows, gathers linked idylls of childhood. Five children, led by the dreamy Edward, play at knights, dragons, and secret worlds, while grown-ups blunder past the magic. The tales follow the children through seasons of make-believe.

Grahame writes childhood from the inside, with humor and a poet's eye for gardens, roads, and rainy days. The book is a sequel to The Golden Age, and its tone is wistful and warm. It suits readers who love childhood remembered well. Grahame's childhood idylls still charm readers of all ages.
1295-ceres-runaway-and-other-essays:
Alice Meynell gathers short essays on art, nature, and life in this 1909 volume. The title piece imagines Ceres, goddess of harvest, fleeing the modern world, while other essays touch on laughter, the sea wall, the daffodil, and the little language of children.

Meynell writes in brief, polished prose, with a poet's eye and a Catholic's quiet faith. Her essays are small and finely made, never loud. The book gives a gentle hour of reflection, and it shows a respected essayist at her most characteristic. Meynell's small essays reward slow, quiet reading.
13088-emerson-and-other-essays:
John Jay Chapman's 1899 essays, reprinted in this edition, take Emerson as their opening and longest subject. Chapman then turns to Walt Whitman, Shakespeare's Romeo, Michelangelo's sonnets, Dante's Inferno, Robert Browning, and Robert Louis Stevenson. The essays are critical portraits, not lives, and they judge each writer by moral force as much as by art.

Chapman quotes Emerson's scorn for flattering the masses, and his claim that moral sentiment builds cities, courts, and colleges. In the Romeo essay he praises the final scenes for their stark natural force, even where stagecraft fails them. The book is a record of an American critic at his most earnest, testing great writers against his own demand for truth spoken plainly.
1309-the-spirit-of-place-and-other-essay:
Alice Meynell gathers essays on place, solitude, and the life of the mind in this 1899 volume. The title piece meditates on how places keep their spirit, while others touch on bells, rain, sleep, and the letters of a French poetess.

Meynell writes in short, fine prose, with a poet's care and a thinker's calm. The essays ask for quiet reading and reward it with insight. The book gives a gentle, thoughtful hour, and it shows Meynell's essay art at its most characteristic. Meynell's essays ask for quiet reading and reward it with insight.
13271-rides-on-railways:
Samuel Sidney's Rides on Railways offers amusing, instructive notes for travelers who care little where they go, bound for Wales, the Lakes, or the Scottish Highlands. Sidney draws on personal observation, notes of former journeys, and histories of towns, mines, and manufactures along the lines. The book is a mid-Victorian railway companion, practical and curious.

At Rugby, eighty-three miles from London, he maps a vast network. Midland arms run to Leicester, Derby, and Nottingham, the Trent Valley line to Stafford, and a line to Leamington in three-quarters of an hour. Later, at Liverpool, he pictures the river ploughed by boats and steamers, with five miles of docks and forests of masts. The book is a lively guide to industrial Britain by rail.
13474-women-and-the-alphabet-a-series-of:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson asks, ought women to learn the alphabet, in the opening essay of this 1881 volume, first printed in the Atlantic Monthly in February 1859. He credits the essay with helping liberal views on women's training, and notes a report that Sophia Smith read it before founding the women's college at Northampton that bears her name.

Other essays, drawn from Common Sense About Women and the Woman's Journal, argue that civilisation has changed the family from a barony to a republic, while law lags behind ideas and manners. Girls admitted to Boston schools only in summer, when boys were too few, later crowded a high school with alarming success until it was abolished after eighteen months. Higginson writes reform with wit and history.
1360-historical-lectures-and-essays:
Charles Kingsley gathers lectures and essays on history: on the Roman Empire, the Middle Ages, and the making of modern England, with a reformer's zeal for the lessons of the past. The pieces range from the fall of Rome to the age of Elizabeth.

Kingsley writes history as moral drama, praising heroes and scolding tyrants, in prose that is vivid if Victorian. The volume shows a popular lecturer at work. It suits readers who like history told with passion and a point of view. Kingsley's lectures show history told with passion and a point of view.
13722-youth-and-sex-dangers-and-safeguar:
A 1919 guide by Mary Scharlieb and F. Arthur Sibly that takes up the dangers and safeguards of sex for girls and boys, in two parts. Scharlieb writes on girls: puberty, sickness, mental and moral training, and the final aim of education, stressing the strain that schooling places on adolescent girls.

Sibly writes on boys, drawing on his own experience and on schoolmasters such as Canon Lyttelton, to argue that impurity was widespread in schools and often hidden by a code of silence. Both authors urge plain, early instruction by parents and teachers rather than ignorance. The book is a document of Edwardian sex education, earnest, clinical, and anxious about youth.
14276-italian-journeys:
W. D. Howells published Italian Journeys in 1867 and again in 1895, tracing a road to Rome from Venice. Chapters run from Padua to Ferrara, through Bologna to Genoa, by sea to Naples, with days in Pompeii and Herculaneum, Capri, and ragged schools. Roman pearls, a pilgrimage to Petrarch's house at Arquà, a visit to the Cimbri, and minor travels to Pisa, Trieste, Bassano, and Mantua follow.

Naples street life fills the liveliest pages. Men quarrel purple over small fish, asses bray above the discord, women roast pine cones at charcoal fires, and children suffer hair-combing agonies. Goats wander, bagpipes play, and balcony watchers look down on the riot. A sea voyage adds comedy: seasickness turns the narrator into the Ancient Mariner, until morning coffee, toast, and a steward's loud Servitor suo restore good humor. Howells writes travel as friendly observation, curious and amused.
1434-essays:
Alice Meynell's essays, in this 1914 collection, range from winds and waters to books, towns, and the small manners of daily life. Titles such as Ceres' Runaway, The Tow Path, and The Little Language show her range: nature notes beside literary reflections, all written in a precise, musical prose.

Meynell watches a rain shower or a railway journey with the same care she gives to a poem, and her judgments are gentle but firm. The essays reward slow reading. Together they form a portrait of a mind attentive to beauty in common things, and a classic of the English familiar essay.
14481-the-function-of-the-poet-and-other:
James Russell Lowell, poet, critic, and diplomat, is the subject of this collection assembled by Albert Mordell from Lowell's magazine writing of the 1870s to the 1890s. The title essay first ran in the Century Magazine in 1894.

Lowell reflects on poetry, humor, satire, and imagination, names Homer, Dante, Cervantes, Goethe, and Shakespeare as indispensable authors, and reviews contemporaries such as Henry James and Longfellow. His criticism joins common sense to wide reading. Mordell's editing gathers fugitive pieces that might otherwise have stayed buried in old magazines. The volume shows a leading American man of letters judging his own tradition.
14519-five-little-plays:
Alfred Sutro's 1922 collection gathers five one-act plays, printed in Edinburgh for Brentano of New York. The contents run from The Man in the Stalls to The Bracelet, each a compact drawing-room piece.

The Man in the Stalls, produced at the Palace Theatre in 1911, opens in a Shaftesbury Avenue flat with a baby-grand piano and a merry fire. A Marriage Has Been Arranged turns on a rich suitor, Lady Aline, and the question of selling oneself for millions. Sutro writes witty, civilized comedy of manners, light in form and sharp in talk.
14588-three-wonder-plays:
Lady Gregory's Three Wonder Plays, published by Putnam in London and New York, gathers folk plays from Irish legend, including The Golden Apple and The Dragon. Gregory, of the Irish theatre, drew on Kiltartan lore.

In The Dragon, Taig refuses the king's guard, takes a sword with silver and gold thread, and boasts he will cut the beast crossways and lengthways and make garters of its body. The plays mix comedy, courage, and wonder in Kiltartan speech. They show Gregory's folk theatre at its most playful, written for stage and reading alike.
14684-mr-dooley-says:
Mr. Dooley, the Irish-American saloon keeper created by Finley Peter Dunne, holds court again in this set of dialect dialogues with his neighbour Mr. Hennessy. Speaking in a thick brogue, Dooley turns the news of the day into bar-room philosophy, sceptical, funny and often shrewd.

Topics range across divorce, woman suffrage, a bachelor tax, panics, ocean travel, work, drugs, the tariff, expert testimony, the Japanese scare, the Hague Conference and Turkish politics. Under the jokes sits a populist eye for power: who gains, who pays and who talks loudest. The pieces capture early twentieth-century America as heard from a Chicago bar, not from a pulpit or a platform.
14734-second-plays:
A. A. Milne's Second Plays, published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York and printed in Edinburgh, gathers five plays by the future author of Winnie-the-Pooh. Milne dedicates the volume with the words so little in return for so much.

The contents are Make-Believe, Mr. Pim Passes By, The Camberley Triangle, The Romantic Age, and The Stepmother. Make-Believe, a children's play, opened at the Lyric Theatre, Hammersmith, on December 24, 1918, with the eleven Hubbards of one family. The Romantic Age debates whether young lovers should be left to find out their own mistakes. The set shows Milne's light, deft stagecraft.
14759-camping-for-boys:
A practical guide from 1911, revised in the years that followed, explains how to run a boys' camp that builds character as well as health. Its first concern is purpose: camp should draw boys outdoors, teach citizenship and leave them steadier than it found them.

Chapters on leadership stress the moral quality of leaders, since boys copy the men in charge. Camp craft, safety, comfort, games and daily routine follow, with advice shaped by an age before nylon tents and gas stoves. Some medical notes are now out of date and should not be followed. As history, the book shows an early ideal of youth work: wood smoke, discipline, friendship and the open air.
1480-tom-brown-s-school-days:
Thomas Hughes's beloved school story follows Tom Brown from his White Horse Vale home to Rugby School, where he learns the code of boy life under Dr Arnold. Through dormitories, cricket fields, and fights with bullies, Tom grows from a shy new boy into a young man of courage and fair play.

His friendship with the gentle Harry East and the kindly influence of masters shape his character chapter by chapter. The book idealises Rugby's muscular Christianity, yet its scenes of school life feel true. It founded the school-story genre, and it still charms readers of all ages.
1486-the-unseen-world-and-other-essays:
John Fiske's essays take up science, religion, and literature with a Victorian American's confidence. The title essay reviews Draper's Science and Religion and argues that faith and evolution need not war. Other pieces contrast two translations of Dante and range across history, philosophy, and the unseen world of the mind.

Fiske writes clearly and warmly, aiming to reconcile new science with old belief for general readers. His arguments are dated in places, but his curiosity is genuine. The volume is a useful window on late nineteenth-century thought, when Darwin and Dante could share one shelf.
15249-outspoken-essays:
William Ralph Inge, Dean of St. Paul's, wrote these Outspoken Essays in a fifth impression of 1920, on discontents, patriotism, the birth-rate, and the future of the English race. Church topics follow: Bishop Gore, Roman Catholic modernism, Cardinal Newman, St. Paul, and institutionalism versus mysticism. Survival and immortality close the set.

Inge writes bluntly, with a scholar's learning and a churchman's worry about modern England. A Euripides motto on soft words versus hard truth fronts the book. Readers who like bold, learned essays will find Inge provocative, even where his views now jar.
15488-woman-s-life-in-colonial-days:
Carl Holliday, professor of English at San Jose State College, published this study of colonial American women, first printed in 1922 and reprinted in 1968 by Corner House. It draws on colonial writings to picture women's daily lives, from religion and work to courtship, marriage, and childbirth. Footnotes, some renumbered for clarity, support the text.

The first chapter treats colonial woman and religion: suffering and privation in early days, described by Prince, Bradford, and Johnson, and a faith both unyielding and repressive. Wigglesworth's Day of Doom, Edwards on hell torment, and Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God show what women were taught about God, love, and punishment. Holliday's book gives a detailed, sympathetic portrait of women who bore a hard world with few rights and much labor.
15653-dorothy-dale-s-queer-holidays:
Margaret Penrose wrote Dorothy Dale: A Girl of To-Day and The Motor Girls. Her Dorothy Dale story appeared in New York in 1910, from Cupples and Leon, illustrated, at sixty cents postpaid. A front picture shows Dorothy bringing out from the closet the ghost, on page 78. The series list names earlier volumes: Dorothy Dale at Glenwood School, her great secret, and her chums.

Twenty-four chapters run from the same old Tavia and what happened to Tavia through a light in the window, the tangled web she wove, and shopping and shoplifters. Who stole the ring, the haunted woods, and a magazine ghost lead to the little woman in black and the thorns of a holly wreath. Gathering evergreens, a scream from the castle, and college boys and Glenwood girls follow. Stormbound at Tanglewood, the ghost that really walked, and the rescue close a Christmas mystery for girls.
15684-the-summer-holidays:
A children's story by Amerel, issued in New York by D. Appleton and Company in 1851. The tale follows a city boy's August visit to his uncle's country house. Amerel writes in plain, moral prose, mixing fun with lessons from nature. Each chapter pairs an outing with something to learn, from rain to corn to bats.

Samuel Reed joins his cousins Thomas and John at Uncle Harvey's home, where walks, a creek, and Daddy Hall's donkey fill the days. The boys watch hawks, locusts, and farm work, and hear their uncle explain each wonder. A hard battle and the return home close the holiday. The book charms as an early American picture of a good summer: fresh air, kind kin, and steady curiosity.
15773-round-the-world-in-seven-days:
A boys' adventure novel by Herbert Strang, illustrated by A. C. Michael and issued in 1910. The tale races round the globe in a week, following a cablegram that sets the heroes eastward. Strang, a popular writer of school and sea stories, keeps the pace at full speed. Chapters jump from Europe to the Gulf, Penang, and Australia without pause.

Lieutenant George Underhill opens the book aboard a survey ship in stormy Solomon Islands waters. Later the party crosses to the Bosphorus, digs at the tomb of Ur-Gur, dodges gun runners, and flees pygmy stalkers. A ship on fire, a rescue, and a midnight vigil raise the stakes. The novel charms as pure Edwardian dash: brave lads, strange lands, and a race against the clock.
15950-wilderness-ways:
A book of animal studies by William J. Long, second series, issued by Ginn and Company in Boston in 1900. Long dedicates the book to Killooleet, Little Sweet-Voice, who shares his camp and makes sunshine as he works and plays. His preface insists the sketches come from years of personal observation in woods and fields. They study animals pure and simple.

Long refuses to give beasts human motives and imaginations, holding any animal interesting enough as an animal. Ways of wood folk fill the sketches, with character drawn from habit, not fancy. The prose stays clear and outdoor. The book still pleases nature readers: a patient watcher, telling what wild neighbours truly do.
15983-read-aloud-plays:
Horace Holley's 1916 volume from Mitchell Kennerley gathers nine short plays meant to be spoken aloud rather than staged with full sets. The contents run from Her Happiness and A Modern Prodigal to The Genius, Survival, The Telegram, Rain, Pictures, and His Luck. A brief introduction opens the book, and each play is short enough for one sitting.

The pieces turn on private moments. A troubled woman slips in from the dark to find Paul. A family stands at odds, luck strikes, and other small crises of love and pride follow. Spoken dialogue carries nearly all the action, with only lean stage notes to set a scene. The book suits readers, actors, and groups who want playable drama without scenery or costumes.
16091-dorothy-dale-s-camping-days:
Margaret Penrose's Dorothy Dale's Camping Days, published by Cupples and Leon in 1911, continues the adventures of a plucky schoolgirl heroine. Dorothy's earlier books took her to Glenwood School and through a great secret, and this volume sends her camping with her lively friend Tavia. Chapter titles promise a hayrick, a disastrous drag, a premature camp, a wild animal, and the disappearance of Tavia.

Boys arrive, mistaken identity tangles the plot, and a sanitarium and a clue deepen the fun before camping days proper begin. Penrose writes brisk, cheerful stories for girls, full of friendship and outdoor high spirits. Young readers who like school and camp tales will find this a bright, fast-moving entry.
16181-young-lion-of-the-woods-or-a-story:
Thomas B. Smith's 1889 Halifax tale, dedicated to his wife as his first work, calls itself a record of facts from early colonial days. Its preface claims only that merit: setting forth duty, religious trust, and the spirit of liberty amid suffering and hardship, in people whose loyalty faced the severest test. A verse by Charles G. D. Roberts praises a Canadian hearth, home, and name growing toward nationhood.

The Young Lion of the Woods thus follows colonial settlers, likely Loyalists, through danger and devotion in a new land. Smith writes earnest, patriotic history-fiction for Canadian readers. The book offers a window on how late Victorian Canadians told their own founding story.
1637-sanitary-and-social-lectures-and-es:
Charles Kingsley's Sanitary and Social Lectures and Essays, from Macmillan in 1880, gather his talks on health and society. Woman's Work in a Country Parish, The Science of Health, The Two Breaths, and Thrift lead the set, with Nausicaa in London on the lower education of women close behind.

Kingsley, a clergyman and reformer, preaches fresh air, clean water, and honest work with muscular energy. His lectures mix science, morals, and practical advice for parishes and homes. The volume is a vivid record of Victorian social reform, earnest, breezy, and full of good sense.
16435-the-atlantic-book-of-modern-plays:
Sterling Andrus Leonard edited this 1921 anthology for students and play readers, with an introduction on how to read plays, notes, and questions for talk after each piece. The bill mixes famous names with lesser-known ones: Lady Gregory, Eugene O'Neill, John Galsworthy, Synge, Yeats, Lord Dunsany, and Harold Chapin all appear.

One-act pieces rule the set, from Riders to the Sea to Spreading the News and The Land of Heart's Desire. The range runs from Irish folk drama to sharp social satire. Teachers meant it for class use, but any reader who likes short plays will find the volume a lively tour of the modern stage near 1920.
16474-lectures-and-essays:
Thomas Henry Huxley gathers his famous lectures and essays in this 1910 volume, with help from Professor H. N. Martin on some pieces. An autobiography opens the book, recalling his 1825 birth at Ealing, then lectures on evolution, the physical basis of life, naturalism and supernaturalism, miracles, and agnosticism follow.

Huxley writes as Darwin's great defender, clear, combative, and witty. The essays argue that science and faith must each keep to its own ground. Readers get the core of Victorian scientific debate in the voice of its sharpest champion, still readable and still provocative.
16495-your-boys:
Gipsy Smith writes from six months among British troops in France in this 1918 book, with a foreword by the Bishop of London. He preached within forty yards of the Germans, slept in a cellar so cold his mustache froze to his blanket, and found comfort in sour bread, Swiss milk, and hot water. YMCA marquees near the roads served hot drinks to thousands of walking wounded.

Smith's point is plain: doing Christian work matters more than preaching about it. His sketches are short, vivid, and full of soldier talk. The book speaks to parents at home, urging them to see what their boys faced and what simple kindness meant at the front.
16614-the-birth-time-of-the-world-and-ot:
J. Joly, Dublin professor of geology, gathers scientific essays in this volume from E. P. Dutton. The title essay asks the birth-time of the world, followed by denudation, the abundance of life, alpine flower colors, mountain genesis, and alpine structure. Other minds than ours, the latent image, pleochroic haloes, radium in medicine, and skating fill out the set.

Joly writes as a working scientist with a gift for clear explanation, and plates of Lucerne and Alpine cliffs illustrate the text. The essays range widely but stay grounded in rock, light, and life. Readers of popular science will find a thoughtful, old-style survey of earth and mind.
16712-some-turns-of-thought-in-modern-ph:
George Santayana brought out these five essays in 1933, most first read or printed in journals and talks. They take up John Locke, fifty years of British thought on ideals, new work in science, Freud, and a French writer on God and the world. Each piece starts from a book or a talk and then widens out.

Santayana weighs old views of sense and mind against new science and new doubt. He asks how much of plain common sense still holds, and what faith and the mind can claim when facts shift. The book suits readers who want short, clear takes on big ideas, with no need to know each thinker first.
1693-dangerous-days:
Mary Roberts Rinehart sets this wartime novel in Pittsburgh, where the Spencer family and their circle live through the years of the First World War. Natalie Spencer runs a busy social life, her husband Clayton works in the world of steel and money. Their daughter Delight comes of age as young men leave for France.

Rinehart follows dinners, weddings, and factory business alongside worry, gossip, and grief, showing how war reaches people who never see a trench. The book's interest lies in that home-front view: comfortable lives strained by duty, rumor, and loss, and by women learning how much of the cost they are asked to carry.
17067-the-house-of-the-combrays:
G. Le Notre's House of the Combrays, translated by Mrs. Joseph B. Gilder in 1902, opens in the winter of 1868 when a father-in-law spots a book on the table. He knew its heroine in life, not as Balzac's saintly Mme. de la Chanterie, but as Mme. de Combray of Tournebut near Gaillon. His tale then runs back to royalist plots, ruined nobles, and the Terror.

The Combrays and their Chouan allies fight, hide, and scheme through Revolution and Empire, with a tower, a chateau, and a web of kin at the heart. Le Notre tells true history in novel form, with names and places kept close to fact. Fans of French historic tales will find a rich, tragic chronicle of loyalty and loss.
17187-three-plays:
Zora Neale Hurston's Three Plays gathers Lawing and Jawing, Forty Yards, and Woofing, transcribed from her own manuscripts with pencilled notes kept in the text. Lawing and Jawing opens in Judge Dunfumy's court at Waycross, Georgia, where a clerk, lawyers, and a crowd await the judge under a red arrow marked To Jail. The other two plays carry the same folk humor and stage craft.

Hurston writes in Black southern speech of her day, with courtroom jokes, quick talk, and sharp character sketches. The plays are short, lively, and made for performance rather than print alone. They give a rare early stage voice from a major writer, and they still play well in a classroom or small theatre.
17522-practical-essays:
Alexander Bain, emeritus professor of logic at the University of Aberdeen, published this collection of practical essays in London in 1884. Bain explains in his preface that the volume is in great part a reprint of articles contributed to reviews. Their principal bond of union is their practical character, beyond which little connects them apart from the author's individuality and the range of his studies.

Bain promises a certain novelty in the suggestions offered across the essays. Readers get a Victorian philosopher writing for practical ends, on education, mind, and conduct, rather than pure theory. The book suits readers of Bain, of Scottish philosophy, and of the review essay at its most useful.
17562-trifles-for-the-christmas-holidays:
H. S. Armstrong published this book of trifles for the Christmas holidays in Philadelphia in 1869 with J. B. Lippincott and Company, entered in 1868 by Henry S. Armstrong. Armstrong dedicates the trifles to Jas. Davidson Hill of New Orleans, a chosen schoolfellow, a staunch comrade in arms, and the true friend of later years. That dedication sets a warm, personal tone.

Readers get short holiday pieces, light in subject and meant for Christmas reading. The book suits readers of Victorian holiday gift books and of Armstrong's minor place in American letters. Its trifles offer a glimpse of Christmas leisure in 1869.
17864-memories-of-childhood-s-slavery-da:
Annie L. Burton wrote this short memoir in Boston in 1909, looking back on her childhood on a Southern farm during the Civil War. She was born enslaved, and she tells her own early years in plain, direct prose, with no grand claims and no bitterness forced on the page.

She recalls ten white children and fourteen Black children at play, food snatched on the way to the fields, whippings by the overseer, and one wooden bowl shared at meals. The war raged far off while the children roamed the farms, half aware of the great change coming. Her voice makes this a rare, first-hand sketch of slave childhood, told by one who lived it.
18048-football-days:
William H. Edwards wrote Football Days in 1916, put out in New York by Moffat, Yard, with a preface by Walter Camp of Yale. Edwards, Princeton class of 1900, recalls the game and the men behind the ball, and he dedicates the book to John P. Poe, who died on a French battlefield.

Chapters run from prep school days and a first glimpse of a varsity team to freshman year, the cannon rush, and great games against Harvard and Yale. Edwards writes with a player's fond pride and a fan's eye. The book is a warm memoir of early college football, before the game grew into the vast sport it is now.
18226-my-young-days:
The author of Evening Amusement and Letters Everywhere wrote this 1872 book of childhood memories, with twenty pictures by Paul Konewka. It appeared in New York from Dutton and in London from Seeley, Jackson, and Halliday. The narrator looks back to a dreary afternoon in a great drawing room at grandmamma's, when the cry I want to go home rose from the bottom of the heart.

Chapters give home sickness, Uncle Hugh's story, and the little stowaway. They cover my home and what it is like, little cousins, and lessons. Holidays, the cottage on the cliff, Susette and her troubles, autumn days, and goodbye to Beecham close the book. Readers get a child's world told by a grown voice: houses, cousins, school, and seaside holidays, with the ache of being away from home running through them all.
18560-chopin-and-other-musical-essays:
Henry T. Finck published these musical essays at New York in 1894, after a first copyright in 1889. The lead essay calls Chopin the greatest genius of the piano, noting that New York dealers sold three times as many Chopin pieces as those of any other romantic or classical writer. Finck argues that Chopin's fame kept growing, yet many of his deepest works stayed little known.

Other essays cover how composers work, Schumann as seen in his letters, music and morals, Italian and German singing styles, and German opera in New York. Finck writes as a keen listener with strong views. The book is a lively guide to musical taste in the 1890s.
18780-shakespeare-and-the-modern-stage-w:
Sidney Lee, author of A Life of William Shakespeare, published these essays at London in 1907 with Constable. The lead essay warns against spectacular staging, urging simpler scenery, trust in the actor, and use of the audience's imagination, with lessons from Kean, Irving, Phelps, and French and German stages. Lee argues for Shakespeare played often and in variety.

Other essays cover the Elizabethan playgoer, oral tradition after Shakespeare's death, Pepys as average playgoer, Benson's company, and the municipal theatre. Lee blends scholarship with stage sense throughout. The book remains a clear, practical guide to staging Shakespeare.
19316-lyra-heroica-a-book-of-verse-for-b:
William Ernest Henley selected and arranged this 1891 book of verse for boys. It is called Lyra Heroica, reprinted in New York in 1920. Shakespeare opens the contents, with Scott's clarion call. Scott writes that a single crowded hour of glorious life outweighs an age with no name. Selections from Whitman, Longfellow, Lowell, Whittier, and Bret Harte appear by permission.

Henry the Fifth visits his host tent to tent, calling men brothers, friends, and countrymen. His cheerful majesty thaws cold fear like the sun. Then comes the march to Agincourt, where French pride meets English resolve. Readers get a stirring boys' anthology of battle, courage, and hero verse.
19826-the-white-christmas-and-other-merr:
The White Christmas gathers merry Christmas plays for amateur performance. Its notes point performers to Denison's Songs Worth While for music. Most carol tunes are familiar to everyone, the editor says. Unfamiliar hymn music can be found in that collection. The volume itself is handsomely printed on non-glossy paper. It measures seven by ten and a quarter inches, bound in stout paper.

Schools, churches, and families staged Christmas plays every December. Publishers like Denison built catalogs for those stages. A white Christmas on stage needs songs everyone can sing. These plays mix sentiment, snow, and goodwill in short acts. The practical notes show the trade behind the tinsel. It is a handbook for homemade holiday theater.
19834-ethel-morton-s-holidays:
Mabell S. C. Smith wrote the Ethel Morton books for girls. Ethel Morton's Holidays, dated 1915, finds the Morton circle at leisure. Helen and Ethel Brown have gone to the West Woods. A wild grapevine there still holds yellow leaves bright enough for decorating. Tomorrow evening's plans send the girls hunting color. Roger accounts for his sisters with a brother's economy.

The Ethel books follow two cousins both named Ethel. Holidays mean clubs, crafts, parties, and small schemes. Smith fills them with doings girls could copy at home. Decorating with grape leaves is typical of the series. Its world is safe, busy, and friendly. Such series trained steady girl readers by the shelf.
19855-louis-school-days-a-story-for-boys:
E. J. May wrote Louis' School Days as a story for boys with a Christian aim. Its ideal schoolboy has affections restored to their rightful Lord. Every thought, in the book's phrase, is brought into captivity to Christ. The boy longs to praise God in his life, not only his lips. School, in this telling, is a place of soul-forming. Lessons matter less than conversion.

Evangelical school stories filled Victorian Sunday libraries. They set games and masters inside a frame of faith. A hero's progress was measured in obedience and prayer. Modern readers may find the piety heavy. The book faithfully shows what such schools hoped to make. It is a period piece of religious education.
19907-around-the-world-in-ten-days:
Chelsea Curtis Fraser wrote Around the World in Ten Days as a boys' adventure. Students pour from the Clark Polytechnic Institute doors in its opening. Two boys pause at a newsboy on the street. The taller buys a newspaper and pockets it in his raincoat. From that small start, a dash around the world begins. Ten days for the circuit is the book's daring wager.

Airplanes made Jules Verne's eighty days look slow. Fraser raced his heroes by every fast conveyance of the 1920s. Schoolboys with grit and timetables were his cast. The story teaches geography at running speed. Each stop is a lesson disguised as a deadline. It captures the decade's faith in shrinking distance.
19952-to-the-front-a-sequel-to-cadet-day:
Charles King wrote To the Front as a sequel to Cadet Days, dated 1908. It opens on graduation day at West Point. A remarkable scene marked that morning's ceremonies. The Board of Visitors watched in full attendance. Officers of the academic and military staff stood in full uniform. Something in the ceremony broke its usual order. King, a West Point graduate himself, knew that stage perfectly.

King's cadet stories follow young officers from academy to frontier. Cadet Days made his school reputation; this sequel graduates the class. The front of the title means active service in the Philippines or West. King's soldiers are professionals, not dime-novel heroes. His books taught civilians how the old army worked. Graduation day here is a true threshold scene.
20070-four-days:
Hetty Hemenway published Four Days in 1917, with the subtitle The Story of a War Marriage. The First World War forms the backdrop for a brief, intense tale. One scene fills a station with troops in khaki climbing from train cars. Feet stamp, and young voices shout and call above the roar.

Four days is a short span, and the title stresses that rush. Love and duty must be weighed while war waits for no one. The book shows how war sped up courtship and parting alike. Readers get a home-front tale told at wartime pace and pitch.
20172-the-flutter-of-the-goldleaf-and-ot:
Olive Tilford Dargan wrote The Flutter of the Goldleaf and Other Plays, a set of dramas. One scene shows a wife tidying a room for a New York specialist. Her husband has been too sick to go to the store for days. She dusts and rattles about, keen to hide any trace of disorder.

Plays in this set turn on home life, work, and mountain folk. Dargan wrote of the South and its hills with a poet's ear. Talk in dialect gives her scenes their bite and warmth at once. Readers get period drama where small rooms hold large hopes and fears.
20389-historical-and-political-essays:
William Edward Hartpole Lecky, the Irish historian, gathered these essays from his work for leading reviews. Pieces on Sir Robert Peel, Henry Reeve, and Dean Milman first appeared in the Edinburgh Review. Other essays ran in the Pall Mall Magazine and the Contemporary Review.

The subjects range across politics and letters. One essay treats Queen Victoria as a moral force in the life of the nation. Another, Carlyle's Message to His Age, weighs the prophet-like writer's hold on his times. The book shows Lecky's calm, balanced way of judging public men and public questions.
21187-dr-jolliffe-s-boys:
Weston School's cricket match against Hillsborough opens Lewis Hough's boarding school novel. The crowd roars as their captain Crawley is given out leg before wicket. Life at Doctor Jolliffe's school in the late nineteenth century fills the book. Rules exist mainly to be broken by boys with energy.

The boys slip out of bounds to a forbidden tuck shop and skate near thin ice on a frozen lake. They also poach on a big estate and try cruel country sports like rat baiting. Hough draws each boy's character clearly, scene by scene. Readers wondered why this warm, well-made school story never became better known.
21238-the-castaways:
A ship founders in a typhoon in the Celebes Sea in Captain Mayne Reid's short tale. Her boat brings only a few ashore: the captain, his two children, the Irish ship's carpenter, and the Malay pilot. Two others in the boat die before land is reached. The landing starts a long walk toward Bruni, hundreds of miles away.

Each chapter takes up a plant, tree, or animal of the region. The upas tree, an orangutan, a fruit that drops like a bomb, and a python all appear. The Malay pilot's skill with a blowpipe, which he makes on the spot, saves the party more than once.
21295-cormorant-crag-a-tale-of-the-smugg:
Two boys on a small offshore island off England's south coast anchor George Manville Fenn's tale of the smuggling days around 1830. One is the doctor's son, the other the squire's. Old fisherman Daygo takes them fishing and warns them off one stretch of cliff, where ships that come too close are said to disappear.

Borrowing Daygo's boat, the boys find the truth: a sea cave big enough to hide a small vessel, stocked with fresh smuggled goods. Found inside days later, they are seized by the French smugglers who run the trade. Fenn then works through captures, escapes, and perils that nearly end the boys for good.
21312-glyn-severn-s-schooldays:
Glyn Severn and Singh, the young Maharajah of Dour, are schoolfellows of fifteen or sixteen at an English boarding school in George Manville Fenn's tale. Glyn's father, a colonel in the old Maharajah's army, is now Singh's guardian. A bully named Slegge makes himself their enemy from the start.

A menagerie owner's elephant sometimes turns dangerous, and the two boys, who know elephants from India, prove best at calming it. Then Singh's heavily jewelled princely belt vanishes, and suspicion falls on boys known to be short of money. Half the book hunts the thief, and the surprise ending reaches well beyond the few days of school action.
2134-utopia-of-usurers-and-other-essays:
G. K. Chesterton gathers essays that attack usury, the servile state, and the new powers of advertisement, eugenics, and bad journalism. A Song of Swords opens the book, and the title essay argues that modern finance has built its own false utopia. Chesterton wrote these essays before the First World War, when finance and empire were changing Britain.

Later pieces cover art, the war on holidays, the prison, the lash for labour, and the poetry of revolution, with Chesterton's usual paradox and fire. The collection suits readers who enjoy polemical essays that defend the common man. His defence of small property and local life runs through the book, against big banks and big states.
21452-ernest-bracebridge-school-days:
Ernest Bracebridge stands at the centre of W. H. G. Kingston's school story Ernest Bracebridge. The book opens on a half-holiday, with boys cheering a fellow who has taken his degree as Senior Wrangler. Old faces, old scenes, and warm handshakes set the tone.

Kingston fills the tale with the staff, customs, and small wars of a Victorian school. Ernest is drawn as a near-perfect hero, brave, kind, and steady. A visit to a second school shows how long such customs lived on. Many judges count the book among Kingston's best, and it reads aloud especially well.
21468-marmaduke-merry-a-tale-of-naval-ad:
Marmaduke Merry tells of naval life in bygone days in W. H. G. Kingston's long tale of that name. Action fills the frame, and inside it sailors spin tales of still more action. The manner recalls Captain Marryat, whom Kingston admired and followed.

Cassell's printed this edition as a course book for learners of English. Sixteen pages of questions and drills close the volume, to guide pupils' reading. Kingston adds a strong dose of faith near the end, as was his habit. The result mixes a rattling sea yarn with a schoolroom tool, a rare blend that still reads well.
21688-scottish-cathedrals-and-abbeys:
The Reverend D. Butler surveys Scotland's great churches in Scottish Cathedrals and Abbeys, in the Guild Library. Principal Story writes the introduction to Butler's handbook. Reviewers praised the series for careful workmanship and scholarly industry.

Nowhere else, the Speaker said, could so clear an array of facts be had in such small compass. Butler packs history and church statistics into a bright, readable form. The book sold at one shilling and sixpence, with interleaved copies for note-takers. Walkers and students of Scotland's kirks get a compact guide to buildings that carry a thousand years of faith.
21933-much-darker-days:
Andrew Lang parodies the sensation novel in Much Darker Days, a comic shocker of 1884 issued under the name A. Huge Longway. The title mocks a real bestseller, Dark Days, and Lang's narrator mocks everything else. He confesses to wallowing in crime: stillicide and mayhem are child's play to him. Throw the book from the railway window if you dislike it, he says; you have paid your money.

The tale burlesques the confessions, curses, and cleared-up mysteries of cheap thrillers. Chapter thirteen arrives before chapter one in the printing, in the joke's spirit. Lang, a scholar of folklore, knew bad fiction well enough to imitate it perfectly. The result is a small, sharp period squib, funniest for readers who know the solemn originals it skewers.
22279-phil-bradley-s-mountain-boys:
Silas K. Boone wrote Phil Bradley's Mountain Boys, or The Birch Bark Lodge, in 1915. The Mountain Boys series sent Phil and his chums into the woods for their holidays. This volume opens with the boys securing a good supply of bait and starting for the canoe. Their fat companion Lub has a comical way of expressing misery, and his ludicrous faces keep the others from taking him seriously.

Camping, fishing, hunting, and the building of a birch bark lodge fill the vacation. Boone writes woodcraft as fact inside the fun. Such series taught city boys an outdoor creed of skill and good humour. Phil Bradley's crowd are typical of the breed.
22298-practical-mechanics-for-boys:
J. S. Zerbe, a mechanical engineer, wrote Practical Mechanics for Boys to put real shop knowledge into boys' hands. The contents promise first how to commence work, then familiarity with tools and the four important things. Fundamental devices follow: belt lacing, grooved friction gearing, and a valve that closes by water pressure. A trammel for drawing ellipses and a crank motion worked by a slotted yoke show his range.

Zerbe explains each device plainly enough for a home workshop. His Boys' books treated engines, electricity, and flight the same way. In an age when boys built their own toys and models, such manuals were treasure. This one survives as a handbook of the mechanical self-education of 1910s America.
22334-in-kings-byways:
Stanley J. Weyman wrote In Kings' Byways, a set of tales set around royal courts. The narrator serves in a great lord's household. One morning, he learns that who climbs may fall.

At the usual hour, Monseigneur left for the Council as always. Soon the whole house was in an uproar. My lord had returned early and called for Prosper. Even the sound of that name passing lip to lip felt ominous. Weyman was known for swashbuckling tales of old France. These byways of kings mix court intrigue, sudden danger, and servants who see power up close.
22410-the-crofton-boys:
The Crofton Boys follows a family of children in their London home. Mrs. Proctor takes her children to the Temple Garden each fine evening. There they walk and breathe air from the river.

Breakfast scenes open the family's ordinary days together at home. The Temple Garden stood not much farther off from their house. Such small geography grounds the story in real London. The boys' lives unfold through home lessons and outings. Period children's books like this taught conduct through example. Readers see siblings learning kindness, patience, and duty in daily rounds. It preserves a gentle picture of Victorian family life from inside.
22675-home-life-in-colonial-days:
Home Life in Colonial Days is Alice Morse Earle's classic study of everyday life in early America. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Earle helped invent the study of colonial daily life, working from houses, inventories, letters, and the objects families actually used.

Her thanks in the preface map her method. Photographers in Boston and Richmond helped, as did the Misses Allen of Deerfield. Many friends and strangers also secured single articles or photographs for her. Fireplaces, spinning wheels, tableware, and dress fill the chapters, each thing tied to the work it served. The book remains a doorway into colonial homes, valued for its detail and for proving that ordinary life is history too.
22700-brittany-its-byways:
Fanny Bury Palliser wrote Brittany and Its Byways, a travel book through the old province of Brittany in western France. The catalog record gives no year. Palliser, known for works on lace and art, here turns guide, leading readers away from railways into lanes, churches, and fishing towns.

The journey begins with a crossing: a fair wind carried the party in six hours from Poole to Cherbourg. Dusk hid the harbor's beauty until morning, when they climbed the Mont du Roule behind the town for the view. Such patient looking sets the book's pace. Palliser mixes history, legend, and close description of dress and custom. Her Brittany is the Celtic, devout, sea-bound province that English travelers loved.
22766-electricity-for-boys:
J. S. Zerbe wrote Electricity for Boys, a practical manual that teaches electricity by having boys build the gear themselves. The catalog record gives no year. Zerbe, a mechanical engineer, wrote a shelf of such books, trusting that a boy who winds his own coil understands more than one who only reads rules.

The contents move from magnets to machines. Early chapters treat magnetic lines of force and the earth itself as a magnet. They explain why the compass points north and south. The peculiarity of a magnet and the action of the electro-magnet come early, with the strange influence around a wire carrying current. Batteries, motors, and telegraphs follow in workshop order. The book captures the moment when electricity was still a hobby a boy could hold, and it remains a clear, hands-on introduction.
23074-a-voyage-round-the-world-a-book-fo:
A father earns worship in A Voyage Round the World, a book for boys. Other boys might have very good fathers, the young narrator grants, but they were not equal to his. The boy's father joins games of cricket, fishing, and shooting like another boy, the narrator says. Yet he is always right about everything, and no finer-looking gentleman exists in the county.

With that father at the helm, the voyage circles the globe in the great tradition of boys' travel books. Ports, storms, and strange peoples arrive in steady sequence, each one turned into a lesson or a marvel. The county's finest gentleman makes an ideal guide. Such books mapped the world for boys who might never leave their shire. The map here is affectionate, imperial, and very much of its century.
23234-semiramis-and-other-plays:
Semiramis and Other Plays, from 1904, collects verse dramas, opening with a queen's anxious court. Guards enter and ask for news of Artavan, who is late. Semiramis sleeps, while a loyal watcher refuses rest, saying her lord shall find her watching night or day.

The watcher has not slept for two nights, yet vows to stay awake for the first hoof-beat from the north. She even swears she would not be called away for the god Bel himself. Readers get old-world court drama: loyalty, waiting, and a sleeping queen whose fate hangs on a rider still out of sight.
23265-the-crofton-boys:
The Crofton Boys follows a family whose home is picked for plain convenience. Their house stands near enough to church that the boys can walk there and back, even in the worst weather, before their shoes get wet. It also sits handy to Covent Garden market in London.

If a friend drops in to dinner without warning, Jane and Agnes can be off to the market at once. They can buy a fowl, or vegetables or fruit, and be back before they are missed. Readers get a warm Victorian family tale, where household geography and small errands shape the children's daily adventures.
23491-the-castaways:
Harry Collingwood opened this sea tale on a wet, dreary October afternoon, as the narrator travels to Gravesend to join the clipper City of Cawnpore as a cuddy passenger bound for Calcutta. Wind from the south east drives rain squalls across his path, setting a gloomy, expectant tone.

Miss Onslow leads the first chapter, and shipboard life, fellow passengers, and the long voyage east follow, with Collingwood's usual skill at sea detail. The title promises castaways, yet the tale takes its own course, and readers may find fewer wreck scenes than the name suggests. Still, fans of Collingwood will enjoy the voyage, the characters, and the steady, seamanlike storytelling that made his books popular audio fare.
23531-marjorie-s-busy-days:
Carolyn Wells, author of the Patty books, wrote this nineteen hundred eight girls' book of Marjorie's busy days, printed by Grosset and Dunlap. A frontispiece shows Marjorie feeding goldfish, trying amusements of many sorts, and finding none that holds her interest, a fitting start for a heroine always on the move.

Chapters run from a jolly good game and an exasperating guest through picnic plans, a novel picnic, first days at school, a Jinks club, and spelling troubles. A real adventure follows, leading to Halloween, Thanksgiving, and a charity bazaar. Wells writes Marjorie with warmth and humour, as a girl whose plans go awry and whose friends set them right. Young readers will enjoy the school, club, and holiday scenes in turn.
23569-christmas-holidays-at-merryvale-th:
Alice Hale Burnett wrote this Merryvale boys' book of six real stories for small boys, each complete, about Toad and Chuck Brown and their friends Fat, Reddy, and others. It faithfully pictures boy life in a small town. Circus day opens the set, as Toad and Reddy earn tickets by watering elephants, harder work than it seemed.

A father's Indian tale brings an unexpected fireside visitor, a picnic in a farm wagon brings trout broiled over a camp fire, and other holiday doings follow in turn. Burnett writes so a boy may read and grasp each tale with ease, with action and talk true to small town boyhood. Young readers will enjoy the circus, the picnic, and the fireside, while grown readers will smile at a vanished, wholesome boy world.
23614-happy-days:
Oliver Herford and John Cecil Clay wrote this nineteen seventeen book of toasts, Happy Days, printed by Mitchell Kennerley. To stern critics opens the set, with a wish that critics may learn the forward lookout beats the stern. Toasts to her shadow, fashion, the typewriter, the floor, music, and the publisher follow.

Here's looking, the dove of peace, the clock, hope, liberty, stairs, Lady Nicotine, editor, creditor, Neptune, waiter, temptation, the maid with fancy free, sweethearts, and readers complete the round. Herford and Clay write light verse for drinking and dining, witty, brief, and good humoured. Readers who love toasts and table talk will enjoy the book as a pocket companion for happy days, to be dipped into and quoted aloud.
23725-viking-boys:
J. M. E. Saxby published Viking Boys in London in 1892, a boys' adventure set among Norse seafarers. Its thirty-two chapters carry saga-style titles, quoted like lines from old poems: calls to work, memories of dealing, farewells, and shield-walls. The frontispiece shows Yaspard trying to light a scene with a sudden flare.

Young heroes, carls on cliff tops, ravens, kinsfolk, and plighted troth fill the story, which moves between voyages, fights, and councils. Saxby, who also wrote The Yarl's Yacht, gives readers the Viking age as Victorian boys liked it: bold, loyal, and full of sea air, with honor tested in war and in parting.
2385-gala-days:
Gail Hamilton, the pen name of Mary Abigail Dodge, writes of Gala-Days: holidays, travels, and the pleasures of a well-spent life. The essays and sketches in this volume mix humor, moral reflection, and sharp observation of American manners, all in Hamilton's brisk, witty voice. She was one of the most popular essayists of her day.

The book's charm lies in its author's personality: frank, funny, and unafraid of an opinion. Modern readers will enjoy its period flavor and its still-fresh jokes. It offers a pleasant sample of Victorian American essay writing.
2418-oldport-days:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson sketches Oldport, his name for Newport, Rhode Island, in essays on its people, seasons, and social life. Oldport Days moves through summer visitors, old families, and seaside scenes, with Higginson's gentle wit and reformer's conscience in the background. The book preserves a resort town before the Gilded Age transformed it.

Higginson, a friend of Emily Dickinson and a colonel of Black troops in the Civil War, writes with broad sympathies. The sketches charm with their detail and their humane tone. Readers of New England literature will find a quiet treasure.
24410-hollow-tree-nights-and-days:
Albert Bigelow Paine, author of The Hollow Tree and Deep Woods Book, wrote this continuation of the Hollow Tree and Deep Woods stories, with pictures by J. M. Condé, published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London, copyrighted in 1915 and 1916. It is dedicated to J. P., a friend of all Hollow Tree people, and its frontispiece carries a line about knowing a way.

Paine explains a map of the Deep Woods, showing many new things: three marks on the Edge of the World, far below, show where the Hollow Tree folk and Mr. Rabbit sat telling star stories. Mr. 'Coon leaned on the tree, hiding his spot, and a little bush marks Mr. 'Possum's curl. Paine's young readers' books also include The Boys' Life of Mark Twain and The Hollow Tree Snowed-In Book. Readers get Hollow Tree nights and days.
24461-third-class-in-indian-railways:
M. K. Gandhi wrote this pamphlet after his return from South Africa, drawing on more than two years of travel in India. For over a quarter of that time he travelled third class by choice, from Lahore in the north to Tranquebar in the south, and from Karachi to Calcutta.

Gandhi describes crowded carriages, dirty stations, and the hardships of ordinary passengers, and he writes to railway managers asking for reform. His account is plain, detailed, and practical, not a speech but a traveller's report. It shows the young Gandhi learning India by riding with its poorest passengers, and it still reads as a sharp piece of social observation.
24603-the-house-of-toys:
Henry Russell Miller wrote this children's fantasy, published at Indianapolis in 1914 with a frontispiece by Frank Snapp. Its chapters are named for plans, a witch, sands, a rescue, good fairies, spells, sanctuary, plots, and a new house. Miller warns at once that this is not a fairy tale, though old friends appear in it.

The witch is a dreadful old being who fools even the wisest folk, and Circumstance is one of her many names. A horde of grisly goblins follows in her train. Miller's story turns a child's house of toys into a stage for luck, choice, and courage, and it ends, as its last chapter promises, happily.
24684-science-and-morals-and-other-essay:
Sir Bertram C. A. Windle, of St. Michael's College, Toronto, published these essays at London in 1919. They had appeared in the Dublin Review, Catholic World, America, and Studies, some as first printed, others almost rewritten. Windle dedicates the book to John Robert and Mary O'Connell, as a token of sincere friendship.

His essays weigh science against morals, faith against materialism, from a Catholic scholar's view. Windle, a doctor and a man of letters, writes with learning and courtesy. Readers interested in the old debate between science and religion will find these essays thoughtful, earnest, and very much of their age.
24808-all-afloat-a-chronicle-of-craft-an:
William Wood wrote All Afloat in Toronto in 1915, volume thirty-one of the Chronicles of Canada. It tells how Canadians moved by water, from birch canoes and voyageurs on misty mornings to sailing craft under French and then British flags. Chapters take up canoes, pioneer ships, and the timber and fur trades that filled Quebec and Montreal.

Wood notes how fish and furs led exports until the War of 1812, when timber took first place, and how Loyalist settlers built the Bluenose craft of the Maritimes. The book mixes trade facts with lively scenes of ports and rivers. It stands as a clear, compact history of Canada as a land of waterways.
24903-molly-brown-s-senior-days:
Nell Speed published Molly Brown's Senior Days in New York in 1913, the fourth book of her college series for girls. Molly's last year brings good news and bad, gossip over teacups, the senior ramble, a campus ghost, and two Christmas breakfasts, closing with the jubilee and farewells.

Speed follows Molly and her friends Judy and Adele through rivalries, stolen visits, and barbed arrows, with four half-tone pictures by Charles L. Wrenn. The tone is bright and good-natured, with school spirit to the fore. Girls who followed Molly from freshman days will find a fond farewell to college life in this closing volume.
24987-girl-scouts-their-works-ways-and-p:
This Girl Scouts handbook, Series No. 5 from headquarters at 189 Lexington Avenue, New York, sets out the movement's works, ways, and plays. The motto is Be Prepared and the slogan is Do a Good Turn Daily. The Promise is to do duty to God and country, help others at all times, and obey the Scout Laws. The ten laws run from trusted honor and loyalty through usefulness, courtesy, cheerfulness, thrift, and cleanliness in thought, word, and deed.

Membership is open to any girl accepting the Promise and Laws, to give girls group experience and outdoor life. A Tenderfoot learns the Promise, Laws, slogan, motto, salute, respect due to the flag, and useful knots. Second Class work adds cooking, housekeeping, animals, birds, flowers, trees, first aid, and health laws; First Class demands finding one's way by compass and judgment alone. The booklet captures scouting's spirit.
25099-historical-essays:
James Ford Rhodes's Historical Essays, published by Macmillan in 1909, collects addresses and lectures by the author of the great History of the United States from the Compromise of 1850. Rhodes, a leading American historian of his generation, writes about the craft of history itself as much as about the past.

Essays take up the nature of history, how history should be written, the historian's profession, and newspapers as historical sources. Portraits of Edward Gibbon and Samuel Rawson Gardiner round out the volume. Readers interested in how history gets made, rather than only in what happened, will find this a thoughtful guide.
25447-mysticism-and-logic-and-other-essa:
Bertrand Russell gathers essays that set clear thought against mystical feeling. He argues that the belief that good and evil unlock the world must be driven from philosophy, or it stays a set of pleasing dreams. Thinkers who set good and evil aside and chase facts alone, he claims, are likelier to reach truth and even to do good. The title essay weighs mysticism's insights against logic's discipline.

Other essays range over knowledge, science, and ethics, in the plain, combative style Russell made famous. The title page lists his many books, from The Principles of Mathematics to A History of Western Philosophy. George Allen and Unwin published the London edition, which keeps Russell's Greek terms transliterated and his equations marked for print.
25540-anecdotes-for-boys:
Harvey Newcomb gathers entertaining narratives and anecdotes for boys in this Boston volume, entered in 1847 and issued in a sixth thousand in 1851. Newcomb, author of How to Be a Lady and How to Be a Man, writes for young people fond of short, striking stories.

His preface notes that such a taste can lead readers to devour all the trash in reach, so he offers anecdotes chosen to illustrate principles and character instead. Each tale aims to fix a moral point in memory through a vivid deed, making the book a tool for parents and teachers.
25586-a-collection-of-stories-reviews-an:
Willa Cather gathers stories, reviews, and essays in this collection, arranged in two parts. Part one holds stories such as Peter and Eric Hermannson's Soul. The Sentimentality of William Tavener, The Namesake, and The Enchanted Bluff also appear. The Bohemian Girl completes the story set.

Peter opens with an old man refusing to sell his fiddle, though his hand trembles and crows laugh at his playing. Part two turns to criticism. Pieces treat Mark Twain, William Dean Howells, Edgar Allan Poe, Walt Whitman, Henry James, Kate Chopin, Stephen Crane, and Frank Norris, closing on the art of fiction.
25865-patty-s-summer-days:
Carolyn Wells sends Patty through a gay summer of weddings, trips, and country fun. The book opens in a lively house full of wedding plans, then moves to Atlantic City, a new home, lessons, a rescue, and a school play. A motor trip steals the show, with Patty riding in a great car called the Flying Dutchman, named for an ancestor from Holland, and marveling that folk can talk at such speed.

Printed in 1906, the tale runs on through a stormy ride, pine branches, a quilting party, a summer Christmas, and a stay at Sandy Cove. Rosabel, the Rolands, and the Crusoes add color, and a Bazaar of All Nations closes the season. Patty stays bright and busy to the last page, and the summer ends as gaily as it began.
25955-the-bronze-eagle-a-story-of-the-hu:
Baroness Orczy sets a romance of the Hundred Days in The Bronze Eagle, printed by Doran in 1915 and first serialized as Waterloo. The tale opens at the landing at Jouan, on a calm spring dawn over headland and sea. It runs through glorious news, the old regime, the emperor's return, the empress's millions, rivals, a crime, and the ascent of the capitol. Revelry by night, the Tarpeian rock, and the last throw close the book.

A later scene shows a duchess and a comte spurning a follower of the Corsican usurper, helping his sister to a carriage while Jeanne stands dazed by fresh terrors. Orczy, known for The Scarlet Pimpernel, writes of loyalty, treason, and love in Napoleon's brief return, with verve and a keen sense of theater.
26098-happy-days:
A. A. Milne's Happy Days gathers short pieces under headings from Margery to Life's Little Tragedies, Three Stories, Out-of-Doors, Indoors, Little Plays for Amateurs, and Successful Men. Early chapters cover a sock, a pianola, a knight of the chimney-piece, the art of conversation, afternoon sleep, and a twice-told tale.

Later pieces weigh a crown of sorrows, a lucky month, a rescue, a Portuguese cigar, and the things that matter, beside a Christmas story in the making and a seaside novelette. A golfing sketch pits the narrator against Thomson, whose ball rests in a bunker he had forgotten. The collection is light, wry, and domestic, finding comedy in small daily events.
26144-the-unicorn-from-the-stars-and-oth:
William B. Yeats and Lady Gregory's 1908 volume gathers plays from the early years of Dublin's Abbey Theatre. Notes in the book record first stagings: Cathleen ni Houlihan at St. Teresa's Hall in 1902, The Hour-Glass at Molesworth Hall in 1903, and The Unicorn from the Stars at the Abbey itself in November 1907.

The plays draw on Irish legend, country life, and moral fable, with casts and stage notes that show how the Abbey company worked. Together they give a clear view of the Irish stage revival at its height, when Yeats and Gregory were shaping a national drama from folk tales, peasant speech, and old myth.
26410-peak-s-island-a-romance-of-buccane:
Ford Paul's 1892 romance opens on September 27, 1607, with a wreck on a rocky shore. The British ship Queen Elizabeth, bound for Virginia with general merchandise, breaks up in a gale, and bodies and cargo wash onto the beach. A smaller vessel wedges between rocks nearby, while survivors, among them Mrs. Carleton, Miss Vyvyan, and a child, find shelter in a castle.

The story follows how the castaways divide their new life, with one taking charge outside the castle, fetching wood and water and salvage from the wreck. The other keeps the household within. The sea that wrecked them stays a presence throughout, and the tale mixes shipwreck survival with the bold color of buccaneer days.
26660-plays-complete-edition-including-t:
This short hosted text contains only the front matter of Leo Tolstoy's Plays, complete edition including the posthumous plays, translated by Louise and Aylmer Maude. Funk and Wagnalls published the fourth impression at New York in 1919, printed in Edinburgh. A note from Tolstoy praises the Maudes as translators without equal for knowledge of both languages and penetration into meaning.

The contents list three plays published in Tolstoy's lifetime: The Power of Darkness, The First Distiller, and Fruits of Culture. Three posthumous plays follow: The Live Corpse, The Cause of It All, and The Light Shines in Darkness. A transcriber's note explains that the plays themselves appear as separate e-books. Readers should treat this entry as the edition's gateway, not as the plays.
26714-the-captain-s-bunk-a-story-for-boy:
M. B. Manwell published this story for boys with the Religious Tract Society at London in 1898, with coloured illustrations. It is set in Northbourne, a quaint fishing village tucked under a long stretch of downs, reached by railway to Brattlesby town and then a tramp on foot. A few small thatched cottages sit in a semicircle round a tiny bay, facing the open ocean.

Two gentry houses finish the half-circle and stare across the bay at each other. The Bunk holds Captain Carnegy, an elderly half-pay naval officer, and his motherless boys and girls, including Geoff and Alick, Binks's plaguey pair. The Vicarage holds Mr. Vesey, his invalid wife, and terriers Splutters and Shutters. Chapters run from mutiny at the bunk and Theo's haven to arrest, a tangled web, peril on the sea, and no place like home.
270-dream-days:
Kenneth Grahame returns to the children of The Golden Age in eight dreamlike tales. Dream Days opens on the twenty-first of October, with schoolroom lessons, dead languages, and scales hammered out in tears. The children escape into imagination whenever adults turn away.

The Reluctant Dragon, the best-known tale, gives a peace-loving dragon and a boy who saves him by staging a fight. A saga of the seas, a magic ring, and jasper walls follow. Grahame's prose is playful, wistful, and precise. The collection charmed readers before Wind in the Willows.
27135-the-vaudois-of-piedmont-a-visit-to:
Reverend J. N. Worsfold's The Vaudois of Piedmont, published in London in 1873 with a map of the valleys, visits the Waldensian valleys and sketches their remarkable history as a church and people. Worsfold, vicar of Christ Church, Somers Town, meant a pocket volume for tourists.

He follows the large learned works of Muston, Monastier, and Gilly, answering Tischendorf's call for little books on great subjects. The book also seeks help for the Vaudois work, especially contributions toward a memorial church near the site of an ancient one. His Latin motto means the hammers are broken but the anvil remains. The book was printed at 48 Paternoster Row, London.
2788-little-men-life-at-plumfield-with-j:
Louisa May Alcott wrote this sequel to Little Women, dedicating it to Freddy and Johnny, the little men to whom she owed some of her best and happiest hours. Their loving Aunt Weedy, Jo herself, runs Plumfield school with her husband.
