Nat arrives first, then the boys, Sundays, stepping stones, and patty pans, with Naughty Nan and a firebrand or two. Alcott writes with humor and tenderness about a school where kindness is the curriculum. The book endures as a classic of childhood, and of Jo March grown into a teacher.
27901-jewish-literature-and-other-essays:
Gustav Karpeles published Jewish Literature and Other Essays in Philadelphia in 1895 with the Jewish Publication Society of America. The essays survey the Talmud, women in Jewish literature, Moses Maimonides, Jewish troubadours, humor and love in Jewish poetry, and the Jewish stage.

Karpeles opens by rebuking Heine for condemning Jewish women ignorant of their poetry's golden age, noting that popular knowledge of the field was only fifty years old. The book remains a readable nineteenth-century guide to a literature Karpeles compares to a Hebrew Pompeii newly unearthed. Later essays treat the Jew's quest in Africa, a Jewish king in Poland, Leopold Zunz, and Heinrich Heine.
2821-the-story-of-the-gadsbys:
Rudyard Kipling wrote this story of the Gadsbys as an awful warning, addressing Captain J. Mafflin of the Duke of Derry's Hussars in the preface. Poor Dear Mamma, The World Without, and The Tents of Kedar follow a young officer's courtship and marriage.

With Any Amazement, The Garden of Eden, and Fatima carry the tale through love, army life, and disillusion in India. Kipling writes in scenes and dialogue, with wit and bite. The book offers a sharp, early portrait of Anglo Indian society, and of a marriage under strain.
29130-billy-topsail-company-a-story-for-:
Norman Duncan wrote this 1910 boys' story, Billy Topsail and Company, published by Fleming H. Revell in New York, Chicago, Toronto, London, and Edinburgh. The book continues The Adventures of Billy Topsail, which the Brooklyn Eagle praised for portraying actual Newfoundland life without invention. Every boy who knows Billy, the publisher says, will welcome this continuation among the hardy sons of the sea.

A frontispiece shows Bill o' Burnt Bay and the boys of the Spot Cash unable to fathom the mystery of the Black Eagle. Duncan, author of Doctor Luke of the Labrador, writes clean, pure, and stimulating adventure, true to life. Readers get a stirring Newfoundland sea story for boys, full of boats, boys, and the northern coast.
2920-four-short-plays:
John Galsworthy collected four short plays under the heading Hall-Marked and Others, drawn from his Six Short Plays. Hall-Marked, a satiric trifle, opens in a bungalow sitting room with French windows, where a dripping woman runs in carrying a wet Scotch terrier. Defeat, The Sun, and Punch and Go complete the set, each running a single sharp situation.

The plays show Galsworthy's range in miniature, from society comedy to wartime feeling. One later scene has a young officer refuse a girl's kiss, then bend to her forehead, only for her to press her mouth to his and cling. The collection suits readers who want Galsworthy in brief, where a whole social world fits inside one room and one evening.
2940-evolution-and-ethics-and-other-essa:
Thomas Henry Huxley collected Evolution and Ethics and Other Essays around his Romanes Lecture at Oxford, the second in the series founded by George Romanes. Huxley mourns Romanes, dead in the flower of his age, a friend valued for kindly nature and zeal for knowledge. He recalls receiving Romanes's early work as a secretary of the Royal Society and rejoicing at the accession to the little army of workers in science. The essays restate the patent facts of variation.

Domestic plants and animals vary widely under favorable conditions, and interbreeding can fix a variety into a race that comes true from seed. Such races may differ as widely as admitted species. The book asks how ethics can stand against a natural process that favors self-assertion, and it remains Huxley's most philosophical work.
29420-american-rural-highways:
Issued in the Agricultural Engineering Series under consulting editor E. B. McCormick, this manual treats the purpose and utility of rural highways in America. A preface dated at Ames, Iowa, in August 1920 frames the transport problem as national in scope, and chapters work from first principles toward practice. The book speaks to engineers, farmers, and county officials building roads for a motor age.

Its pages cover road purpose, design, and use, with the technical care of a college text, including notes on grades, loads, and surfaces. The aim is practical: better farm-to-market roads for a growing nation. Historians of transport and rural America will find a detailed record of how highway science was taught just as cars remade the countryside.
29444-the-machinery-of-the-universe-mech:
A. E. Dolbear, professor of physics and astronomy at Tufts College, wrote this 1897 book in the Romance of Science series, printed by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London and E. and J. B. Young in New York. Dolbear sets out mechanical conceptions of physical phenomena: how energy, motion, and forces might be pictured as machinery of the universe, from imponderables to transformations of light and electricity.

Chapters trace antecedents of electricity, the nature of what is transformed, and the series of changes that yield light, with positive and negative electricity weighed in turn. The prose is that of a teacher speaking to general readers. Students of Victorian science will find a clear window on how physicists pictured nature just before the electron age.
29515-the-battle-of-the-bays:
Owen Seaman's 1902 book of verse, printed by John Lane at the Bodley Head in London and New York, takes its title from its opening sequence, The Battle of the Bays. Its poems include a song of renunciation, verses for the albums of crowned heads only, Marsyas in Hades, the rhyme of the kipperling, a ballad of a bun, and a Vigo-Street eclogue. An ode to spring in the metropolis follows.

Seaman, known also for In Cap and Bells and Horace at Cambridge, writes light verse with a sharp, classical edge. His battle of the bays is a witty contest of poets, fought with rhyme. Readers of Edwardian light verse will find a clever, polished collection, funny and learned at once.
30007-a-dear-little-girl-s-thanksgiving-:
Amy E. Blanchard wrote A Dear Little Girl's Thanksgiving Holidays, part of the Dear Little Girl series, printed by the Whitman Publishing Company of Racine, Wisconsin. The copyright, held by George W. Jacobs and Company, is dated 1912, and this printing is dated 1924. Edna comes home from school one Friday afternoon to find a letter from grandma, with no real news but an invitation of the Thanksgiving kind.

Grandma wants the whole family for an old-fashioned Thanksgiving, like those of her youth, since she and grandpa grow old and may not gather them all again. Edna and her mother plan to go a day or two ahead, while Celia, the boys, and father follow, father not free until Wednesday afternoon. Twelve chapters follow: the invitation, Reliance, a missing key, a hearty dinner, the red book, the old house, the mill stream, Jetty's party, and farewells.
30198-nirvana-days:
Cale Young Rice gathers poems in two groups, non-dramatic and more or less dramatic, in a Doubleday volume dated 1909 in Roman numerals. Early lyrics include an invocation, the fairies of God, and a song of the old Venetians. The title poem Nirvana Days joins pieces from off the Irish coast, at Stratford, and before the great Buddha of Kamakura. A vision of Venus and Adonis, a serenata magica, and a Japanese tale of O-Shichi and Moto widen the range.

Dramatic pieces follow, with titles such as Uncrowned, Written in Hell, At the Helm, Dead Love, Mortal Sin, Sea-Mad, and a quatorzain sequence on quest and requital. Rice, author of Yolanda of Cyprus and David, writes in a high, musical style, fond of myth, the sea, and the soul's return. The book suits readers who like late Romantic verse with a wide, wandering eye.
30469-a-tale-of-the-summer-holidays:
G. Mockler presents a children's holiday tale published by Thomas Nelson and Sons in 1899, built around the four younger Danvers children. Two days after the holidays begin, they receive a note from Drusie. It summons them to a secret gathering the next morning at half seven in the summer house.

Chapters follow a friend in need, Hal finding a friend, disappointed hopes, and a fort in the wilderness. Pictures show Jim scribbling yes on paper, Jumbo washing his face, and a boy throwing a lasso with deadly aim. Mockler writes for young readers who enjoy clubs, codes, and outdoor building, keeping the fun brisk and the friendships warm.
30509-the-railway-builders-a-chronicle-o:
Oscar D. Skelton writes The Railway Builders, a chronicle of overland highways, published in Toronto in 1916. A frontispiece shows a surveyor, often an explorer as well, striking into the wilderness in search of a mountain pass or lower grade, from a drawing by C. W. Jefferys.

Contents move from the coming of the railway and early travel in Canada to the call for the railway and Canadian beginnings. The Grand Trunk era, the Intercolonial, and the Canadian Pacific beginnings follow. Skelton tells how rails crossed a continent, through surveys, companies, and politics, in a clear national chronicle.
3068-washington-square-plays:
Washington Square Plays, volume twenty of the Drama League series, gathers four one-act plays from the Washington Square Players, with an introduction by Walter Prichard Eaton. The Clod by Lewis Beach, Eugenically Speaking by Edward Goodman, Overtones by Alice Gerstenberg, and Helena's Husband by Philip Moeller make the set. Doubleday, Page published the volume in 1925 from copyrights of 1913 to 1916.

A scene from one play has Una ringing a bell, primping at a mirror, and teasing George, a car conductor, for his politeness. The plays show the little-theatre movement's range, from folk drama to psychological comedy. The collection suits readers interested in American experimental theatre of the nineteen teens.
30953-the-boy-scout-and-other-stories-fo:
Richard Harding Davis wrote this collection of stories for boys, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1917, with copyright in 1891, 1903, 1912, 1914, and 1917. Its five stories are The Boy Scout, The Boy Who Cried Wolf, Gallegher, Blood Will Tell, and The Bar Sinister. The frontispiece shows a boy demanding how he is to get ashore.

The title story opens with a rule of the Boy Scouts: every day to do someone a good turn. It applies not because the copy-books say it deserves another indeed, but in spite of that pleasing possibility. Until a true Scout has performed his act of kindness, his day is dark. He is as unhappy as a grown-up who has begun the day without shaving or reading the daily New York Sun. It is a spirited collection of Davis's best boys' tales.
30966-miss-mouse-and-her-boys:
Mrs. Molesworth wrote this children's book, published by Macmillan in London and New York in 1897, with pictures by L. Leslie Brooke. It is dedicated to the memory of her brother-in-law, Sir Craven Charles Goring, whose unfailing interest in her work encouraged her through many years. The frontispiece shows a room full of boys, captioned, Oh, what a lot of boys.

Twelve chapters run from What a Lot of Boys and Pat and Pets through Guests at Tea, Wanted: A Sister, Bob, and Ferrets and Fairies. They continue with Nance's Story, Miss Mouse at Home, and The Story of the Lucky Penny. They end with A Great Sacrifice and Out on the Moor. Pictures include a hand-and-pat game down a hill, Nance with stories in her head, and a boy throwing little suns to catch. It is a old-fashioned tale of Miss Mouse and her boys.
3108-nine-short-essays:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote Nine Short Essays on gardens, truthfulness, happiness, literature, and the stage. A Night in the Garden of the Tuileries recalls June 18, 1868, under the Second Empire. It was the longest night Warner ever saw despite short summer nights, spent lounging in Paris gardens and giving none of the balmy nights to sleep. Other essays treat simplicity, the English volunteers, and Nathan Hale. A literature-and-stage essay asks whether the divorce of stage from literature is permanent.

It wonders whether the stage has degenerated or evolved into an independent art, a vinculo or only a mensa et thoro. Warner doubts any recent play carries literary quality. The essays show a thoughtful American man of letters weighing art against popularity.
31278-the-history-of-freedom-and-other-e:
Lord Acton's History of Freedom and Other Essays, edited by John Neville Figgis and Reginald Vere Laurence, was published by Macmillan in 1909, first edition 1907. It gathers seventeen essays reprinted from the Quarterly Review, the English Historical Review, the Nineteenth Century, the Rambler, and other journals. Its title essays trace freedom in antiquity and in Christianity, followed by pieces on Erskine May's democracy in Europe, the massacre of St. Bartholomew, and the Protestant theory of persecution.

Later essays take up political thoughts on the church, Goldwin Smith's Irish history, nationality, Döllinger on the temporal power and his historical work, and Cardinal Wiseman. They go on to conflicts with Rome, the Vatican Council, the Inquisition, the American Commonwealth, and historical philosophy in France. The editors, drawing on Acton's letters to Döllinger and Lady Blennerhasset, present a great historian's liberal mind at full range.
32224-tom-brown-s-school-days:
Tom Brown's School Days, by An Old Boy, was published in New York by Macmillan and Company in 1880. It carries drawings by Arthur Hughes and Sydney Prior Hall, and is the classic Rugby school story. Its frontispiece shows Tom chaired in the quadrangle. The author dedicated the book, without her permission, to Mrs. Arnold of Fox Howe, to whom he owes more than words can repay.

Its contents follow Tom from The Brown Family and The Veast through Sundry Wars and Alliances. The Stage Coach and Rugby and Football lead to After the Match and Settling to the Collar. A War of Independence and A Chapter of Accidents lead into a second part. There the tide turns, a new boy arrives, Arthur makes a friend, and a fight and a fever test the school. Readers get the founding boys' school tale, with football, friendship, and bullying at its heart.
32267-a-century-of-english-essays:
A Century of English Essays, chosen by Ernest Rhys and Lloyd Vaughan for Everyman's Library, number 653, edited by Ernest Rhys, is an anthology of English essayists across a century. Its publishers offer lists of published and projected volumes across travel, science, fiction, theology and philosophy, history, and classical works. They continue through books for young people, essays, oratory, poetry and drama, biography, reference, and romance, in cloth, leather, and library bindings.

The volume's apparatus shows its scholarly care. A small number of printer's errors were corrected by reference to other editions, footnotes moved to just below the referring paragraph, and author lines regularized to appear one line below each essay. Readers get a century of English essays in one Everyman volume, from the essay's classic practitioners, chosen and ordered for general readers.
32334-jacko-and-jumpo-kinkytail-the-funn:
Howard R. Garis's bedtime book tells stories of Jacko and Jumpo Kinkytail, the funny monkey boys, for reading aloud to small children each night. The volume belongs to Garis's long Bed Time Stories series, which also includes Sammie and Susie Littletail, Johnnie and Billie Bushytail, and the Uncle Wiggily books. Each volume in the series holds thirty-one stories, one for each night of the month, with eight coloured illustrations.

Jacko and Jumpo get into the small scrapes and jokes that suit very young listeners, with animal characters, clear morals, and gentle humour. Louis Wisa's pictures accompany the text. Parents and teachers looking for short, nightly read-aloud tales will find this volume in the same friendly pattern as the rest of Garis's animal bedtime books.
32453-molly-brown-s-sophomore-days:
Nell Speed's girls' novel, copyrighted in 1912, follows Molly Brown through her sophomore year at Wellington, where she returns gladly to Queen's Cottage. Molly swings off the bus with her suitcase, running in without ringing the bell, and soon meets juniors and freshmen she knew by sight the year before. Chapters follow Otoyo, a clashing of wits, a tempest in a teapot, an unwilling eavesdropper, and two long-distance calls.

Later the year brings a glee club concert, a Japanese spread, vespers, a great sleet, a skating carnival, and a thaw. Christmas plots, a surprise, and news about how O'Reilly's became Queen's carry Molly toward the turn of the wheel and a garden scene. Speed, author of the Tucker Twins and Carter Girls series, writes warmly about school friendship and growing up.
32496-helen-grant-s-schooldays:
Amanda M. Douglas's Helen Grant's Schooldays, published in Boston in August 1903 with illustrations by Amy Brooks, opens the Helen Grant books. A frontispiece shows Helen telling her dreams to an old apple tree. Chapters begin with Helen herself, an excursion to Hope, air castles with foundations, and the planting of small seeds, in the pattern of Douglas's popular girls' series.

Later volumes in the series follow Helen Grant's friends, Helen at Aldred House, Helen in college, Helen senior, Helen graduate, Helen teacher, and her decision and harvest year. Douglas, author of the Kathie stories and Larry, writes warmly about school, friendship, and growing up. Young readers get a period picture of American girlhood, with dreams, duties, and the slow work of becoming.
3250-how-to-tell-a-story-and-other-essay:
Mark Twain opens this set with his famous essay on telling a story. The humorous story, he claims, is an American development, distinct from the comic story and the witty story. He disclaims the power to tell a story as it ought to be told, but claims to know how it ought to be told, having kept company with expert storytellers for years. The wounded soldier and the golden arm follow as examples.

Mental telegraphy again and the invalid's story round out the volume. Twain's rule is patience: let a story pause, wander, and arrive in its own time. The essays still teach comic timing better than most textbooks. They show a master explaining his craft in the act of practicing it, with jokes that prove each point as he makes it.
32679-geographic-variation-in-red-backed:
E. Lendell Cockrum and Kenneth L. Fitch study red-backed mice of the southern Rocky Mountains in a Kansas Museum paper dated November 15, 1952. Cockrum was drafting a synopsis of North American voles, while Fitch had written a thesis on Wyoming mice, and together they weighed many skins and skulls.

Their work names two subspecies new to science and clarifies two more. The wide-ranging Clethrionomys gapperi galei was typed from Ward, Colorado, at nine thousand five hundred feet. It varies in coat from Wyoming to the Tetons. Northern and southern forms differ in stripe, sides, and skull traits.
32972-round-the-world-in-eighty-days:
Jules Verne's Round the World in Eighty Days appears here in Henry Frith's English translation, transcribed from an 1879 Routledge edition. The story opens in 1872 with Phileas Fogg taking on Passe-partout as his servant, and the wager that follows sends them racing around the globe in eighty days. Trains, steamers, and narrow escapes carry them from London through Asia and America and back again.

Frith's version keeps its own period spellings and turns of phrase, which give this edition a flavor distinct from the better-known Towle translation. Verne's plot, though, needs no help: a cool, exact hero, a loyal servant, and a clock that never stops. It remains one of the great adventure novels, built on timetables, geography, and the thrill of a deadline that cannot be missed.
33040-bye-ways:
Robert Hichens's Bye-Ways, published in New York in 1914, gathers short stories that stray from the main road of his novels. The contents open with The Charmer of Snakes. In it, Renfrew lies awake on a camp bed while jackals whine outside his bell tent and fettered mules stamp on rough ground. The contents then move to A Tribute of Souls, written with Lord Frederick Hamilton, An Echo in Egypt, The Face of the Monk, and The Man Who Intervened.

Later stories include After To-Morrow, A Silent Guardian, A Boudoir Boy, and The Tee-to-Tum, each taking a strange or sidelong turn. Hichens, known for The Garden of Allah and Bella Donna, brings his taste for the exotic and the uncanny to these shorter pieces. The collection suits readers who like a story that begins in a familiar place and quietly leads somewhere stranger.
33055-her-season-in-bath-a-story-of-bygo:
Emma Marshall's Her Season in Bath, published in London in 1889, is a story of bygone days set at the height of the Bath season in 1779. The city then felt the full tide of amusement and pleasure each year, as streets, parades, and terraces filled with visitors seeking fashion, music, and company. Marshall's chapters move from coiffeur and the tide of fashion to music, a vase of Parnassus, and a proposal, before the plot thickens.

Later chapters bring brawls, a challenge, an early morning meeting, and a bitter end, followed by a valley of the shadow and, ten years later, 1790. The novel uses Bath's social world as both setting and judge, where a season's triumphs and blunders follow a young woman for years. It is a gentle historical romance, fond of its period detail and its heroine's fortunes.
33087-discoveries-a-volume-of-essays:
William Butler Yeats's Discoveries gathers his thoughts on poetry, drama, and the life of art. It is a volume of essays printed by the Dun Emer Press at Dundrum in 1907 in only two hundred copies. Its contents run from Prophet, Priest and King and Personality and the Intellectual Essences through The Musician and the Orator and A Banjo Player. They go on to The Looking-glass, The Tree of Life, and The Play of Modern Manners. The essays ask why the blind man in ancient times was made a poet.

Later pieces treat saints, drama, asceticism, and symbolic art, closing with the holy places. Yeats writes from his work with a small theatrical company in the west of Ireland. He argues that drama must root itself in folk life and symbol rather than in drawing-room talk. The book is a key document of the Irish revival.
33213-the-fun-of-cooking-a-story-for-gir:
Caroline French Benton's Fun of Cooking, a story for boys and girls published by the Century Company in 1915 with illustrations by Sarah K. Smith, teaches cooking through story. Its chapters run from the day before Christmas and supper at the house in the woods through Jack's school luncheons and a birthday picnic. They go on to Sunday night supper, Mildred's school party, strawberry time, and camp, before jams and jelly, a Hallowe'en supper, and a time when Mother Blair was sick.

Later chapters bring a doll party, Thanksgiving supper, candy for the fair, and examination day, with an index. Benton, author of A Little Cook Book for a Little Girl, writes for children who want to cook, not merely watch. The book remains a delightful period introduction to the kitchen, where a picnic, a party, and a sick day all teach something useful.
33309-through-the-postern-gate-a-romance:
Florence L. Barclay's Through the Postern Gate, a romance in seven days, was published in 1912. It reached a hundred and forty-sixth thousand printing. Barclay, author of The Rosary, structures the tale by days. Day one brings the story of Little Boy Blue, then Miss Charteris takes control, a boy invades the kitchen, and Christobel signs her name. Guy Chelsea takes control on day five, and Miss Ann has much to say on day six.

The romance's appeal lies in its gentle, domestic magic, where a postern gate opens to love and second chances. Barclay writes with warmth and faith, in a style that made her books bestsellers. For readers who enjoy Edwardian romance, Through the Postern Gate offers a sweet, well-told tale of a week that changes lives.
3331-the-diary-of-samuel-pepys:
Samuel Pepys kept this diary through the 1660s, and it remains the liveliest record of Restoration London. A naval official by day, Pepys wrote at night in shorthand about everything: plays, dinners, quarrels with his wife, office politics, and the great events that broke over the city. Plague in 1665 and the Great Fire in 1666 pass through the entries as personal news.

The diary's charm is its candor. Pepys records his vanities and fears alongside his work, and no entry feels written for posterity. Readers meet Charles the Second's London from the inside: coffee houses, theaters, and streets, all in one man's daily shorthand. It is history as gossip, and gossip that happens to be true.
33389-a-pair-of-schoolgirls-a-story-of-s:
Angela Brazil's Pair of Schoolgirls follows two girls through school days, in the author's familiar, lively style. Brazil, praised for writing schoolgirl tales that other schoolgirls loved, sets the story among classes, games, and friendships, where a pair of heroines learn loyalty, pluck, and fun. The book joins a long shelf of Brazil school stories, from Captain Peggie to The Luckiest Girl in the School.

The tale's charm lies in its true school detail and its warm, comic voice, catching the talk and trials of girls together. Its heroines, by turns bold and kind, carry readers through term-time scrapes. For fans of classic school stories, A Pair of Schoolgirls offers a bright, old-fashioned term with two girls worth knowing.
33421-the-speech-of-monkeys:
R. L. Garner's Speech of Monkeys, in Heinemann's Scientific Handbooks, asks whether monkeys have a true language of their own. Garner, who studied apes at close range, sets out his experiments and his claims for monkey speech, in a book that stirred both wonder and debate. The volume belongs to a series of handbooks that aimed to bring science to general readers.

The book's interest lies in its early, bold attempt to listen to animals as speakers, not just as beasts. Garner's tone is earnest and curious, and his methods, though dated, opened a field still studied today. For readers of animal behavior and science history, it is a fascinating, pioneering work on the border of language and nature.
33521-little-frankie-at-his-plays:
A volume in A. R. Baker's Little Frankie series, this small book follows a young child through his games and playtime lessons. Frankie learns by doing: trying out toys, inventing pastimes, and discovering how to share, take turns, and mind others in play. The simple episodes are written for very young readers, with short scenes and clear morals tucked inside the fun.

As one of several Frankie books covering home, cousins, father, journeys, and school, this volume suits early readers and families reading aloud. Its old-fashioned charm lies in its gentle pace and its belief that play itself teaches patience, kindness, and good manners. The book preserves a nineteenth-century style of children's literature at its most domestic and affectionate.
33668-springtime-and-other-essays:
Sir Francis Darwin gathers essays on nature, books, music, and people in this illustrated 1920 volume. The title essay argues, against governesses who gave each season three months, that spring should take February as well as March, April, and May. That leaves winter a short link of December and January. Darwin writes with a naturalist's eye and a gentle, digressive humor.

Further essays discuss names of characters in fiction, the antiquary Thomas Hearne, recollections, old instruments of music with illustrations of psalteries, lutes, crwths, and recorders, traditional names of English plants. A procession of flowers closes the book. Readers who enjoy reflective, well-informed essays will find Darwin an agreeable companion.
33880-the-land-of-lost-toys:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote this children's book, published in Boston in 1900 with pictures. It opens with an earthquake in the nursery: Sam, a boy with a knack for breaking toys, scalps his twin sister Dot's new doll to roof a wigwam made from bed curtains. Dot, fat, resolute, hasty, and devotedly unselfish, bears the loss with tears and clenched fists.

Later tales follow lost toys and the children who loved them, in Ewing's warm, observant style. She writes for children without talking down to them. The book remains a charming classic of nursery storytelling.
339-old-indian-days:
Charles A. Eastman, Ohiyesa, dedicates these stories of old Indian life to his daughters. Old Indian Days divides into the warrior and the woman, with tales of love, famine, and the white man's errand. The love of Antelope opens on Eagle Scout Butte.

Winona the woman-child, Snana's fawn, and the war maiden follow, with a glossary to close. Eastman, a Santee Sioux physician, writes from inside the culture he describes. His stories honor courage and womanly strength alike. The book preserves a world already passing. Eastman's stories preserve Sioux life as he knew it firsthand.
34005-curious-punishments-of-bygone-days:
Alice Morse Earle wrote this book on old punishments, first published in 1896 and reprinted by Loompanics Unlimited, with pictures by Frank Hazenplug. Earle found her material in old court records, newspapers, diaries, and letters while writing colonial history. A drunkard's cloak fronts the volume.

Chapters run from bilboes, the ducking stool, the stocks, and the pillory through punishments of authors and books. Later chapters treat the whipping-post, the scarlet letter, branks and gags, public penance, military punishments, and branding and maiming. Earle writes with curiosity and a touch of humor. The book gives a vivid look at justice long past.
34267-the-morality-of-woman-and-other-es:
The Morality of Woman and Other Essays is a set of essays by Ellen Key, the Swedish thinker. Mamah Bouton Borthwick made this authorized translation from the Swedish. The Ralph Fletcher Seymour Company of Chicago published it in 1911. Two companion essays treat the woman of the future and the conventional woman.

The title essay opens with a saying of Almquist on counterfeit love. The law hangs men who counterfeit banknotes, in that sharp comparison. A man who marries without love counterfeits something far more precious, it argues. From that spark Key states her simplest formula for a new morality. Love is moral even without legal marriage, she holds. Marriage without love is immoral, whatever the law may say. The customary objection, that her school forgets all other duties, is faced at once.
34271-is-polite-society-polite-and-other:
Julia Ward Howe published essays at Boston in 1895, headed by a question: is polite society polite? A signed photograph of Howe fronts the book. Contents place Paris and Greece Revisited after the title essay. The salon in America and Aristophanes follow. The halfness of nature and Dante and Beatrice close the list.

Why do we ask this question, Howe begins, promising to make her reasons evident. Howe, author of the Battle Hymn of the Republic, was America's grand old woman of letters. Her essays draw on European travel and Boston salon life. Lamson, Wolffe published them in her eighty sixth year. The title essay needles fashionable manners.
3499-jo-s-boys:
Louisa May Alcott returns to Plumfield, Jo March's school, in this sequel to Little Men. The chapters follow Jo's boys as young men: Dan, Nat, Demi, Emil, and Josie, with scenes such as Jo's Last Scrape, Dan's Christmas, Nat's New Year, Plays at Plumfield, and Class Day. Marmee's place is now empty, and Meg speaks tenderly of the family that has changed.

Jo, now a teacher and mother figure, watches her pupils face work, love, and loss. Alcott mixes humor with moral lessons, praising kindness, hard work, and courage. The book suits readers who grew up with Little Women and Little Men and want to see Jo's schoolboys become men.
3549-cowley-s-essays:
Abraham Cowley, a seventeenth century English poet, writes essays in this Cassell volume from 1893. An introduction traces Cowley from his father Thomas, a London stationer who died in 1618, through a childhood of early verse. One piece discussed is a sixteen stanza work with songs, first printed in his little Poetical Blossoms at the age of thirteen.

Cowley's essays treat gardens, solitude, work, and the good life with the ease of a man who loved retirement and study. He writes in the plain, personal manner that helped shape the English essay. The volume suits readers who want to meet an early master of the form, before Addison and Steele made it famous.
35539-is-the-bible-worth-reading-and-oth:
Lemuel Washburn wrote Is the Bible Worth Reading, and Other Essays, published by the Truth Seeker Company in New York in 1911. The Truth Seeker was the leading American freethought paper, and Washburn writes in its spirit. The title essay asks plainly whether the Bible deserves the place given it.

Dozens of short essays follow. Their titles show the range: A Cruel God, What Is Jesus, Religion and Morality, and Christianity and Freethought. Others treat the American Sunday, the danger of the ballot, and whether poverty can be abolished. Washburn argues for deeds over professions and for truth over creeds. The book is a freethinker's handbook, brisk and combative, aimed at readers ready to question the faith around them.
35591-the-daughter-pays:
The Daughter Pays, by Baillie Reynolds, is a novel of love and sacrifice. Burt issued the New York printing under Doran arrangement in 1915 rights. A Louvre statue of Love bears this motto: whoever thou art, thy lord is he. Chapter one sets two girls before a portrait in a London gallery.

Gallery Sixteen at Hertford House glows in late June sun as they gaze. Virginia at home and the two Virginias set up the heroine split life. Gaunt terms, a trap, and Andromeda mark the fall into trouble ahead. Renouncement, the final test, and the last ride together drive the close. Three escapes are promised by the chapter list before the mastery ends it.
35689-anti-suffrage-essays:
Anti Suffrage Essays, by Massachusetts women, was printed at Boston in 1916, with a lead note by Ernest Bernbaum of Harvard University. The book is given, with thanks, to the 295,939 Massachusetts men who backed the women stand at the vote of 1915.

The writers were famed speakers, writers, and organizers in the 1915 fight against votes for women. A front essay calls the result the anti suffrage victory in Massachusetts. It notes their poll topped the best party poll the state had seen, and won by 133,447 votes. The essays set out why these women held the vote would harm home and state. Readers get the losing side of a great fight in its own strong words, one year before the tide turned for good.
35860-essays:
Essays, by Arthur Christopher Benson of Eton College, was published by William Heinemann in London in 1896 and dedicated to Henry James. Benson gathers studies of quiet, scholarly lives: John Hales of Eton, Henry More the Platonist, Andrew Marvell, Vincent Bourne, Thomas Gray, and William Blake, the last printed here for the first time. Most of the pieces had appeared in reviews.

Benson writes with a gentle, reflective touch, opening the Blake study in the stillness of the Eton churchyard and letting each subject's character unfold from small scenes. His gratitude to a Cambridge friend who revised the whole book hints at the care taken. The volume helped make Benson's name as an essayist of the contemplative school, a writer later loved for his diaries and lyrics.
36078-literary-byways:
William Andrews gathers light essays on books and writers in a volume issued at London in 1898. William Andrews and Company published it at Farringdon Avenue. Three chapters first ran in Chambers's Journal.

The contents roam widely over small literary game. Authors at Work opens the book, and The Earnings of Authors follows. Declined with Thanks treats the rejected manuscript. Later pieces list epigrams on authors and poetry written on window panes. Folk rhymes, toast lists, and menu-card verse get their turns. Anne Bradstreet appears as the earliest American poetess. Mary Pyper is named a poet of the poor. James Nayler, the mad Quaker who claimed to be the Messiah, closes the odd crew. Andrews wrote for readers who liked print lore.
36120-essays:
Essays, by David Hume, appears in an edition from John Long of London with a biographical introduction by Hannaford Bennett. The introduction retells Hume's life from his own short memoir. Hume was born at Edinburgh on April 26, 1711, son of a minor Scots laird who died in his infancy. He entered the university at twelve.

The essays range over taste, politics, and manners. They treat the liberty of the press, the first principles and origin of government, and parties in general and in Great Britain. Others take up superstition and enthusiasm, civil liberty, and eloquence. One asks whether politics may be reduced to a science. The set shows Hume's calm, sceptical temper at work on public questions.
36176-nan-sherwood-s-summer-holidays:
Nan Sherwood's Summer Holidays, by Annie Roe Carr, was published in 1937 by the World Syndicate company of Cleveland and New York. Thirty chapters carry Nan Sherwood of Tillbury and her friend Bess from a New Year's Eve secret across the Atlantic. A storm at sea, a stay in the ship's hospital, and a hunchback who keeps turning up fill the crossing.

Chapter one opens on New Year's Eve. Nan says she has pinched herself a dozen times and pulled her own hair. She has told her mirror again and again that the thing is a fact. Next spring she sails to Scotland. Later chapters bring Scottish games and tunes, an accident near a castle, Nan's disappearance, and London on holiday for a coronation. Carr writes a brisk girls' travel tale.
3667-wolfville-days:
Alfred Henry Lewis writes tales of Wolfville, a fictional cattle and mining town in the Arizona desert, in this collection. Wolfville's cowboys, gamblers, miners, and storekeepers fill stories told in the drawling voice of an old cattleman. The town's saloon, poker games, and street encounters provide the stage for humor, violence, and sudden kindness.

Lewis, a journalist who knew the West, writes with a love for frontier talk and for characters who live by their own code. His stories mix tall tales with sharp observation of a rough society. The book suits readers who enjoy classic western humor and the days when Wolfville stood for the whole wild Southwest.
36984-fifty-contemporary-one-act-plays:
Frank Shay and Pierre Loving chose these fifty short plays from the whole world's stage. Stewart and Kidd printed the set at Cincinnati in 1920. Each play stands whole in one act, sorted by the land it came from.

Austria leads with Hofmannsthal and Schnitzler. Belgium gives Maeterlinck's The Intruder. France, Germany, and Great Britain fill long lists: Bennett, Dowson, and Wedekind stand among them. Lady Gregory flies the flag for Ireland. India sends Mukerji's Judgment of Indra. A one-act play then was the live form of the little theatre age: short, sharp, and fit for one set. Shay, a famed seller of plays, built a shelf of the best in one thick book.
3706-the-valiant-runaways:
Gertrude Atherton sets this boyhood tale on a great cattle rancho in old California, where two sons of a rich landowner chafe under their father's rule. Roldan, the elder, paces the verandah in a fury at the start, and soon he and his younger brother slip away from home to seek their own fortunes. The rancho world of adobe walls, silver spurs, and grazing herds frames a story about pride, kinship, and the lure of the open road.

Once free, the runaways cross brush country by night, lose their way among owls and bats, and press on toward the nearest town with no shelter in sight. Hunger, fear, and stubborn courage take turns driving them forward. The book suits readers who like frontier adventure told at a brisk pace, with the boys learning that freedom costs more than they had guessed.
37154-songs-of-heroic-days:
Songs of Heroic Days is a book of war verse by Thomas O Hagan, printed at Toronto in 1916. O Hagan gives the book to the brave Canadian hearts that beat and battle for freedom and the safety of the Empire. The date on his note is January 20, 1916.

A letter from the King of Belgium stands near the front, in thanks for verses in his honor. Poems hold I Take Off My Hat to Albert, Louvain, and The Kaiser Favorite Poems. Other verses name mothers, the trenches, and Langemarck, where Canadians stood fast. One poem treats the song of the Zeppelin, and one the bugle call. Readers get Canada war feeling in verse, hot from the first years of the Great War.
3716-mrs-general-talboys:
Anthony Trollope sends a formidable Englishwoman to Rome for the winter of 1859 in this comic tale. Mrs General Talboys claims she comes to drink at the living fountains of classical poetry, though friends suspect a domestic tiff sent her south. Once among the English colony she declaims on the Capitol for Italian unity, praising martyrs' blood and Rome immortal in tones that leave even sympathizers gasping.

The narrator, an Englishman on the spot, admires her fire and winces at her flight, since she soars so high that no plain listener can follow. The tale satirizes grand talk with gentle malice, and Rome itself, with its ruins and revolutions, plays a full part. It is a short study of enthusiasm, and of how a good cause can still make its champion hard to bear.
37249-the-city-of-numbered-days:
City of Numbered Days is a novel by Francis Lynde, published by Scribner at New York. Becher illustrated the volume for its author in this edition. Lynde, an engineer turned novelist, set many of his tales in the West of railways and mines. The city of the title is a camp whose days are numbered by its boom.

His novels turn on water rights, mine titles, and the men who fight for a town future in the courts and in the street. The Numbered Days of this one count down a reclamation or mining camp toward the date when its fate is sealed. The book belongs to the shelf of Western business novels. Its romance is in the survey, the ditch, and the bond issue, as much as in any love story of the camp.
37272-stage-coach-and-tavern-days:
Stage-Coach and Tavern Days, by Alice Morse Earle, author of Home Life in Colonial Days, was published in New York in 1900 by Macmillan. A front plate shows travel in the South in the thirties. Nineteen chapters run from the Puritan ordinary through tavern fare, signs and symbols, and the tavern in war, to turnpikes, packhorses, and the stage-driver's trade.

A motto poem grieves for the travelers of the old coach: the youth and his bride and the gray three-score, all passed under the tavern door. Earle reconstructs early American travel from records and lore: what coaches cost, what taverns fed, what signs hung over doors. Her social history treats the road as a world of its own, already vanished when she wrote.
37434-the-motor-maids-school-days:
Katherine Stokes wrote this girls tale of school days and a motor car. The book came out in New York in 1911 with Hurst. Nancy Brown teases her friends at the High School gate at the start. She promises them the surprise of their lives in ten minutes.

The car called the Comet drives picnics, storms, and a fire scare. Chapters add a ghost party, rumors at school, and a home visit. Mary faces judges, and Belle makes a confession near the end. The tale mixes fun, school bonds, and mild peril for young readers.
37672-from-school-to-battle-field-a-stor:
From School to Battle-Field is a boys' tale of the Civil War by Captain Charles King, published by Lippincott at Philadelphia in 1899. Violet Oakley and Charles Stephens drew the pictures. The story opens on a rainy Saturday in New York, before the war. Two boys lean at a window, hating the east wind that spoils their ball game against the Murray Hill crowd.

The pictures promise the road ahead: a boy pulled from a horse, a wounded head lifted on a knee, and a girl weeping over Snipe's letter. One plate hails the first capture of the advancing Union arms. Talk in the tale turns on school exams and hard Latin, soon to be traded for the battle-field.
379-worldly-ways-byways:
Eliot Gregory, writing as An Idler, gathers forty short essays on manners and society in this 1899 volume. Topics run from charm, dress, and hosts to Paris, Newport, hotels, and the climber's art. Gregory, who knew diplomatic and high society circles, writes as an amused onlooker rather than a reformer.

His pieces poke fun at snobs, dandies, and social exiles while praising ease, wit, and good form. Some essays look back at old Newport or old Paris; others catch new wealth on the move. The book reads as a period guide to how polite folk lived, talked, and judged each other at the century's end.
37911-the-motor-girls-at-lookout-beach-o:
Margaret Penrose wrote The Motor Girls at Lookout Beach in 1911. Its subtitle calls the tale an quest of the runaways. Summer plans open the contents of the girls' holiday. A strawberry patch, a strike, and arbitration follow in the heads. Cora's queer plight and a clue at the spring house come next.

Bess Robinson bubbles with enthusiasm in the first chapter. Her sister fears she will blow up without repression. The Robinsons live at Chelton, a New England town, the opening says. A startling discovery and complications fill the middle contents. Lost on the road and boys to the rescue stand in the list. A shadow in the hedge and an inn follow. Lookout Beach itself, and a struggle with the waves, close it. The two orphans and the whole truth finish the contents. Penrose gives motor girls a seaside mystery.
37967-more-portmanteau-plays:
More Portmanteau Plays is a set of plays by Stuart Walker, published at Cincinnati in 1919. Stewart and Kidd issued the volume, edited with an introduction by Bierstadt. Walker is shown with the working model of his Portmanteau Theatre in the frontispiece. 

The series list names three volumes of the plays in the set at the front. Portmanteau Plays is the first, and Portmanteau Adaptations the third of the three volumes. This second volume carries the heading Jonathan Makes a Wish in the series list. Walker theatre toured America with a company and a stage in trunks, playing short plays in towns without theatres. His books let schools and little theatres do the same with print. The plays here are short, actable pieces, made for a stage that packs into boxes and an audience that has never seen a curtain rise before.
38290-speciation-and-evolution-of-the-py:
Speciation and Evolution of the Pygmy Mice, Genus Baiomys, is a zoology monograph. Packard wrote it for the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. It ran in volume nine, number twenty three, pages 579 to 670, in 1960. Four plates and twelve text figures show skulls, teeth, and forms in detail.

Pygmy mice are the smallest cricetine rodents in North America, Packard notes. Their range runs from Nicaragua into the southwestern United States in the north. Fossil kinds open the study, then living variation by age and sex. Two living species, musculus and taylori, get full systematic accounts of races. Evolution, speciation, and conclusions close the technical work.
38767-spanish-highways-and-byways:
Spanish Highways and Byways, by Katharine Lee Bates, was held under a 1900 copyright and printed by Macmillan in New York. Bates had written on American letters and on the English church drama. Many plates from photos fill the book.

Chapters move from the lazy Spaniard myth and a nonstop carnival to the Alhambra at Granada. Later parts treat Seville in Passion Week, marks of the Inquisition, and a bull fight. Bates writes on gypsies, the route of the silver fleets, and Murillo cherubs. She gives the book to her mother in a short Spanish note at the front. Travel readers get Spain town by town, with art, faith, and street life in clear view.
39114-doesticks-what-he-says:
Philander Doesticks, the pen name of Mortimer Thomson, gathered his comic pieces in this book. Livermore and Rudd printed Doesticks, What He Says at New York in 1856. A plate shows Doesticks and his friends at the front.

The title page jokes at full length. The book is neither history, romance, life-drama, life story, nor post mortem probe, it swears. It is a set of unpremeditated literary extravaganzas, written without malice aforethought. Thomson wrote them purely for his own glorification, and the publisher printed them solely for his own profit. In a literary point of view the book claims nothing, says the maker. It amounts to nothing, the reader will conclude. Doesticks was a star of the comic press.
39243-six-one-act-plays:
Six One-Act Plays is a set of short plays by Oliver, put out at Boston in the mid nineteen teens as part of a set for American play wrights. A note at the front warns that the print form is for home readers alone. Stage use, pro or not, calls for the authors leave in writ form, and all stage rights are held in law.

The six plays bear names that span faith, place, and crime. A prophets hand, the young of Granada, a dove of peace, and a group of young men stand in the list. A strike play and a dark tale of a womans death close the set. The book is made out to a named friend of the author by first marks.
39266-theological-essays:
A volume of freethought essays by Charles Bradlaugh. A London edition appeared in 1895, after his death. The contents range widely. Heresy, Its Utility and Morality opens the book. A Plea for Atheism follows. New lives retell Abraham, Jacob, Moses, David, and Jonah. Other essays ask when the gospels were written. One answers Gladstone in a debate over Christianity.

The first essay poses a sharp question. Why does society pardon vice yet persecute the open heretic? Bradlaugh sorts famous supposed atheists into true classes. Voltaire and Paine, he notes, were theists. Each generation's heretics often become a later age's saints. Bradlaugh sat in Parliament after a famous struggle. He had fought for the right to affirm rather than swear a religious oath.
39949-the-place-of-science-in-modern-civ:
Place of Science in Modern Civilisation and Other Essays gathers papers by Thorstein Veblen. A list of his books stands at the front, from The Theory of the Leisure Class onward. The New York edition is dated nineteen nineteen. Contents open with the title essay. The evolution of the scientific point of view follows. Why economics is not an evolutionary science takes the third place.

Preconceptions of economic science fill three long essays in the middle. Professor Clark's economics and the limitations of marginal utility take their turns. Industrial and pecuniary employments and the nature of capital close the list shown. In the part printed, the claim that modern Christendom is superior to all other systems of civilised life is weighed. Other ages are spoken of as lower or less mature by contrast, it notes.
39954-with-americans-of-past-and-present:
With Americans of Past and Present Days is a book of memories by Jusserand, ambassador of France to the United States. It was published in New York by Scribner's Sons in 1916. The dedication looks back thirteen years. A new French ambassador then gave his credentials to the youngest president the Republic had had. Their first talk had a great many successors, he writes. In thirteen years the Union grew from forty-five states to forty-eight. Its trade with France doubled, and its navy more than doubled in tonnage.

The Panama Canal, not yet American when he came, was dug in his time. The aeroplane was unknown then. Jusserand counts that he has seen an eleventh part of the nation's whole life. The book gathers his talks and studies of Americans, from the founders to his own day. It is a fond, sharp portrait by a friend in office.
4006-yesterdays:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox's book of poems looks back on days gone by with a moral creed set in verse. Speak no evil, cause no ache, and guard the tongue, she urges, since words are adders when hearts are stung.

The poems move along rough pathways toward the grave, yet they counsel thoughtfulness and bravery rather than gloom. Wilcox writes in plain, musical lines meant to be read aloud and remembered. Readers who like old-fashioned verse with a clear lesson will find short poems for quiet hours, each carrying a small rule for living well.
4035-greek-studies-a-series-of-essays:
Walter Horatio Pater's essays on Greece move from springs and myths to the spirit of Greek art. A fountain of Dirce, haunted by the virgins of Thebes, becomes typical of the coolness of all springs, and the infant god washed there stands for a whole world of myth.

Pater reads Greek story as poetry, finding in rivers, gods, and portents a distant echo of old tumult and wonder. His prose is fine and allusive, meant for readers who know the classics or wish to meet them anew. The essays offer a Victorian critic's loving map of Greece, where myth and art explain each other.
4059-miscellaneous-studies-a-series-of-e:
Walter Pater's miscellaneous essays gather studies of art, poetry, and faith, from Raphael's Disputa to the beauty of pagan philosophy. Pater argues that philosophy and faith, truly apprehended, are as beautiful as Plato thought they must be.

The Disputa, a council of all ages, embodies an idea of truth through art, while other essays weigh antiquarian detail against grace. Pater's technique is perfect in its care, yet beauty stays his ruling test. Readers who like criticism that reads like poetry will enjoy these late essays of a master stylist. Each piece rewards slow reading.
40590-a-century-of-science-and-other-ess:
Century of Science and Other Essays gathers pieces by John Fiske, issued at Boston and New York in eighteen ninety nine. A line from Longfellow stands as the book's motto. A dedicatory letter to Thomas Sergeant Perry opens the volume. Perry taught English literature at a college in Tokyo, the letter notes.

Fiske says he long wished to make his friend the patron saint of some book of his. A chatty, wandering book fits the purpose, he writes. It would remind Perry, in his exile at the world's eastern rim, of quiet evenings of old. Over October ale and Virginia pipes, with Yule logs crackling, they roamed in fancy through the universe. The volume may serve as a record of many such sessions, he hopes. His theory of prolonged human infancy is tied to those talks, he adds.
4063-peter-plymley-s-letters-and-selecte:
Sydney Smith's Peter Plymley letters defend Catholic emancipation with wit and plain sense. Smith marvels at servile addresses poured on the throne, and at treating a great question of justice as nothing more than a matter of the monarch's private feelings.

The essays around the letters carry the same voice: a clergyman who argues in clear English, with jokes that cut and logic that holds. Readers who enjoy political satire of the Regency age will find Smith a lively guide to church, state, and tolerance, still readable for his humor and his fairness.
41311-five-plays:
Lord Dunsany wrote these five short plays of gods, kings, and doom. Little, Brown printed them at Boston in the Modern Drama Series, edited by Edwin Björkman. The Lost Silk Hat, the lightest of them, stands last in the book.

The Gods of the Mountain leads the set. The Golden Doom and King Argimenes and the Unknown Warrior follow. The Glittering Gate takes fourth place. Dunsany's plays made the little theatres of two continents: short, strange, and built on one twist of fate each. Beggars who play at gods, a gate to a heaven that is not there — his irony is the cold kind. The print is for readers, the rights page warns, and no stage use comes free.
41348-boys-and-girls-of-colonial-days:
Boys and Girls of Colonial Days is a story collection by Carolyn Sherwin Bailey, printed at Chicago by the Flanagan Company with copyright of 1917. Uldene Shriver illustrated the book. Its frontispiece is the youngest soldier of the Revolution. The stories teach colonial history through the children who might have lived it.

Fourteen tales make the contents. The Pink Tulip and Big Hawk's Decoration open the book. The Soap Making of Remember Biddle and The Beacon Tree follow. The Jack-O'-Lantern Witch and The Iron Stove bring in folklore and the hearth. A Boston Tea Party gives the Revolution its famous night. The Deacon's Grasshopper, Patience Arnold's Sampler and The Star Lady come next. Bailey wrote for the schoolroom market, where history was learned as story. Her colonial children make soap, stitch samplers and watch empires change.
41474-the-dixie-book-of-days:
The Dixie Book of Days, published in 1912, is Matthew Page Andrews's calendar of Southern memory. For each day of the year it sets poems, short notes and birthdays of noted Southerners. A frontispiece shows the founding of the first lasting English colony at Jamestown, Virginia, in 1607.

January first offers a sonnet by Paul Hamilton Hayne and verses by James Ryder Randall. January second marks Nathaniel Bacon, the first American rebel, born in 1647. A note calls his epitaph the single true poem made in America for a hundred and fifty years after Jamestown. January third gives Madison Cawein and the birth of Alfred Mordecai in 1804. The book keeps Southern letters and arms in daily view.
41631-a-dear-little-girl-s-summer-holida:
Dear Little Girl Summer Holidays is a girls story by Amy Blanchard. Whitman Publishing of Racine issued this printing in nineteen twenty four. The copyright rests with George Jacobs in nineteen eleven on the tale. Twelve chapters run from The Invitation to Home Again at the close.

Edna and her friend Dorothy Evans sit under trees on a hot June morning. They sew doll clothes in their thinnest frocks, hair pinned in pug knots. Dorothy throws down her work, too sticky to sew another stitch today. A porch party, a little bungalow, fog, and a sailing party fill the summer. A fire, a Boston trip, a bazar, and Old North Church follow them.
41653-seven-short-plays:
Lady Gregory wrote seven short plays, issued in New York and London in 1916 and dedicated to W B Yeats. She offers him a play for every night of the week. The set opens with Spreading the News and Hyacinth Halvey. The Rising of the Moon and The Jackdaw follow.

The Workhouse Ward, The Travelling Man, and The Gaol Gate complete the seven. Copyright dates run from 1903 to 1909. A notice reserves all acting rights and directs would be performers to Samuel French. Gregory's plays draw on Irish speech and village life. The short forms suit small stages and amateur companies as well as the Abbey stage.
4202-quotations-from-diary-of-samuel-pep:
A book of quotations from Samuel Pepys's diary gathers his most vivid lines, shorn of dates and context. Upon a small temptation, one line admits, he could be false to her, while another frets at his wife's neglect in leaving her scarf.

Waked between four and five by his blackbird, vexed by maids, and over head and ears in getting his house up, Pepys speaks in fragments that still sound whole. The collection suits readers who want Pepys in small bites, for browsing or for finding a line to carry away. It offers the diary's flavor without its full bulk.
42382-the-wilderness-castaways:
Dillon Wallace wrote this boys tale of castaways in the Labrador wilds. McClurg printed the book in Chicago, first in 1913, here in 1936. Henry Watson drew the plates of hunts, camps, and river trips. Chapter one brings Dan Rudd under Captain Bluntt sharp tongue at sea.

Contents promise a first bear, a husky camp, and a ship wreck. Castaways drift on an ice pan and face starvation in cold. A death struggle, a lonely Christmas, and wolf stalks follow in turn. Paul and Dan at last reach Winnipeg and make good there.
42946-live-toys:
Live Toys is a book of true tales of pets for young readers. Emma Davenport wrote it, and Harrison Weir drew the plates. It came out in London in the year 1862 in fine form. The tales are those of the pets of a boy and a girl.

The book is given to a kind friend of the two young ones. The first pet the writer calls to mind is a big white rabbit. It was kept when the two were small, by the sea. A pony, two small birds, and a parrot have tales of their own. Each tale is short and tells what the pet did in the home. The tales were meant to be read aloud to the young.
42975-medi-val-byways:
Mediaeval Byways is a set of studies of the lighter side of the Middle Ages by Salzmann. Houghton Mifflin issued the book in 1913 with pictures by George Kruger. Salzmann had written on English industries of the Middle Ages before this volume. A dedication jokes that his wife lightens his own middle age with her care.

Forewords admit that record office research looks dull to polite friends of the author. Yet old legal papers hide jokes, feuds, and odd customs worth the digging. Church courts, manors, and town life supply the byways of the title here. Readers who fear dry history gain a merry door into medieval England.
43102-the-rope-of-gold-a-mystery-story-f:
Roy Snell wrote The Rope of Gold, a mystery story for boys, for Reilly and Lee in 1929. Rights date from that year. Chapter one, The Dangling Ladder, opens at night on a mountainside in Haiti. Far below, the valleys are lost in darkness. The massive fortress called the Citadel hangs like a cliff above a boy. Hot from climbing, he throws himself on moss at the foot of a mahogany tree.

Even three thousand feet above the sea, Haiti is hot and dry, he thinks. Then he stares: a ladder dangles from a small, dark opening in the fortress wall. It hangs some forty feet up the sheer face above him. Contents promise native drums, a hidden pitfall, a voodoo drum, and a jeweled monkey. A chest of secrets, a queen's ruby, and a battling giant fill the close.
43144-scamp-and-i-a-story-of-city-by-way:
Meade wrote this tale of London by-ways for young readers, and Shaw printed this edition in 1891. Scamp and I opens at the height of the London season of 1875. I'd Choose to Be a Queen heads the first chapter.

Parks, streets, and shops crowd with pleasure seekers in the first scene. Garden parties, operas, and theatres fill the rich world's round. Regent Street, Piccadilly, and Eaton Square shine with wealth. Money seems the one god of that bright world, the tale says. Against that gloss Meade sets her young cast and the dog Scamp, in the back streets where the poor live their own full lives.
43263-the-arrow-of-fire-a-mystery-story-:
The Arrow of Fire, a mystery story for boys by Roy Snell, was published at Chicago in 1930 by the Reilly and Lee Company. Thirty-three chapters run from The Squad Call through a running battle, talking in the dark, and mysterious violence, to The Show-Down. Johnny Thompson stands at the center of the tale.

Chapter one opens at midnight. The waters of Lake Michigan are like smooth blue-black glass, the stars burning queer bright holes in it. A long, low freighter glides with scarce a ripple, and at the prow stands Johnny Thompson, gazing at the skyline of his beloved city. Three years have passed since he last heard its rumble and saw its lights. Now he glides slowly forward toward mystery and romance. Snell's pages fill with clues, shots, a card from the underworld, and a secret number.
43293-the-secret-cache-an-adventure-and-:
The Secret Cache is an adventure and mystery story for boys by Brill, issued at New York in 1932. A pictured caption shows a boy looking back just in time, as one of the giants springs up out of the rocks. Brill's two other northern tales are listed with it in the series. The contents open with a letter written on birch bark.

A sloop called the Otter, a drive before the gale, and an island in the great lakes follow in the early heads. A half breed brother, a blood stained tunic, and a giant Iroquois carry the tale onward. A fire lit orgy, a hungry porcupine, and a painted thwart vary the run. The rift in the rock and the cache come at the middle, then a sealed packet and a fleeing canoe. Brill sets his boys among the lakes and old fur trade country of the north.
43556-i-mary-maclane-a-diary-of-human-da:
I, Mary MacLane is a diary of human days by Mary MacLane, printed in New York in 1917. MacLane had won fame with The Story of Mary MacLane. She writes in the first person, in short, hot bursts, from Butte in Montana.

The book opens on a dark July night, with gray hills and a low sky. MacLane says she meets herself face to face, with hate, despair, and keen watch. She calls herself rare, vain, false, and deeply herself, and sets herself in a pot of her own making to be tried. The diary aims to show the woman inside her in full detail. Readers meet one of the boldest self portraits of her age, frank and strange by turns.
436-the-master-key-an-electrical-fairy-t:
L. Frank Baum gives a boy inventor three electrical gifts in this fairy tale of early science. Rob, keen on batteries and motors, meets a Demon of Electricity who grants him devices for travel, food, and force. Rob tests them on cannibal isles, pirate ships, and foreign courts, learning their limits as he goes.

Baum frames the tale as a wonder that may soon prove true, since yesterday's marvels become today's tools. Rob saves a republic, serves a king, and at last gives up his treasures by choice. The book charms as a bright, hopeful story of science as magic for a new century.
43714-the-boy-spies-with-the-regulators-:
The Boy Spies with the Regulators, by James Otis, tells how two boys helped the Carolina patriots drive the British from that state. A L Burt of New York published it under a copyright of 1901. The narrators are Sidney Hubbard and his cousin Clare Butler, who tells the tale in the first person and makes no pretense at a scholar's story.

The boys lived in 1768 on the Alamance, near the ground where the first battle of the colonies' struggle was later fought. A frontispiece shows Sandy looking around to see Sidney standing with his rifle aimed, resting on a tree branch. Chapters run through a treasonable act, a rescue, a stay at Brunswick, a siege, and Tryon's demonstration. A trial, a proclamation, declared war, a convoy, and the battle close the book. Otis wrote history as boys' adventure.
43853-the-galloping-ghost-a-mystery-stor:
A boys' mystery novel by Roy J Snell, published at Chicago in 1933. The Reilly and Lee Company held the copyright. Red Rodgers is the young hero. Thirty-three chapters race from Kidnapper's Island to a football finish. The flea flicker and seventy thousand witnesses close the contents. Sport and detection share the plot throughout.

Red wakes on a vibrating floor, deafened by motors. Silence then seems total, and panic rises in him. A wild, mad, hilarious laugh pierces the quiet. At least he is not stone deaf, he tells himself. The laugh was almost human, but not quite. Red is a city boy, and the wild places are sealed books to him. Isle Royale, moose riding, and a branded bullet await.
43904-mystery-wings-a-mystery-story-for-:
Mystery Wings is a mystery story for boys by Roy Snell, published by Reilly and Lee of Chicago in 1935. Johnny Thompson is its hero.

A wrinkled stranger accosts Johnny in a park at dusk: pardon, my young friend. His drawl reassures the boy, who sits down again. The stranger reads him: he thinks hard, he worries, he thinks baseball. The town and its team are everything to Johnny, he says. Chapter titles promise a thought camera, Johnny's think-o-graphs, and a place of magic. A mystery ship, strange passengers, and a green-eyed dragon follow. Baseball returns with a steel-fingered pitcher and a flying ball team. Ether and moth-balls, liquid air, and a smoke screen close the tale.
44031-the-talisman-a-tale-for-boys:
The Talisman is a tale for boys, put out at Boston in eighteen twenty nine. Its front is a form of law: the writ of the clerk of the shire. That writ tells the day the title of the book was laid in the clerk's desk. It tells the act of the land by which the right in the book was held. A plate past the title leaf shows a group at the first spring of a boat.

The tale starts with a boy named Frank. Frank had heard a great deal of the town, the tale says, but he had never seen it. For he lived more than a mint of miles from New York. He lived still more far from Boston than that.
44094-civilisation-its-cause-and-cure-an:
Edward Carpenter wrote Civilisation: Its Cause and Cure, published by George Allen and Unwin in London. The title essay first appeared in 1889, and edition followed edition until this complete one of 1921. Carpenter, the author of Towards Democracy, argues that civilisation itself is a kind of disease of society, with a cause that can be found and a cure that can be imagined.

Eight other essays share the volume. Carpenter criticises modern science and forecasts the science of the future. A defence of criminals questions the morality that punishes them. Lamarck is set against Darwin in a paper on exfoliation, and custom, humane science, and the new morality each get an essay. An appendix describes pre-civilised peoples. The book made Carpenter a prophet of the simple life for readers who doubted industrial England.
44154-swatty-a-story-of-real-boys:
Swatty, a Story of Real Boys, by Ellis Parker Butler, was printed by Houghton Mifflin in 1920. Butler gives the book to Fred Ernst Schmidt of Muscatine, Iowa, the faithful companion of his boyhood. The tale is told by one of the boys himself.

The narrator chums with Swatty and Bony along the big river. He opens with a thought on school lickings, and how teachers might lick less if they knew how things turn out. Miss Murphy, a good looker yet a tartar with the rod, means to lick Swatty. The narrator sister Fan is engaged to Swatty brother Herb and loves to tease the boys, then slip them a dime. Boys and grown readers get river town fun in true boy voice.
44341-minimum-gauge-railways:
Minimum Gauge Railways, by Sir Arthur Percival Heywood, treats the fifteen inch gauge line. A third edition was printed for private circulation in the author lifetime. It tells the origin and growth of the line at Duffield Bank near Derby. A similar line at Eaton Hall near Chester gets its own account in the book.

Objects of the fifteen inch gauge opens the contents after the introduction. Construction of the Duffield Bank line and details of the Eaton Hall line follow. Locomotives, then wagons and cars, fill the middle chapters of the work. The Duffield Bank workshops and scientific considerations come next in the list. Remarks on narrow gauge railways and an appendix close the contents. An estate toy that hauled real loads argues for tiny railways in earnest.
44352-the-shadow-passes-a-mystery-story-:
Roy J Snell wrote The Shadow Passes, a mystery story for boys set in Alaska. The Reilly and Lee Company issued the book in Chicago in nineteen hundred thirty eight. Johnny Thompson leads its young cast of seekers. Blackie, a tale teller of Matanuska Valley, opens the book.

Boys crowd the store stove at night for Blackie’s wild tales. A shadow craft that glides in fog with no sound tops them all. His fast boat roared in chase and may have cut it in two. Too swift for a whale, he swears, and too sly for plain craft. Some eastern boat, he guesses, haunts the salmon runs in May. Crutches by his chair will go by spring, he vows to the boys. Coast Guard work calls him back to speed and open sea. Silver fox hunts and blue bear caves fill the boys’ own chase.
44418-italian-days-and-ways:
Italian Days and Ways is a travel book by Anne Hollingsworth Wharton. The third edition came out in 1906, with eight plates. Much of the book is cast as letters from the road.

The route starts at Genoa, which she calls La Superba, and runs along the Riviera. Rome takes up a large share, with the Via Appia and the great churches. Later letters reach Assisi, Florence and Fiesole. Small mishaps, such as being captured by a cabman, keep the tone light. The book gives a warm, close view of Italian towns and daily life. Photos by Dr Bertha Lewis show the Bay of Naples and the road to Paestum.
44586-diplomatic-days:
Edith O'Shaughnessy, author of A Diplomat's Wife in Mexico, wrote this illustrated account of her years in Mexico, published by Harper and Brothers in November 1917. The contents begin with first impressions of the tropics, the shipboard journey by Havana and Vera Cruz, and the climb up to Mexico City, eight thousand feet high.

The chapters then follow the revolution as a diplomat's wife saw it: Diaz's resignation wrung from him, President de la Barra sworn in, and a first reception at Chapultepec Castle. Madero's triumphal march, three days of adoration, a first bull-fight, and a typical earthquake fill the early pages. Later chapters give the Grito de Dolores ceremony, the election of Madero, the Day of the Dead, and first glimpses of Zapata and General Huerta. Dinners at legations and notes on Mexican housekeeping fill out the picture.
44844-the-evolution-of-culture-and-other:
The Evolution of Culture and Other Essays is a set of anthropological essays by the late General Pitt-Rivers, founder of the Pitt-Rivers Museum. Myres edited the volume, and Henry Balfour, the museum's curator, wrote the introduction. The Clarendon Press at Oxford published it in 1906 with twenty-one plates. Its contents gather lectures across a decade: Principles of Classification of 1874 and On the Evolution of Culture of 1875.

Three papers on Primitive Warfare, from 1867 to 1869, and Early Modes of Navigation complete the set. Balfour's introduction tells how an army officer applied lessons from his professional experiments to a far wider field. Pitt-Rivers had worked on the improvement of firearms. A passage preserved in the copy gives his key insight. He noticed the unfailing regularity of gradual change in firearms, each step a trifling improvement on the one before.
44864-coaching-days-ways:
Coaching Days and Ways is a book by Cuming in the British Sport Series, printed by Hodder and Stoughton. Armour drew the illustrations. The opening chapter treats John Palmer, who changed the coach team from three horses to four. Before Palmer, travellers were content with the unicorn team.

Palmer showed that the coach could carry letters faster and more safely than the post-boy. His Bath to London journey in 1784 ran at nearly seven miles an hour. The four-horse team then spread to almost every road in the country. Fast coaching did not wait for macadam roads, Cuming argues. A Sporting Magazine note of June 1807 records ninety miles in nine hours and four minutes on the North road.
45037-hebrew-humor-and-other-essays:
Hebrew Humour and Other Essays, by Chotzner, was printed in London in 1905. Chotzner had been Hebrew tutor at Harrow, and the book is given to his wife. The title essay leads a set of sixteen pieces on Hebrew letters and life.

Chotzner calls the Hebrew Bible the Book of Books and finds true flashes of humour in its pages. Its humour, he says, differs from the broad fun of Sterne, Cervantes, or Heine, and has a stamp of its own. Other essays treat the Bible and the ancient classics, art among the old Hebrews, and the life of Hebrew women of old. A sketch of the Talmud follows. Later pieces treat Yedaya Bedaresi, Immanuel of Rome, and the pull of Hebrew letters on Heine.
45376-the-old-world-and-its-ways:
The Old World and Its Ways is a travel book by William Jennings Bryan, printed at St Louis in 1907. It describes a tour around the world and journeys through Europe. Bryan says in his preface that the book answers many requests. Its aim is to put his observations on the old world in lasting and handy form.

More than two hundred pictures go with the text, from photographs gathered at the places visited or taken by his party. Chapters one to forty-six were written from time to time during the trip. Bryan travelled with his wife and their two younger children. The party reached San Francisco on 27 September and got home to Lincoln on 5 September 1906, sixteen days short of a year away. The book shows a famed American orator and statesman looking at the old world with a plain man's eye.
4581-the-thrall-of-leif-the-lucky-a-stor:
Ottilie A. Liljencrantz sets this Viking story in the days of Leif the Lucky, when Norse ships reached new western lands. Chapters open where wolves thrive better than lambs, then follow a maid in a silver helmet, a gallant outlaw, a Viking lair, and the ire of a shield-maiden. Leif himself appears as cross-bearer and king's guardsman, while Eric the Red holds his own domain and tales of the unknown west grow bolder.

The hero, a thrall or bondman, must win his way through courts, battles, witch dens, and voyages, with Helga's wooing and a familiar blade in a strange sheath among his trials. The closing chapters reach Vinland the Good, the green western shore the Norse sought. Readers get a stirring historical adventure for young and old, full of ships, swords, loyalty, and the hard road from bondage toward freedom.
46209-concord-days:
Concord Days, by Bronson Alcott, was published at Boston in 1872. Roberts Brothers issued the volume. Entries run by month, from April to September. April opens with diaries: Alcott comes again into his study. An open fire burns in the east room. He blames himself that his full diaries hold too little life. A boyhood sight of his mother's journal, he recalls, first set him keeping his own. The habit of the day held for life.

Short pieces fill each month like entries in a journal. Thoreau, Emerson, and Margaret Fuller appear in April and May. Hawthorne, Swedenborg, and Goethe take summer pages. Walden Pond, Plato, and Socrates close the set. The book gives Concord thought at home: quiet, bookish, and sure of the inner life.
4652-escape-and-other-essays:
Arthur Christopher Benson published Escape and Other Essays in 1915. It opens with a Thomas Gray line about people who leave traces of their journey behind them, and advises readers to do so while they can. The contents run from Escape, Literature and Life, and The New Poets. They go on to Walt Whitman, Charm, Sunset, and The House of Pengersick. Then come Villages, Dreams, The Visitant, That Other One, Schooldays, Authorship, Herb Moly and Heartsease, and Behold, This Dreamer Cometh.

Benson's introduction walks down by the river Cam, a stream slighted by lovers of wild scenery. Its chief merit for schoolboys is that it nears a canal in straightness and slow lapse, and so suits their manoeuvres. That quiet manner marks the whole book. Readers get a set of gentle essays on books, places, and moods, by a writer who finds escape in attention to a life close at hand.
47451-the-putnam-hall-rebellion-or-the-r:
The Putnam Hall Rebellion, or The Rival Runaways, is a boys' school story by Arthur Winfield, printed at New York with copyright in 1908. Grosset and Dunlap issued it. Winfield also wrote the Rover Boys series, under the same hand. This tale is the fourth in the Putnam Hall series, and complete in itself.

His introduction says the series began at readers' request. Boys and girls who loved the Rover Boys wanted to know what happened at Putnam Hall before the Rovers arrived. Thirty chapters run from target practice to a case of tit for tat. Pepper plays a joke, blank cartridges turn up, and cadets are locked in the dormitories. The rebellion ends with the boys back at school.
47596-four-short-plays:
