Four Short Plays is a set of wee stage works by Lady Bell, put out at London in the early nineteen twenties. All rights were kept, and the print was made in Scotland. Its gift word makes it out to a famed stage dame of the day.

A tale of a wife comes first, in one act. A sketch in three scenes of a north girl comes next. A fun piece in one act on a fall from the sky by cloth bag takes third place. A fun piece on a duke of the second class closes the set. The first play sets its cast at the front: a sea chief of near fifty and his wife of half his years, in their snug draw room.
48378-fireplaces-and-chimneys:
Farmers Bulletin Number 1889, Fireplaces and Chimneys, came from the United States Department of Agriculture at Washington. The bulletin takes the place of Bulletin 1649 on the same theme. A first line notes that hearth means home in many tongues. Much of home and camp joy centres on an open fire, it says.

The book aims to give home folk and builders a working grasp of sound rules. It treats how to plan and build hearths and chimneys that draw well and stay safe. A well built hearth can heat one room, or two with a heat unit. Looks count too, the text says. A good chimney still needs care and repair in time. The rules suit farm homes most of all.
48823-spies-and-secret-service-the-story:
Spies and Secret Service: The Story of Espionage, Its Main Systems and Chief Exponents is a survey by Hamil Grant, published in London in 1915. A portrait of Fouché, Napoleon's police minister, fronts the book. The first chapter treats the ethos of the spy. It argues that spies are always with us, from prehistoric ages onward, and weighs what makes an efficient spy.

The second chapter follows the spy through the ages. Spies in the Bible, the stratagems of Frontinus, and the carrier-pigeons of the ancients appear. Hannibal and Caesar used spies, and Frederick the Great is named the real founder of modern espionage. Napoleon and his leniency toward spies close the survey. The third chapter turns to Le Caron, the famous Fenian spy. Its contents trace his alias, his work in Paris, and his part in the Fenian movement and the invasion of Canada.
49061-rambles-on-railways:
Rambles on Railways is Sir Cusack P Roney's tour of the railway world, with maps, diagrams, and appendices. Effingham Wilson of London published it in 1868. A long preface of corrections shows the book's character: figures checked, names mended, and the Board of Trade returns waited for.

Roney substitutes for his early pages an exact analysis of the railway capital of the United Kingdom at the end of 1865. The total ordinary capital stood at £219,598,196. Traffic receipts and net earnings for 1865 come under the same care, with the dividends on unguaranteed capital reckoned better than he first assumed. Even small facts are set right: Australian railways at 669 miles, not 480, and empty cabs do pass through the Euston portico. The ramble is a Victorian stocktaking of the steam network in money and miles.
49064-inventing-for-boys:
Inventing for Boys, by A Frederick Collins, teaches young readers how to turn ideas into working inventions and patents. Collins was the inventor of the wireless telephone. Frederick A Stokes published the book in New York in 1916, with many pictures and diagrams.

A word to the boy opens the case: every boy is a born inventor. Collins calls inventing the most fascinating game a fellow can take up, better than wireless, baseball, or chess, because it builds something from nothing. He walks the reader from the first rough sketch to the finished machine in wood and steel. Then he turns to the sordid part, as he jokes: making money from the thing. The book is dedicated to his son, John Roller Collins, a thinker of new and novel thoughts.
4917-the-kellys-and-the-o-kellys:
Anthony Trollope's novel of the Kellys and the O'Kellys opens amid the excitement of Dublin's State Trials in early 1844. O'Connell, his son, repeal newspaper editors, Tom Steele, and Father Tierney stand indicted for conspiracy, and the city follows every proceeding with absorbing interest.

Against that political backdrop, the Kellys and O'Kellys pursue love, money, and family standing in an Ireland stirred by the Repeal movement. Trollope mixes courtroom drama with domestic comedy. Readers get a Victorian Irish novel where public agitation and private ambition keep colliding, told with Trollope's usual patience for character.
49170-summer-days:
Summer Days is a girls’ story issued at New York by Dodd, Mead in 1880, with pictures. It opens on the fifteenth day of June, the last day of school. Alice Grey has just said her last good byes to the other girls. On her homeward way she hears a voice behind her calling her name.

Susy Lee runs up, begging her friend to wait a minute. Let us go on together, says Susy, there is no use in walking alone. Alice laughs and asks to creep under Susy’s big sun umbrella. The one has an umbrella and the other has none, in her teasing. Vacation, friendship, and small adventures fill such a summer tale. Books of this kind were the standard holiday reading of schoolgirls.
4922-bar-20-days:
Clarence E. Mulford's Bar-20 Days sends two tired but happy punchers into a coast town on an errand from their boss Buck, and the pleasures of town life soon overtake the business. Horses stabled and sleeping quarters arranged, the cowboys set out to enjoy what a small city can offer two active young men.

A voice hailing them as cow-wrestlers opens the first of many scrapes, and Mulford keeps the humor rough and good-natured. The stories belong to the Bar-20 ranch world, where loyalty to the outfit matters more than any single adventure. Readers get short, sunny western tales about work, play, and the code of the range.
49488-the-history-of-the-2nd-dragoons-ro:
Edward Almack wrote The History of the Second Dragoons, Royal Scots Greys, issued in London in nineteen eight. Forty four illustrations fill the book. Lady Butler Scotland for Ever fronts it, by kind permission of the artist. A long list of subscribers opens the volume. Aberdeen University Library stands first among them. Officers of the regiment fill page after page of the list.

Lieutenant E H Bonham and Lieutenant M Borwick of the Royal Scots Greys subscribed, the list shows. Major C B Bulkeley Johnson and Major W F Collins subscribed too. Captain H R H Prince Arthur of Connaught appears among the names. The Army and Navy Stores of London also took a copy. Military readers get a subscription regimental history of the famed Scots cavalry, famous for the charge at Waterloo.
4953-revolution-and-other-essays:
Jack London's Revolution and Other Essays opens with a letter from Arizona signed Yours for the Revolution, and London answers in kind, counting hundreds of thousands of American socialists behind the greeting. The title essay argues that revolution is not a distant dream but a movement already numbering its adherents.

Other essays follow on the planet's linkage, the house beautiful, gold hunters of the North, the Yellow Peril, and what life means to the author. London writes as a propagandist and a storyteller at once, blunt and vivid. Readers get the socialist London at full stretch, before the novels made his name a household word.
49906-the-daft-days:
The Daft Days, a novel by Neil Munro, came out in a shilling edition from William Blackwood and Sons in 1909. Munro also wrote John Splendid and The Lost Pibroch, tales of the Highlands. Press praise at the front ranks him among the few novelists whose work counts as literature.

The tale opens on a winter morning at New Year time. The town bell rings with queer jolts and pauses, as if Wanton Wully Oliver, the ringer, had been jovial the night before. The narrator calls it a blithe, daft, scatter brained bell, with no solemn reminders in its tune. That cheery note sets the key for a Scots tale of the daft days round the New Year.
50284-boyville-a-history-of-fifteen-year:
Boyville is a history of fifteen years' work among newsboys by John Gunckel, published by the Toledo Newsboys' Association in Ohio. The book was copyrighted in 1905 and is dedicated to the newsboys of America and their friends. Its frontispiece shows the president talking to the newsboys.

The book is built in seven parts and forty chapters. That scale suits its subject: not one season of charity but fifteen years of organised work with the boys who sold papers on city streets. Gunckel's association in Toledo gave those boys a centre, and the record follows the building of that work part by part. Illustrations run through the volume. Boyville is at once a memoir of reform, a report to supporters, and a portrait of the newsboy's world at the start of the twentieth century.
50596-quinneys:
Quinneys is a novel by Horace Annesley Vachell, first published by John Murray in May 1914. The edition history at its front lists reprint after reprint through the war years to March 1917. It is dedicated to Cyril Maude, the actor manager of that age. Contents divide the tale into two books of nine and more chapters.

Book one opens with The Sign, The Dream Cottage, and The Pleasant Land of France. The Installation, Susan Prepares, and The Visitor Arrives move the household into place. Book two begins with Bludgeonings, a sharp turn in tone for the story. The novel turns on the Quinney firm of antique dealers and the faked and genuine treasures of that trade. Its long reprint run through the war shows how a tale of shops, cottages, and connoisseurship held readers far from the trenches.
5060-six-short-plays:
John Galsworthy's Six Short Plays gathers one-act and short dramas, opening on a November evening in Keith Darrant's study. The room is large and dark-curtained. A single reading lamp falls on Turkey carpet and books beside an armchair. A deep blue-and-gold coffee service makes an oasis before a log fire. Darrant sleeps there in Turkish slippers and an old velvet coat.

A curtained door opens softly, and Larry Darrant enters, half lost in the curtain, thin and worn. The short form suits Galsworthy's compressed conflicts of family and conscience. Readers get six compact plays, each a single situation pressed to its turning point, ideal for an evening's reading.
50800-bimmie-says:
Bimmie Says is a science fiction story by Sydney Van Scyoc, first printed in Galaxy Magazine in October nineteen sixty two. Its narrator keeps a diary at the order of her young husband Bimmie. Bimmie says people are stupid and that he can help them, the opening repeats. He wants the diary kept for when he is famous.

The entry is dated June twenty seventh, nineteen eighty two, in a future of scarcity. The narrator is sixteen, short and a good cook, and wed just twenty two days. Bimmie is eighteen, tall and skinny, and hungry. She has barely seen a book, yet must write one. A post collapse marriage frames a tale of brains and need.
5085-characters-of-shakespeare-s-plays:
William Hazlitt's criticism, first published in 1817, takes Shakespeare's plays one by one. It asks what makes each leading figure live on the page and stage. Julius Caesar, Timon, Antony and Cleopatra, Hamlet, Falstaff, Lear, and many others receive short, forceful essays that judge character, motive, and language together.

Hazlitt writes as a reader and theatregoer, not a scholar of sources, and his enthusiasm made the book a model for later Shakespeare criticism. Anyone wanting to read the plays with sharper eyes will find here a lively guide, opinionated and quotable. It treats the characters as people to be understood rather than puzzles to be solved.
50915-the-connecticut-wits-and-other-ess:
The Connecticut Wits and Other Essays, by Henry Beers, professor of English literature emeritus at Yale, was published at New Haven in 1920 by the Yale University Press. The essays are reprints from the Yale Review. The volume was the first published on the Oliver Baty Cunningham Memorial Publication Fund. The fund honors a Yale man of the class of 1917 who fell as a captain of field artillery.

Eleven essays make the book. The title essay treats the Connecticut Wits, the Hartford poets of the early republic. Others take up the singer of the Old Swimmin' Hole, Emerson's journals, and the art of letter writing. Thackeray's centenary, the English drama, Sheridan, the Cavalier poets, Cowley, and Milton's tercentenary follow. A last essay treats Shakespeare's contemporaries. Beers writes as a Yale man of letters on English and American themes.
51596-aloys:
Lafferty wrote this short tale of Professor Aloys, a man of brief great fame. The tale ran in Galaxy Magazine in August 1961. Aloys flared up more brightly than any man in memory. Then he sank from sight, though his ghost still walked.

Aloys grew up poor, in shoes part cardboard and a worn coat. The coat had been his father and grandfather before him. Fame brought an award and a hall of great men to face. Shame and dread grip him as he waits to speak there. The tale asks why such a bright star so soon went dark.
52231-little-folks-christmas-stories-and:
Ada Skinner edited this set of Christmas tales and plays for young readers. Rand McNally printed the book in Chicago and New York in 1915. A Dickens quote on Christmas as a kind, open heart time leads. The foreword stresses good will toward men and peace on earth.

Part one holds tales simple for a child to read alone at home. Part two holds harder tales for a teller to read aloud. Fun and jollity mix with the blessings of the Christ Child birth. Thanks name Maud Lindsay, Ruth Sawyer, and others who gave reprints.
52297-medical-women-two-essays:
Medical Women is a pair of essays by Sophia Jex-Blake, published at Edinburgh in 1872. The first essay treats medicine as a profession for women. The second treats the medical education of women. It is dedicated to Dr Lucy Sewall. From her daily life, Jex-Blake first learned what blessings a woman doctor may confer. A verse from Aurora Leigh heads the argument. It claims a woman's license in the work she can do.

The essays attack the easy faith that what is, is best. Customs held good in one age are held evil in another. The plea is for fixed rules of right in place of mere custom. Jex-Blake was a leader of the fight to open British medical schools to women. These essays state her case in print, with fact and reason for the public ear.
52560-the-fortune-of-the-landrays:
Vaughn Kester wrote a novel with pictures by the Kinneys, issued in New York in 1905. McClure Phillips and Company brought out The Fortune of the Landrays that year. The contents list runs past fifty chapters of road and town life. A boy and his father ride the box of a coach at the start.

The boy is sick of travel, of hot dust, noise, and like towns in a row. Freight wagons haul pork, flour, and hides north to a lake port. Traders ride south to Baltimore with Spanish dollars on pack horses. Kester paints the old road world in full before the fortune plot takes hold.
52615-the-two-marys:
Two Marys is a pair of stories by Mrs Oliphant, published by Methuen in 1896. The tales first ran in Macmillan Magazine and in Good Words for their readers. Contents give The Two Marys in two parts, then Grove Road Hampstead as companion. My Own Story opens in the voice of Mary Peveril, the first narrator.

Her father held a proprietary chapel between Holborn and the New Road in London. Wealth and comfort mix with penury and pain in those streets, she says. No grandeur and no abject misery mark the region she calls home in the tale. Oliphant quiet domestic art turns on two women of one name.
5262-curly-and-floppy-twistytail-the-fun:
Howard R. Garis's bedtime book introduces Curly and Floppy Twistytail, the funny piggie boys, in short stories for small children. The tales tell how Curly and Floppy got their names, how Curly helped his mother. He met an elephant, went to school, and was vaccinated. He played with a spinning top, a turtle, chestnuts, and a big apple.

Garis, creator of Uncle Wiggily, writes simple animal stories with gentle lessons and mild mischief. Illustrated by Louis Wisa, the book offers young listeners brief, cheerful episodes, each complete before bedtime, in the familiar world of Garis's animal families.
5264-patty-s-butterfly-days:
Carolyn Wells's Patty's Butterfly Days follows Patty and her friends through a summer of house parties, garden parties, and pageants. Chapters move from Mona's plan and Susan to the rescue, through a dinner party, Aunt Adelaide, Big Bill Farnsworth, a short spin, the worst storm ever. A welcome shelter follows, toward an apple blossom dance and a forced march.

Wells writes light, cheerful stories for girls, full of friendship, flirtation, and small adventures. The book offers a sunny portrait of American girlhood in the early twentieth century, where butterfly days are days of gaiety, freedom, and growing up.
53169-ignorant-essays:
Ignorant Essays is an anonymous book of humorous literary essays, published by Ward and Downey in London in 1887. The contents page lists eight pieces. The first is The Only Real Ghost in Fiction, followed by The Best Two Books and Lies of Fable and Allegory. My Copy of Keats, Decay of the Sublime, and A Borrowed Poet come next. The English Opium-Eater and A Guide to Ignorance close the set.

The opening essay starts with an ingenious friend's question. Would you be richer if you had the ghost of sixpence, or if you had not the ghost of sixpence? The friend is ready to take either side, but gives preference to the ghost. If he has not the ghost, he has nothing at all; if he has it, he is richer by a ghost.
53202-a-mechanical-account-of-poisons-in:
Richard Mead, physician to Saint Thomas's Hospital, wrote a mechanical account of poisons in several essays, here in a second edition revised with additions, printed at London in 1708. The preface says an exact account of how poisons act is no easy matter. Yet their effects, Mead argues, can be shown to follow from more than bare heat or cold.

Mead finds the footsteps of mechanism in effects once ascribed to occult principles. He aims to trace symptoms up to their first causes. The task is hard, he says, because the animal machine is finely made. The minute bodies of poisons can force sudden, violent changes in it. The essays mark early toxicology.
53348-some-irish-yesterdays:
Somerville and Martin Ross, authors of The Real Charlotte and Some Experiences of an Irish Resident Magistrate, gathered these Irish sketches. Somerville illustrated them, and Longmans, Green and Company published the book in 1906. The pieces first appeared in magazines, and the authors thank the editors for leave to reprint them.

Fourteen sketches make the contents: An Outpost of Ireland, Picnics, Boon Companions, The Biography of a Pump, Hunting Mahatmas, and A Patrick's Day Hunt among them. The book closes with Slipper's ABC of Fox-Hunting. The first sketch belongs to Miss Gerraghty, who serves tables in a Galway lodging-house though nature meant her for a lady. Her visitors get a list of bath holidays, Twelfth Day now added. Her own private list seems one infinite bath holiday, and she denounces them thrash of baths to the kitchen audience. Pictures of Aran fishermen and Connemara fill the plate list.
53524-a-persian-pearl-and-other-essays:
Clarence S Darrow wrote A Persian Pearl and Other Essays, issued in Chicago by C L Ricketts in MDCCCCII, with a copyright of eighteen ninety nine. Five essays fill the book. A Persian Pearl stands first, at page nine. Essays on Walt Whitman and on Robert Burns follow. Realism in Literature and Art and The Skeleton in the Closet close the volume.

Darrow opens by noting that readers are ever reminded there is nothing new under the sun. A rare gem of thought, he says, often proves an old diamond polished anew. The rich mine where it was first found soon lay spent, but the gem shines on as common property. He calls Nature the great communist for that sharing of genius gifts. He then notes a rise of a pessimistic school in current books. Readers get Darrow in a humane, musing vein, far from the courtroom.
53602-a-taxicab-tangle-or-the-mission-of:
A Taxicab Tangle is a boys' story by Stanley Matthews, issued in 1909. It appeared as number 362 of the Brave and Bold Weekly. Street and Smith published the five-cent paper in New York. The heroes are Motor Matt and his chum Joe McGlory. The frontispiece shows a surprise beside a taxicab. Long yellow hair streams from the fallen Granger's head.

The first chapter opens with a letter and a surprise. The boys have spent five days touring New York by motor. Coney Island, Tarrytown, and Fort Lee mark their range. A power boat showed them the bay and the sound. Matt, raised in the Berkshires, pilots his cowboy partner. Dime weeklies of this kind ran on speed and novelty. The motor car was the new marvel of the hour. Matthews built a series on that craze.
53705-harper-s-outdoor-book-for-boys:
Harper and Brothers issued an outdoor book for boys in 1907 as part of a crowded practical list. The front matter advertises the house's Tell Me How books: gasoline engines, aircraft, wireless, and electricity. A practical series adds books for young gardeners and naturalists. Boating, camping and scouting, machinery, and indoor books complete the shelf.

A handy book for girls balances the boys' line. The outdoor book taught camping, woodcraft, and open air skills to its readers. Such how to volumes were Harper's answer to the new century's boy culture. They sold competence: engines, boats, camps, and tools explained for beginners.
54116-castle-blair-a-story-of-youthful-d:
Castle Blair is a children's novel by Flora L Shaw, issued by D C Heath of Boston in 1902 with an introduction by Mary A Livermore. John Ruskin praised it in words printed at the front. He called its child the best description of a noble child he had ever read.

Livermore's introduction sets the scene in Ireland. A bachelor uncle makes a home at Castle Blair for his brother's children. Their father serves in India, and the children arrive untrained and lawless. An orphaned niece from France, older than her cousins, keeps the house. Her motto is peace on earth and good will toward men. His agent Plunkett, hard and disagreeable, manages the estate. The first chapter opens on a rainy night, the hall door blazing with firelight. Children dance in the golden mist at the doorway.
5428-a-defence-of-poetry-and-other-essay:
Percy Bysshe Shelley, the English Romantic poet, argues for the power of poetry and the imagination in this collection of essays. The title essay, A Defence of Poetry, stands beside shorter pieces on love, life, a future state, the punishment of death, metaphysics, morals, and the literature and manners of the Athenians. A piece on Plato's Symposium rounds out the volume.

Shelley opens On Love by asking what love and life even are, then builds toward his larger claim that poets shape how societies perceive the world. Readers get Shelley's philosophy in short form: bold, idealistic, and often lyrical. It suits anyone who wants the poet's mind beyond his verse.
54294-charlie-codman-s-cruise-a-story-fo:
Charlie Codman's Cruise is a sea story for boys by Horatio Alger. Hurst and Company published it in New York. Its preface says the author wrote a story of the sea at the wish of his young friends. It is the third volume of his Campaign Series, after the tales of Frank Frost and Paul Prescott.

Charlie faces trials severer than those of the earlier heroes, the preface promises. He meets them with the same manly spirit and the same resolve to be faithful to duty at all hazards. Alger owns that a landsman may blunder in sea matters. His boys' books taught that pluck and honesty carry a poor boy through storm and shipwreck alike.
54455-light-science-for-leisure-hours-a-:
Richard Proctor wrote Light Science for Leisure Hours, here in a new edition of 1886. Longmans, Green and Company published the book in London. The subtitle calls it a series of familiar essays. Their subjects are science and natural phenomena.

Proctor's first preface states his rule plainly. He would present science in a light, readable form. He would keep exact hold of the facts all the same. He explains as he would wish others to explain new things to him. Later prefaces track the book's changes across editions. An essay on Britain's coal cellars was added. Two essays urging government aid to science were cut. Proctor had changed his mind, fearing more mischief than gain from such aid. The fifth edition removes only what new research proved wrong.
54672-les-bijoux-indiscrets-or-the-indis:
Denis Diderot's first novel hides behind a playful false imprint in this English edition of seventeen forty nine, falsely claiming translation from the Congese and printing at Monomotapa. Its scene is the court of Mangogul, sultan of Congo, an idle monarch at Banza.

A genius gives Mangogul a magic ring. Turned on a woman, it forces her private jewel to speak the truth about her love life. Trial follows trial at court: at the altars, at a private supper, at play, at the opera, among devout ladies and lapdogs. Diderot uses the bawdy device to mock court manners, false devotion, and the science of the Banza academy, whose sittings fill two chapters. The book is a libertine satire of the French court in African dress, clever, indecent, and aimed at targets its first readers were meant to recognize.
55142-rough-and-ready-or-life-among-the-:
Rough and Ready is a boys tale by Horatio Alger, book four of the Ragged Dick set. Its next name calls it life among the New York news boys in full. A Philadelphia house of Coates brought out this form of the tale. The tale first ran in parts in the Schoolmate, a youth sheet of its day. Two past books of the set ran in that same sheet, the note says.

Alger long list of sets crowds the front leaves of the book. Ragged Dick, match boy Mark, and the Tattered Tom set head that list. Campaign, luck, and pluck sets follow in the same stout mold. Brave and bold, Pacific, and Atlantic sets crowd the last ranks. Each set runs to three or four small cloth books of like kind.
55769-robert-greene-six-plays:
Six plays of Robert Greene fill a school set with an essay and notes. Thomas Dickinson edited the set for a known stage text line. The book came out in London and New York in nineteen hundred and nine. A portrait of Greene from an old print fronts the volume.

The plays run from a king tale and a London glass to a friar romp. One play tells of a green clad pinner who aids a Scots king. The lead essay sorts Greenes pamphlet wars from his stage work in tone. It finds his late street tales bold, harsh, and close to their low world. That same split marks his plays as the stage moved toward home drama.
5618-six-plays:
Florence Henrietta Darwin wrote Six Plays, country plays collected in a 1921 Cambridge edition with an introduction by Cecil Sharp and a memoir and portrait of the author. The six plays, sold in paper covers, are Lovers' Tasks, Bushes and Briars, and My Man John. Princess Royal, The Seeds of Love, and The New Year follow, with the middle two bound together.

Sharp introduces them as country plays, rooted in English rural life, song, and custom. Darwin writes for village stages, with folk feeling and plain speech. Readers get a charming set of short plays, suitable for reading aloud or performing, from a writer close to the folk-song revival.
56758-anton-tchekhov-and-other-essays:
Anton Tchekhov, and Other Essays is a book of criticism by Leon Shestov, rendered from the Russian by Koteliansky and Murry. Maunsel and Company published it at Dublin and London in 1916. The title essay, on Tchekhov, is subtitled Creation from the Void. A line from Baudelaire stands as its motto, bidding the heart resign itself and sleep.

Shestov opens by saying Tchekhov is dead, so men may now speak freely of him. Critics, he charges, kept to commonplace and stock phrases while the writer lived. The other essays treat the gift of prophecy, penultimate words, and the theory of knowledge. The contents page also lists Shestov's earlier books, including his study of Dostoevsky and Nietzsche.
56939-making-tin-can-toys:
Edward Thatcher, instructor of metal working at Teachers College, Columbia University, from 1904 to 1919, wrote a book on making tin can toys, printed at Philadelphia and London in 1919. His wife Isabel Thatcher made the drawings and painted his models. An army truck built wholly from used tin cans stands in a picture. A former pupil's letter opens the book in praise.

She ran a Red Cross workshop for patients at a nerve hospital in France, and the shop began work the day after she arrived. Their first need was a charcoal furnace to heat the soldering coppers. It was made from two large square tins with an interlining of brick, and a bit of old grate completed it. Toys, carts, boats, and stoves follow in set lessons. Waste tin becomes playthings and therapy at once.
57523-confidential-chats-with-boys:
Confidential Chats with Boys, by William Lee Howard, a doctor, was printed in New York in 1911. Howard also wrote Plain Facts on Sex Hygiene and a matching book for girls. The talks grew out of sessions at boys clubs and prep schools. He says many grown men fail from bad early training, not from lack of gifts. Fathers, he argues, often gave money and little else.

Chapters treat the body as a machine, the skin, and how life begins. Later talks cover care of self at puberty, night emissions, and bad habits. Quacks get a sharp warning. A chapter on choice of work and one on disease close the book. Howard writes in a plain, direct tone for boys and parents.
57558-walking-essays:
Walking Essays is a book of essays on walking by Sidgwick, published in London by Edward Arnold in 1912. The book is dedicated, in long comic verse, to the companions who walked with the author on hill and plain. The dedication begs their pardon and insists that a tale of walks should not go unrecorded.

The verses set out the walker's creed that the essays develop. Against the hard high road, Sidgwick sets the path that twists at will through wood and field and up the hill. Walking, for Sidgwick, is a way of seeing: the rhythm of striding mends the soul. The essays grew out of real walks with real companions, and the dedication's mix of apology and gratitude gives the book its tone.
57673-the-garden-god-a-tale-of-two-boys:
Garden God, a tale of two boys, is a novel by Forrest Reid, in a second impression of 1906. David Nutt published the book in London from Long Acre that year. Reid earlier work, The Kingdom of Twilight, is named at its front for the reader. 

Reid dedicates the book to Henry James, as a slight token of respect and admiration in his words. Two boys and their friendship in an Irish country house form the centre of the story. Reid wrote of boyhood with a delicacy that made him a writers writer in his generation. The Garden God of the title broods over a garden where the friendship flowers and fades in one summer. Henry James admiration for the young Ulster novelist helped the book find its first readers among those who prize tone and nuance above event in fiction.
58755-a-lost-leader-a-tale-of-restoratio:
Dorothea Townshend wrote A Lost Leader, a tale of Restoration days, put out by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge at London. Harold Piffard drew the plates, and the front plate shows Astbury facing a great horse pistol. The prologue asks, under which king, on a December evening in 1648 at Farnham. Troopers fill the town, and crowds stare at steel-coated men. A house of some rank draws the thickest press of watchers.

Chapters take up a fallen regicide, a noble foe, and the queen's return to Hunstanton. An escape, a candid minister, and the ghost of Hunstanton Place follow. Notes close the book. Townshend sets a tale of loyalty, loss, and hidden worth in the storm years that closed the Civil War. Readers get history dressed as a brisk, grave romance.
59004-burgess-unabridged-a-new-dictionar:
Gelett Burgess, author of the Goops, coins a dictionary of words he says readers have always needed. Frederick A Stokes Company issued it at New York in 1914. Herb Roth drew the cover and the pictures inside.

Each entry invents a word, then defines it in one dry line. Alibosh is a glaringly obvious falsehood. Bimp is a disappointment, a futile rage, a jilt. Blurb is praise from oneself, and that word stuck in the language. Splooch is the acme of ineptitude. Tashivate names indulgent inattention to dull chatter. The frontispiece Wowze shows a tango dancer swollen with vanity. Burgess loved word play of every kind. His joke dictionary treated slang-making as a fine art, with pictures to match.
59191-four-mystery-plays:
Four Mystery Plays, by Rudolf Steiner, came out in New York and London in 1920. Three translators shared the work, with the author's leave, and Putnam's Sons printed the book. The four plays are The Portal of Initiation, The Soul's Probation, The Guardian of the Threshold, and The Soul's Awakening.

The public, a note says, has never been let in to a staging of these plays. The English editor still gives hints of dress and scenery for readers. The first play is summed scene by scene: a debating room, Theodora's vision of the coming Christ, and Johannes in meditation among the mountains. Know thou thyself is his watchword there. Later scenes move through a rock temple and the spirit world, ending with a great mystic utterance by Benedictus.
59443-a-day-with-a-tramp-and-other-days:
A Day with a Tramp and Other Days, by Walter Wyckoff, was published in New York in 1901. Wyckoff taught political economy at Princeton and wrote The Workers. Five pieces make the book. They cover the tramp day itself and days with Iowa farmers. A stint as a section-hand on the Union Pacific follows. Work as a burro-puncher and incidents of the slums close the set.

Wyckoff explains that he wandered eighteen months as a wage-earner, from the Atlantic to the Pacific. In all that time he spent just one day in a tramp's company. His man was Farrell, an American of Irish stock. Farrell was twenty-two, six feet tall, and straight as an arrow. They met on the Rock Island Railway west of Morris, Illinois. The sketches report labor from inside, as social study.
59654-our-common-land-and-other-short-es:
Our Common Land, by Octavia Hill, was published in London in 1877. Macmillan issued the short essays that year. Eight pieces make the volume. The title essay leads, on common land. District visiting and words to volunteer visitors follow. A more excellent way of charity is the fourth. Good citizenship, open spaces, and effectual charity come next. The future of our commons closes the book. The first essay opens on a bank holiday. Crowds stream out of London by every road and train. Vans, carts, and gigs choke the ways for miles. Dust hangs over all in one dull cloud.

Yet the day gives intense enjoyment, Hill writes. Epping, Richmond, Greenwich, and Hampstead swarm with happy crowds. A mounted policeman keeps tolerable order on the drive home. Open air, she argues, is the poor man's holiday wealth.
60057-the-uses-of-diversity-a-book-of-es:
The Uses of Diversity is a book of essays by Chesterton, first issued at London in 1920. His other books crowd the front page: lives of Dickens, sets of essays, and a ballad of a white horse. The contents open on seriousness, lamp posts, and spirits. Pieces on Tennyson, Meredith, and the home life of detectives follow close behind.

The Irishman, Japan, lawyers without law, and our Latin relations fill the middle of the list. Pigs as pets and the romance of Rostand sit beside wishes and the futurists. Divorce, Mormonism, pageants, stage dress, and Christmas all get their essays before Dickens again closes the march. Chesterton's method is the same throughout: take a small or scorned thing, turn it over, and show the wonder inside it.
60167-three-plays:
A A Milne gathered three of his plays in one volume. Chatto and Windus issued Three Plays in London in 1923. The plays stand in the order they were written, the contents note states. The Great Broxopp leads, then The Dover Road, then The Truth About Blayds.

A mock review of Hamlet as a new play fronts the volume in jest. The pretend critic faults Shakespeare for killing seven or eight leads. Milne had written Mr Pim and The Red House Mystery before this set. Theater readers gain three polished, witty plays from a master of light comedy.
60226-ships-ways-of-other-days:
Ships and Ways of Other Days is a history of ships and seamanship by Keble Chatterton, printed at London by Sidgwick and Jackson in 1913. Chatterton had already written Sailing Ships and Their Story. The book holds one hundred and thirty illustrations. Some come from manuscripts in the Pepysian Library at Magdalene College, Cambridge. Others are drawn from works on the Viking age and on Venetian ships.

Thirteen chapters run from the birth of the nautical arts to the nineteenth century. Mediterranean progress and Rome and the sea come first. The Viking mariners follow, then seamanship and navigation in the middle ages. The period of Columbus leads to the early Tudor period and the Elizabethan age. The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries close the survey before the nineteenth. A glossary and an index end the volume.
60267-five-minute-sermons-volume-ii-for-:
Five-Minute Sermons, Volume II, gathers short sermons by priests of the Congregation of St Paul, published in New York in 1886. The sermons were preached at the Church of St Paul the Apostle in New York. They had already appeared weekly in the Catholic Review.

Each Sunday of the year gets three brief sermons for low masses. Advent opens the volume: the spirit of Advent, fair-weather Christians, and the total abstinence pledge. Bad company, penance, and preparation for Christmas follow. Later sermons treat the Christian home, profanity, and living up to the faith. The preface says the pieces aim to edify and stir the moral sense. Any of them can grow into a longer discourse with more stories and scripture. The volume served busy priests who needed sound, short teaching every week of the year.
6029-spring-days:
George Moore looks back on Spring Days, a book omitted from his acknowledged works after public and private criticism showed it no mercy. When Henry Vizetelly went to prison for publishing Zola, Walter Scott took over Moore's novels and reprinted all except this one, and Moore himself had lost faith in it.

All the welcome it found was a few contemptuous press paragraphs and an insolent Academy article he never saw, described by a friend in the Strand. Moore recalls dedicating the book to a great reviewer after a night of listening to him quote Greek, English, and Latin classics. The preface frames a novel returning from exile.
60866-on-the-margin-notes-and-essays:
On the Margin, notes and essays by Aldous Huxley, was copyrighted in 1923 and published in New York by Doran. A list of the author's other works names Mortal Coils, Crome Yellow, Limbo, and Leda. Twenty-seven short pieces run from Centenaries and a re-reading of Candide through Accidie, Water Music, and Pleasures, to Verhaeren, Edward Lear, Wren, Ben Jonson, and Chaucer.

A note explains that most of the essays first appeared in The Athenaeum under the title Marginalia, over the signature Autolycus. The rest ran in the Weekly Westminster Gazette, the London Mercury, and Vanity Fair. Huxley ranges widely in a few pages each: bibliophily, democratic art, polite conversation, nationality in love, and how the days draw in. The book catches the young Huxley in his essayist's mode, dry, learned, and amused.
6105-their-yesterdays:
Harold Bell Wright dedicates Their Yesterdays to Mrs. Elsbery W. Reynolds, in admiration of a motherhood that gave the race wealth of manhood in her sons and riches of womanhood in her daughter. The book opens at Relay Heights in June 1912, under Pope's lines on a child pleased with a rattle, youth with louder toys, and age with beads and prayer books.

The proem begins simply: there was a man, and it happened that this man went back into his days that were gone, again and again. An illustration shows a woman seeing her home warm with holy love in a fire's glowing heart. Wright follows memory backward, asking what yesterdays still burn in us.
6129-healthful-sports-for-boys:
Alfred Rochefort arranges Healthful Sports for Boys by season, opening in spring with marbles, how played, where and how made, games, terms, and skill. Whip tops, peg tops, kites and their practical uses, hoops, wheels, buzzers, and stilts follow, with fishing, bait, outfit, and care.

Summer brings boating and canoeing with don'ts to observe, small sail boats to make and manage, and swimming in styles, floating, diving, and water games. A chapter on things boys should know covers choosing sides in contests. Rochefort writes a practical, cheerful manual for outdoor play, season by season.
614-across-the-plains-with-other-memorie:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers travel memories and essays in this volume, arranged by a friend from papers written before his South Seas years. Across the Plains recounts an emigrant train from New York to San Francisco, crowded with bewildered folk from four ships. Later pieces treat Fontainebleau, dreams, beggars, and a Christmas sermon.

Stevenson writes with keen, personal prose, even when, as his friend notes, the lights seem turned down by sickness. The volume shows his range: reportage, reverie, and moral talk in one. It serves as a fine companion to his better-known travels, quieter yet just as true.
6141-peck-s-bad-boy-with-the-cowboys:
George W. Peck sends Peck's Bad Boy with the cowboys. The book relates amusing experiences and laughable incidents of a strenuous American boy and his Pa among cowboys and Indians in the Far West. Exciting hunts and adventures mingle with humorous situations and laugh-provoking events, fully illustrated.

The pictures promise Pa kicked by a dog and a grizzly big as a brewery horse. Three cheers for Pa follow, with squaws seeming to worship Pa, and a horse stumbling and throwing Pa over its head. A boy dinosaurus picks up a steer, the pair are captured by Curry's gang, and Pa preaches reform. Peck turns western travel into farce.
62377-alcatraz-of-the-starways:
Albert dePina and Henry Hasse wrote a space tale that ran in Planet Stories in May 1943. Venus was a world enslaved, the blurb cries. Then came a warrior princess fanning the flames of revolt. In her mind lay dread knowledge of a weapon used but once in the history of the universe.

Purple, Mark Denning almost sobbed, a purple Josmian. His hand held up a mud dripping globe the size of a baseball, iridescent in the Venusian night. The glow that bathed the endless swamp in ghastly green struck rainbows from the dark sphere. Two more of those and you're free, lower species, an ironic voice with the sweetness of a cello issued from the haze. Slaves dig magical lilies under alien masters.
62708-canal-reminiscences-recollections-:
George Bagby told tales of trips on the James River and Kanawha Canal. His book came out in Richmond in 1879. He first thought to print the tales in a news sheet, he says. Papers in hard times could pay no fee for such work, he notes. In fat years the Dispatch paid him glad cash for trifles.

Richmond folk were free and warm in those good days, he recalls. Will such days come back, he asks with a blue heart. Fear of worse trade and civil strife haunts his front words. Yet the tales at hand are of calm boats and slow days. Canal past fans get a lost road's own voice. Wit and rue mix in it.
6314-biographical-essays:
Thomas De Quincey, author of the Confessions of an English Opium Eater, opens his Biographical Essays with Shakespeare, protagonist on the great arena of modern poetry and glory of the human intellect. Born at Stratford upon Avon in 1564 and baptised on April 25, Shakespeare's birth day rests on tradition, with Malone inferring April 23. De Quincey writes with high praise and close reasoning, weighing fact against legend.

The volume sits in a series whose first book held the Confessions and Suspiria de Profundis, with a third volume of magazine papers promised. De Quincey's essays treat familiarity as a problem, for audiences seeking relaxation often banish Shakespeare, while closets and craving minds return to him. The book is criticism as biography, learned, digressive, and fond of paradox, by a writer who knew opium dreams and English prose alike.
63354-a-garden-of-girls-or-famous-school:
A Garden of Girls, or Famous Schoolgirls of Former Days is a biographical book by Concannon, published in 1914. Longmans, Green issued it at London and abroad. Its frontispiece shows Thomas More with his daughter Margaret. From his prison window they watch monks going to execution. Nine heroines fill the contents. Darlugdacha, a little schoolgirl of Brigid's Ireland, opens the set around the year 490.

A German schoolgirl saint of the Middle Ages follows her. Cecilia Gonzaga represents the Italian Renaissance at school. Margaret More carries the story to Tudor England. A schoolgirl of Saint-Cyr and two eighteenth century diarists come next. One diarist wrote in Paris; the other, Anna Green Winslow, in Boston. Lady Edward Fitzgerald's schooldays and Scott's pet Marjorie Fleming close the garden.
63454-how-to-make-sock-toys:
Pack-O-Fun issued this guide to making sock toys at home. The 1958 booklet from Park Ridge, Illinois, sells at one dollar. Over fifty toys for bazaars, gifts, shut ins, and fun fill it. All designs may be used for gifts or sale by makers.

The book is given to a monkey whose body is a sock. Reader letters in 1955 asked how to make that monkey. Nelson Knitting of Rockford held the Red Heel Sock Monkey directions. A deluge of mail forced a separate folder reprint at once. The monkey heart hides somewhere in cotton stuffing, the dedication says of the toy.
64102-flowers-from-shakespeare-s-garden-:
Flowers from Shakespeare's Garden, a posy from the plays pictured by Walter Crane, was issued by Cassell in 1909. The book is inscribed to the Countess of Warwick, whose old English garden at Easton Lodge suggested it. Each page pairs a flower speech from Shakespeare with one of Crane's pictures. Perdita's speech from The Winter's Tale opens the gathering: daffodils, dim violets, pale primroses, oxlips, and the crown-imperial. Her later distribution of hot lavender, mints, savory, and marjoram follows.

Ophelia's mad scene from Hamlet gives rosemary for remembrance, pansies for thoughts, fennel, columbines, rue, and a daisy. Oberon's bank of wild thyme, woodbine, musk roses, and eglantine comes from A Midsummer Night's Dream. Ceres speaks in The Tempest of wheat, rye, and barley in her rich leas. The result is a picture book built wholly from the flower lines of the plays.
6414-lectures-and-essays:
Thomas Henry Huxley, son of an Ealing schoolmaster and self made intellectualist, stands in his editor's note as the nineteenth century's most noteworthy thinker. His fields were biology, controversy, and pungent criticism of convention. His researches and his attacks on conventional belief probably influenced English science more than any other scientist's work. This 1908 People's Library volume gathers his lectures and essays for a general audience.

Contents run from knowledge of the causes of organic nature, past and present, through Darwin's Origin and hereditary transmission. Man's place in nature follows, with man like apes, fossil remains, and relations to lower animals. Nautilus lives from oldest formations to newest, and Loligo, the modern squid, appears in the lias barely changed. Huxley writes science as argument, clear, combative, and confident that evidence, not authority, must decide.
64325-landscape-in-history-and-other-ess:
Sir Archibald Geikie wrote Landscape in History and Other Essays, published by Macmillan at London and New York in 1905. Ten essays fill the volume. Three treat landscape directly: in history, in the imagination, and in literature. The origin of the scenery of the British Islands follows. The centenary of Hutton's Theory of the Earth and an essay on geological time come next.

The life and letters of Charles Darwin and the work of Hugh Miller have their essays. Science in education and the Roman Campagna close the set. The first essay opens on the origin and spread of the races of men. Climate and geography, Geikie argues, have shaped the branches of mankind. A country's mountains, plains, rivers, soils, and coast work on its people across ages. Geikie, a geologist, reads human history off the ground itself.
64359-spoilers-of-the-spaceways:
Spoilers of the Spaceways is a tale of war in space by W Martin. It first ran in a planet tale magazine in July of nineteen fifty three. Its tag line sends a changed Earth man to a far world of an empress. Mad men there die glad for her, the blurb warns in bold words.

The fight back starts the day a great ship from Trygon lands on Earth. Three envoys give Earth just fifteen days to yield to their world rule. Earth scorns the terms, and the fleet then crushes its weak guns fast. Lost notes leave the tale of that first claim dim in the text. Ross, the hero, wakes to a world held by the star born foe.
64592-harper-s-electricity-book-for-boys:
A practical handbook of electricity for boys by Joseph H Adams. Harper and Brothers published it in 1907. Adams wrote and illustrated the book himself. It stands second in Harper's Practical Books for Boys. A frontispiece shows Thomas Edison dictating to his graphophone. Joseph B Baker adds an explanation of electric light, heat, power, and traction. A dictionary of electrical terms closes the volume.

Early chapters explain the basics and list cheap tools. Later chapters teach the making of cells and batteries. Push-buttons, switches, and home apparatus follow. Boys of that era wired houses for bells and alarms. Wire, jars, and patience were their kit. The book treats that work as serious, learnable craft.
64692-australian-essays:
Australian Essays, by Francis W L Adams, was printed and published by William Inglis and Company of Melbourne in 1886, with Griffith, Farran and Company as London publishers. The price was two shillings and sixpence. Adams also wrote Leicester, an autobiography. He dedicates the book to Matthew Arnold, in a verse letter of glad homage sent across the sea.

Five essays and a dialogue make the contents. Melbourne and Her Civilization opens the book, and Sydney and Her Civilization answers it later. The poetry of Adam Lindsay Gordon gets a study of its own. The Salvation Army is treated as a sign of the times. An essay on culture follows. The dialogue, Dawnwards, closes the volume in six parts. Adams writes as a young colonial man of letters weighing his new country against the old.
64944-in-colonial-days:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote In Colonial Days, put out by Page at Boston. Rights were held in 1896 by one house and in 1906 by Page itself. This third impression is dated March 1911 in the front pages. Merrill drew the pictures, with color plates among them. The front plate shows personages descending toward a door in old Boston.

Plate names map the tales: Howe's masquerade, the old province house, and Randolph's portrait. An elderly gentleman, a balcony scene, and Colonel Joliffe with his granddaughter stand in the list. One title quotes a plea: the fault is none of mine, your honor. A stout man in rich and courtly attire walks another plate. The tales gather round the province house of royal governors in Boston. Hawthorne retells its legends of masks, portraits, and proud men.
65060-wit-humor-and-shakspeare-twelve-es:
Wit, Humor, and Shakspeare is a book of twelve essays by John Weiss. It came out in Boston in 1876 from Roberts Brothers. The contents set out a study of laughter and of the comic in the plays. The first essay is The Cause of Laughter, and the second Wit, Irony, Humor.

The third essay takes up Dogberry, Malvolio, Bottom, and Touchstone, with Ajax from Troilus and Cressida. Falstaff and his companions, with Americanisms, stand fourth. Hamlet stands fifth. The sixth treats the Porter in Macbeth, the Clown in Twelfth Night, and the Fool in Lear. Women and Men, with Maria, Helena, Imogen, and Constance, stands seventh. Lord Bacon and the Plays, Love in Shakspeare, and Portia stand later in the list. The book is a work of literary study from the age of Emerson.
65221-the-martians-and-the-coys:
Martians and the Coys is a comic science fiction tale by Mack Reynolds. The story ran in Imagination for June nineteen fifty one. Lem Coy hates guarding the still while Paw and the boys go feuding. He wants a shot at some Martins too, the blurb jokes in dialect.

Maw Coy climbs the south pasture fence with a bundle on her shoulder. She fords the creek where Hank old coon dog died by a boar. Revenue agents grow thick and uppity, she thinks, hunting honest still folk. She lights her pipe and scans the draw before heading up it. Paw and the boys will be hungry as hound dogs by now, she reckons.
65274-chance-love-and-logic-philosophica:
Chance, Love, and Logic is a volume of philosophical essays by Peirce, the American thinker. It stands in the International Library of Psychology, Philosophy and Scientific Method. Ogden edited that series for its London and New York publishers. Wittgenstein, Jung, and Russell appear in its lists around this book.

Peirce was by antecedents, training, and occupation a scientist above all. His father Benjamin was the great Harvard mathematician of his day. The boy was brought up, by his own favourite claim, in a laboratory. At the Lawrence Scientific School he took his formal training in science. His contributions reach from mathematical logic into many fields besides. The essays gathered under this triple title show the range of his thought. Chance, love, and logic name the poles between which his system moves.
65693-the-forgotten-man-and-other-essays:
The Forgotten Man and Other Essays gathers essays by William Graham Sumner, edited by Albert Galloway Keller. Yale University Press printed it in 1919, after Sumner's death. Keller's preface tells of the mass of notes and papers Sumner left behind. Some essays in the book are not on economic themes but were kept for their worth.

Keller also tells of a large body of manuscript from the years 1899 to 1905. In it Sumner had worked on a survey of the growth and life of human society, drawn from thousands of notes gathered over many years. The title essay gives Sumner his best known phrase for the plain citizen who pays for schemes made by others. The volume preserves the thought of a leading American sociologist and economist. His essays argue for free trade and against state meddling in the lives of working men.
6570-lectures-and-essays:
Goldwin Smith reprints papers first given as talks or set in journals, at the wish of friends who asked for back numbers they could not find. He leaves politics out on purpose, so the volume stays free of party heat, and he notes that a fuller work on his political thought may come later. Papers on Quebec's conqueror, a king's wirepuller, a captain of industry, and Lincoln's early years lead the set.

Most of the pieces first saw print in Canada, and several came back to Canadian journals, giving the book a clear Canadian cast. Smith writes with the ease of a man used to a lecture hall, keen to inform rather than to stir. Lectures and Essays thus reads as a sampler of a busy mind, kept for friends and now open to all.
6587-king-arthur-s-socks-and-other-villa:
Floyd Dell gathers short plays first staged in Greenwich Village, at the Liberal Club and by the Provincetown Players. The set runs from a five-minute morality play and a comedy on Joseph to a tragic fantasy, a domestic talk piece, and a spoof on Ibsen. King Arthur's Socks, the title comedy, sits among them as a village joke on legend.

Dell calls the plays souvenirs of a witty play-time, now past, and asks for a not-too-solemn memory of it. The pieces are short, talky, and full of the Village spirit of his day. This volume suits readers who like small, clever plays that can be read in an evening or staged with few props.
65993-scouting-for-boys:
Robert Baden Powell wrote a handbook of scouting for boys in 1908. Part one gives scoutcraft and scout law: the duties of boy scouts, their secret signs, laws, badges, and war dance. Part two treats observation and tracking, woodcraft and knowledge of animals. Part three holds campaigning and camp life, pioneering and resourcefulness.

Part four gives endurance and health, chivalry and brave deeds, and discipline. Part five holds saving life and first aid, patriotism and loyalty. Part six closes with scouting games, competitions, and plays. By the term instructor I mean any man or lad who takes up the training of a patrol or a troop, the foreword says. Baden Powell hopes anyone, even without previous knowledge of scouting, may teach it to boys by this book, in town as well as country. The boy scout movement starts on these pages.
66074-mere-literature-and-other-essays:
Woodrow Wilson's Mere Literature, and Other Essays was published by Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York in 1896, priced at a dollar fifty. Wilson dedicates the little volume to Stockton Axson, by every gift of mind a critic and by every gift of heart a friend. Eight essays stand in the contents: Mere Literature, The Author Himself, and On an Author's Choice of Company among them. The Interpreter of English Liberty, on Burke, is printed here for the first time.

A Calendar of Great Americans and The Course of American History close the book. The title essay attacks the scientific age's sneer in the phrase mere literature: nothing but talk, fabrication, pastime. Wilson warns that colleges under the positivist spirit command literature to assume the phrases and methods of science. The essays had appeared in the Atlantic Monthly, the Century, and the Forum.
66177-half-hours-with-modern-scientists-:
Half Hours with Modern Scientists holds talks and essays by great science men. Huxley, Tyndall, Cope, and two more hands lend their names to the set. The head of Yale College wrote the front talk for the set. The book came out at New Haven in the year eighteen seventy two.

Huxley leads with a talk on the stuff base of life in plain terms. Force ties of life and of dead stuff form the next talk in line. A reply on first slime, then a talk on the growth guess, follow in turn. Keen minds clash in print on the great doubt of the age. The set served homes that craved sound science in short reads.
66202-a-queen-of-nine-days:
A Queen of Nine Days is a historical tale of Lady Jane Grey, told by her gentlewoman Margaret Brown. Kenyon edited it and put it into modern English. The Religious Tract Society printed it at London. Its contents run from leaving home to Lady Jane's execution.

A prologue sets the writer's duty. The late Lady Jane, she says, laid it on her to set forth the true story of her short, sad tragedy. Jane held that loving eyes see further and more truly than the mere critic's. Chapters follow the heroine through hiding, the Tower, and Wyatt's insurrection. The book gives the nine days' queen a voice from inside her own household.
66237-no-time-land-a-story-for-girls-and:
Mary Fulton wrote this tale for girls and boys at Leith in Tasmania, and the Examiner office at Launceston printed it in 1901. She gave it to her nephews, nieces, and all small readers. A Happy New Century is her wish at the front, dated December 1900.

Guy, come and play with me, begs little Tina in the first line. Guy has no time; he is off fishing with Urie Cass. You never get time, Guy, the small voice wails. His mother's sad face haunts him all day, and the fishing turns sour. No-Time-Land, the land Guy lives in, is the tale's theme: a boy too busy for love learns his fault.
66522-learning-and-other-essays:
Learning and Other Essays, by John Jay Chapman, came out in 1910. Moffat, Yard published the volume at New York. Twelve essays make the contents. Professorial Ethics follows the title piece. The Drama, Norway, and Doctor Howe come next. Jesters and The Comic stand close together. The Unity of Human Nature and the Doctrine of Non-Resistance follow. Climate, the Influence of Schools, and the Aesthetic close the book. The first essay opens at the Metropolitan Museum. An expert praised an engraved Greek gem there. His tone thrilled Chapman more than his words. The gem itself was badly placed, near invisible. Even seen well, its merit would pass most viewers by.

Chapman stood to it as Petrarch stood to his Greek Homer: owning a treasure he could not read. What education is, he then asks.
6666-hello-boys:
Wilcox wrote most of these war verses in France, during seven months spent among American soldiers in camps and hospitals. She says she shaped them in the simplest manner, from close contact with soldiers' minds and hearts, with no thought for critics' rules. Scores of copies were asked for, with autographs, by the men who heard them.

The poems greet the boys by name, cheer them, mourn with them, and send them home in verse. Their plainness is the point: they were made to be spoken aloud in a camp. Hello, Boys is a warm, period book of wartime verse, best read as a voice from the front's waiting rooms.
67391-gilbert-weather-bureau-meteorology:
Gilbert Weather Bureau is a book of meteorology for boys by Alfred Gilbert, published at New Haven in 1920. Gilbert, a Yale graduate of 1909, founded the company that made Gilbert science sets for boys. His book teaches weather study through simple experiments. It opens by attacking the silly notion that the weather knows no laws.

People think the weather man a conjurer, Gilbert says, and nothing could be further from the truth. Weather is a science like electricity or chemistry, with uniform laws. The weatherman reads instruments and reasons from what they show. The book trains boys to observe clouds, winds, and pressure for themselves, in the Gilbert hands-on manner.
67397-the-rockspur-eleven-a-fine-footbal:
Burt Standish wrote a school grid tale of the Rockspur team for boys. The book's rights date to 1900 with Street and Smith. Standish wrote the Merriwell tales with great fame in his day. A house note in front sings the long tale gainst short mag fare. Short tales end just as zeal grows, that note holds in scorn.

A full book lets a boy spend long hours in one world, it says. Paper books stand crown in their class, the note crows with pride. Each day sees a fresh name join that house's long list. On the field, Rockspur's boys fight for school pride and grit. Plays, foes, and wins fill the tale's fast pace. Boys of that age tore in.
67534-the-black-star-a-school-story-for-:
Andrew Walpole wrote The Black Star, a school story for boys, for the Cornstalk Publishing Company of Sydney in 1925. The scene is Deepwater College, and the tale opens at the station as the boys return from holidays.

Jack Symonds waits on the platform for his friend Billy Faraday, whose train from Melbourne has not yet come in. Two strange men in the crowd catch Jack's eye and unsettle one another at sight. The chapter list promises a bully-killer, a broken bootlace clue, a chase for the star, a boy who walks in his sleep, and a vanishing. Walpole spins a school mystery in which the boys themselves unravel the secret.
67682-stories-for-boys:
Stories for Boys is a collection of tales by Richard Harding Davis, published by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York in 1915. The stories themselves date from 1891. Davis dedicates the book to his brother C. Belmont Davis, who was a boy about the same time he was.

The contents lead with The Reporter Who Made Himself King, Davis's famous tale of an American journalist enthroned abroad. Midsummer Pirates, Richard Carr's Baby, and The Great Tri-Club Tennis Tournament follow. Sport runs through the volume: a baseball club story, a jockey story, a boating race. The frontispiece shows a king sitting on a log in the rain, discovered by a boy who never expected royalty there. Davis wrote brisk, manly adventure for the young, and these stories were his gift back to boyhood.
67753-don-miguel-lehumada-discoverer-of-:
Sue Greenleaf wrote this occult romance of Mexico and the United States. Dodge printed Don Miguel Lehumada in New York, copyright 1906. Contents open with Don Miguel arrival from Kansas City in Chihuahua. A scene in the scientist study frames his sun ray liquid.

Marriet Motuble tells Julio Murillo of his first incarnation next. Death of President Diaz and annexation of Mexico fill chapter three. A plunger takes memory fluid and remembers a past life whole. Governor Lehumada lectures on liquid from the sun rays in chapter five. A tomb visit and arrests of conspiracy leaders fill the later chapter heads of contents.
67788-through-colonial-doorways:
Anne Hollingsworth Wharton wrote Through Colonial Doorways, here in its seventeenth edition. J B Lippincott published it at Philadelphia, with copyright in 1893. Wharton dedicated the volume to the memory of Margaret N Carter, whose sketches adorn its pages. Her preface opens on the revival of interest in colonial and Revolutionary times. The literature of those periods had grown, she notes, and private research with it.

Readers want more than councils, congresses, and battles, she argues. They wish to know how their ancestors lived and loved, not only how they wrought and died. Wharton sounds the heavy brass knocker and leads the reader through broad doorways into the homes within. Friends lent her letters and manuscripts for the work. Parts had appeared in the Atlantic Monthly, Lippincott's Magazine, and the Philadelphia papers.
68209-george-bernard-shaw-his-plays:
Mencken, then a young critic, wrote this study of Shaw's plays for Luce of Boston in 1905. It was among the first full books on Shaw in English. A quote from Nietzsche on talent heads the opening: talent is a name for practice and time.

Mencken works through the plays one by one. Mrs Warren's Profession, Arms and the Man, and The Devil's Disciple lead. Candida, Man and Superman, and John Bull's Other Island stand in the list. Major Barbara comes last of fourteen. The novels and other writings get a part of their own. A life sketch with dates, and a head-to-head of Shakespeare and Shaw, close the book. Mencken writes with his known bite, in praise of a playwright still more whipped than read.
6909-old-caravan-days:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood sets this tale on the road in 1857, when a caravan starts out with wagons, folk, and children. The contents list a tavern, the Susan house and its cellar, a little old man with a bag, and a great camp meeting where a child's cry sounds at night. Fairy Carrie and the pig headed man, a minstrel, a toll woman, and robbers cross the road in turn.

Jonathan and Thrusty Ellen, Zene's man and woman, and a house with log steps fill the middle chapters with humor and worry. The caravan pushes forward through Sundays on the road, a country Sunday school, and a night picture of home. Catherwood writes a warm road tale of a young America moving west by wagon.
69251-stories-for-children-a-book-for-al:
Stories for Children, edited by Colman, is a book for little girls and boys. Howe and Ferry issued it at New York in 1860, rights first held in 1844. Innocence, a poem by Rufus Dawes, opens the set with a child in heaven. Lambs, birds, and flower bowers fill that vision of the angel home.

The Fairy of the Rose, also by Dawes, follows with Corinne story in prose. Corinne obeys her parents and loves her brothers and sisters in the tale. Lilla Dream, a child dream among flowers, and Childhood fill the middle. The King of the Swans and Corinne close the eight piece set.
69426-history-of-a-literary-radical-and-:
Randolph Bourne wrote the essays gathered in History of a Literary Radical and Other Essays. Van Wyck Brooks edited the book and wrote the opening essay. B W Huebsch issued it in New York in nineteen hundred twenty. Most pieces had first run in magazines such as The Atlantic Monthly and The Dial.

The title essay traces the thin schooling of a young reader named Miro. Later pieces give six portraits of people Bourne knew. Other essays take up the Midwest, talk as a habit, and the art of Theodore Dreiser. Trans-National America closes the main run of essays. A fragment of a novel ends the book.
69602-the-riddle-club-through-the-holida:
The Riddle Club Through the Holidays is a children's book by Alice Dale Hardy. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York, with a 1924 copyright. Walter Rogers illustrated the volume. Hardy also wrote The Riddle Club at Home and The Riddle Club in Camp. The full title promises the club's doings and how the riddles were solved. It also promises what the snowman revealed at the end. The contents list chapters from Halloween to Christmas.

Early chapters plan parties and play Halloween tricks. Jess has luck, tables turn, and Polly faces a problem. Moving day, camp again, and a special meeting follow. Detective Margy and a riddle chap appear in the middle chapters. Lost treasures and a practical joke raise the stakes. The book closes with Merry Christmas and a storm adventure. The club format mixes puzzles with school holiday fun.
69776-four-little-blossoms-through-the-h:
Four Little Blossoms Through the Holidays is a story for children by Mabel Hawley, with copyright in 1922 at New York. Robert Gaston Herbert drew the pictures, one showing the children decorating a snow figure named White. The book is the fifth of the Four Little Blossoms books, after Brookside Farm and Apple Tree Island.

The contents promise a full holiday run: Thanksgiving gifts, a football game, Christmas at school and at home, and a party. The first chapter finds Meg hunting soap and a scrubbing brush for work in the cellar, while Twaddles dodges an errand. The children, she tells the cook Norah, are packing Thanksgiving food for school, to be given to the poor.
69825-an-apology-for-idlers-and-other-es:
An Apology for Idlers and Other Essays gathers four pieces by Robert Louis Stevenson. Mosher published the volume at Portland, Maine, with editions from 1905 to 1916. The title essay defends idleness against the gospel of work. El Dorado, The English Admirals, and Child's Play complete the book.

Stevenson opens by noting that all are now bound to take up a money making trade. Enthusiasm just short of madness is the price of respect, he mocks. Idleness, he argues, is not doing nothing at all. It is doing much that the ruling dogmas do not count. The busy man's resentment of the loafer gets a sharp portrait. Alexander slighted by Diogenes stands as his case in point. The essays show Stevenson the charmer at his most quotable.
70-what-is-man-and-other-essays:
Mark Twain asks whether human beings are machines shaped by training and habit. What Is Man? and Other Essays gathers the title dialogue with fifteen shorter pieces. An Old Man argues his case to a Young Man, who tests each claim in turn.

The other essays range widely: the death of Joan of Arc, the turning point of Twain's life, and how to make history dates stick. Pieces on Switzerland, Wagner, tobacco, the bicycle, and Shakespeare follow. Twain's humor sharpens a serious question about free will. The collection shows his late mind at its most argumentative.
70568-debating-for-boys:
Debating for Boys is a handbook on argument by William Horton Foster. It was issued in New York by Sturgis and Walton in 1915, with ties to the Boy Scouts of America. The author holds that a boy's debate is a small copy of debate in Congress.

The chapters build the skill step by step. They treat what debate is, what to debate, and how to get ready. Terms, issues, evidence, and the brief each get a chapter. Refutation and delivery close the course. A story part then shows how the boys of Fairfield formed a club and ran a town meeting at Ford Hall. Appendices give questions for debate, rules for judging, and a table of the rules for meetings.
70669-aesthetical-and-philosophical-essa:
Aesthetical and Philosophical Essays is a volume of Friedrich Schiller's essays in English. The contents open with the Letters on the Aesthetical Education of Man. Essays follow on the sublime, the pathetic, and grace and dignity. A dissertation on the connection between the animal and spiritual man gives the book its second title.

Other pieces treat the stage as a moral institution and the tragic art. Schiller asks why tragic objects give us pleasure. His philosophical letters, the Theosophy of Julius among them, close the collection. These essays made Schiller, the German dramatist and poet, a teacher of beauty as a path to freedom. The volume served English readers as his main prose work.
7150-science-education-essays:
Thomas Huxley's Science and Education essays gather speeches and addresses from more than thirty years, and his preface apologizes for repetitions more needfully than in the first volume. Speeches on one topic, given at intervals to widely distant hearers and readers, could hardly avoid repeating. The oldest piece, on the educational value of the natural history sciences, holds crudities Huxley repudiated when it was first reprinted twenty years before.

Yet much of his later work merely develops propositions from that early, sadly imperfect piece. A recent attempt to disturb the compromise on teaching dogmatic theology, solemnly agreed by the first School Board for London, prompts the fifteenth essay and others. Huxley argues for science in schools, honestly taught and free from sectarian control.
71543-the-wonder-island-boys:
The Wonder Island Boys, Capture and Pursuit, a boys adventure tale by Roger T Finlay, was copyrighted in 1914 by the New York Book Company. It is the fifth of six Wonder Island Boys volumes, sold at sixty cents each. Two boys and an aged professor, cast away on an island with nothing but their clothes, form the party. Step by step they build every device of the mechanical arts.

The publisher promises two thousand things every boy ought to know, taught without technical terms. This volume opens with a fight at the savages' camp. Harry returns in excitement, a new band arrives, and the wagon is set to resist attack. John and George circle the camp and meet the warriors by surprise. The professor scouts to the north while tribes gather. A ruse, an attack, and a repulse carry the action.
71708-the-bird-boys:
John Luther Langworthy wrote this tale of two young sky pilots and their first air voyage. Donohue of Chicago printed The Bird Boys in 1912, when flight was still a fresh marvel. A front plate shows a biplane tossed by slants of wind.

The plate tells the tale's pitch: the small craft makes wild dashes this way and that. Her broad planes catch each gust as the boys fight to hold her. Boys of 1912, fed on tales of canoes and house-boats, here got wings at last. The same page puffs woodcraft books for Boy Scouts, full of woods lore and wild beasts. Langworthy gives his young pilots a first voyage to match that thirst for risk.
71776-an-old-master-and-other-political-:
Woodrow Wilson wrote An Old Master and Other Political Essays at Princeton. Charles Scribner’s Sons issued the book at New York in eighteen ninety three. Wilson taught jurisprudence at Princeton when the essays came out. Congressional Government and Division and Reunion stand on his title page.

The Study of Politics and Political Sovereignty fill the next two parts. The Character of Democracy in the United States takes the fourth place. Government Under the Constitution closes the grave set of five. Two essays first ran in the New Princeton Review, the notes own. Two more first ran in the Atlantic Monthly, by leave of its house. An Old Master asks why no one has praised the lecture art. Class rooms now trade old lectures for bare data lists, Wilson laments. Robert Bridges takes the book’s warm gift page at its front.
71823-percy-s-holidays:
Percy's Holidays, or Borrowing Trouble, is a children's story by Lucy Ellen Guernsey, issued by the American Sunday School Union. The copyright entry dates it to eighteen seventy two, and Guernsey's many other tales for the young are listed. A frontispiece shows a child told there is nothing there to cry about. The book belongs to a set called the Round Spring Stories.

Percy's holiday trouble is of the kind a child borrows by worry and mischief before any real harm comes. Sunday school fiction of this kind taught conduct through small home scenes, not sermons alone. Guernsey was a steady hand in that market. A short tale with a clear moral is the form.
71838-essays:
Essays is a gathering of the essays of Winthrop Mackworth Praed. The pieces were gathered and set in order by Sir George Young. An opening essay by Henry Morley, a professor of English literature at University College, London, stands at the front. The book came out in London in 1887 from George Routledge and Sons, as part of Morley's Universal Library.

The front pages list the first books of that library to show its scope. Sheridan's plays stand first, then plays from Moliere by English hands, and Marlowe's Faustus with Goethe's Faust. The Chronicle of the Cid, Rabelais, and Machiavelli's Prince stand in the list as well. The volume at hand gives Praed's essays a place in that cheap set of classics for the plain reader.
72020-janet-s-boys:
Janet's Boys is a tale by Annette Lyster, the author of A Leal Light Heart and Midshipman Archie. It was put out in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, with pictures by W. S. Stacey. A front picture shows Janet and the broker. A note states that odd and mixed spellings stand as printed.

The contents set out the course of the tale. An opening chapter stands first, then The Road to Ruin and In Liverpool. Kelmersdale and All the Way to Gattigo stand next in the list. Mrs. Rayburn's Cap, The Boys' Escape, and The Babes in the Wood carry it on. In the New Home and Frank's Message to Muddie stand later, and Mrs. Rayburn's Le— breaks the list. The book is a moral tale of boys, loss, and a new home, from a Christian house.
72354-the-lindsays:
The Lindsays, a romance of Scottish life by John Leys, reaches its third volume in the 1888 London edition. This volume opens at chapter twenty seven with two conversations. Solicitor Hatchett drives back to his office in a brown study in the first scene. He sends for Mr Beattie and asks after Mr Lindsay at once.

Lindsay has been shut in the house with a bad cold for over a week. The draft of his uncle will cannot be found in the office files. That loss is no surprise, as the coming chapters show in full. Trouble draws near, a police court scene follows, and then a full trial takes the centre. Chapters after the trial bring a fugitive back and jump two years ahead. Law, family, and suspense carry the close of the tale.
72769-half-a-dozen-boys:
Half a Dozen Boys is an every day story by Anna Chapin Ray. Its full title in plain words calls the tale an every day story. A front print shows one boy half dragged from smoke by his pal. Rights date the work to the year eighteen ninety.

The front note owns the tale has no wild flights or close shaves. School, games, pranks, and small rows make the sum of its boys days. The author holds that hot tales make plain life seem dull to boys. She aims to show that the plain round has its own worth and fun. A gift page names the true boy who stood as the mold for Rob.
7324-tropic-days:
E. J.
