Banfield's Tropic Days, from 1918, follows My Tropic Isle with another instalment of sketches from an island off North Queensland, where a few of the original inhabitants kept their uncontaminated ways. Banfield explains that his earlier books aimed at exact, if prosaic, details of island life. Here he again tries to describe types of a crude race in ordinary habit as men and women, not as ethnological specimens, with a tint of imagination to embolden the better truths.

Peace and silence, combined with the large liberties of nature, set the book's mood, in De Quincey's words. Banfield thanks his brother beachcombers in the dedication, and his sketches favour quiet scenes over sensation. The volume reads as a slow, affectionate portrait of tropic life.
73554-radio-v-rays:
Jan Dirk wrote Radio V-Rays, a science fiction story about two college radio fans. Dick Jarvis and Stan Ross are young engineering students. Opposite types in most ways, they are bound by one shared passion. Radio fills Dick's college room and their free hours.

The friends built a fine superheterodyne receiver as a gift for Dick's father. Its mahogany case gleams on a long shelf under the window. One evening they sit down for a DX half hour of distant listening. Stan spots a strange cone-shaped loop aerial on the bench. Dick explains that he built it to dodge heavy traffic on San Francisco Bay. The headline promises that their listening will reach another planet, with disaster to follow.
73563-tropical-nature-and-other-essays:
Tropical Nature and Other Essays, by Alfred R Wallace, was printed in London by Macmillan in 1878. Wallace had also written The Malay Archipelago and works on how animals spread round the world. He was a great field student of living things.

A poem in praise of the tropics opens the book, with palms, rice, cane, spice, and orange trees in the heat. Wallace spent years in hot lands and wrote from his own eyes, not books alone. His essays treat the wealth and sameness of life near the equator, and set it against the changing north. He asks why hot lands hold such rich life in such fixed forms. Students of nature get classic field thought from a man who shared in the great idea of his age.
73691-reflections-on-the-death-of-a-porc:
Reflections on the Death of a Porcupine is a book of essays by D H Lawrence, published at Philadelphia by the Centaur Press in 1925. The Crown leads the contents, a long essay of 1915. A note tells its birth. John Middleton Murry proposed they do something as the war went deep. The doing was a tiny monthly paper, The Signature, sold by subscription. It came out three times and died. The last Crown essays were never printed at the time.

Lawrence owns the venture meant nothing real to him. In a great issue like the war, he says, there is nothing to be done in that way. The forms of the era must go, and men must change deep down first. The Novel, Aristocracy, and the title essay fill the rest. The book is Lawrence at his most prophetic and strange.
74334-the-green-mountain-boys:
The Green Mountain Boys, or Vermont and the New York Land Jobbers, is a history by Philip Smith, printed at Pawling, New York, in 1885. Smith had written on Acadia and on Dutchess County. In his preface he argues that every locality holds unrecorded deeds of moral heroism.

Such deeds, he says, deserve notice as much as many facts fixed in the history the masses read. In a local history they hide among commonplace matter, and a general history cannot spare them room. His small volume gives one such episode its due prominence. The episode is Vermont's fight against New York's claim to its lands, in the days of Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys. His book tells the land war from Vermont's side.
7470-castilian-days:
John Hay, who had served Lincoln and would later serve as Secretary of State, knew Spain from his years as a diplomat, and Castilian Days gathers his Spanish essays. The holiday edition of 1903, illustrated from a special visit to Castile by Mr. Pennell, omits a few less descriptive chapters from the original but otherwise reprints the text unchanged. Madrid al fresco opens the book.

Later chapters take up Spanish living and dying, the influence of tradition, tauromachy, or bullfighting, and red-letter days in the Spanish calendar. Hay writes with a diplomat's eye and a poet's ear, admiring Spain without romanticizing it. The essays remain a classic introduction to Castile: its light, its customs, and its stubborn, splendid difference from the rest of Europe.
74799-adobe-days:
Sarah Bixby Smith wrote Adobe Days, a true tale of her girlhood in early California. The Torch Press issued a revised form in nineteen hundred twenty six. Smith held the copyright from the year before. She gave the book to her father, Llewellyn Bixby.

She was born on the San Justo sheep ranch near San Juan Bautista. Her father had come from Maine and reached San Francisco in eighteen hundred fifty one. Three young Maine men drove sheep and cattle west in eighteen hundred fifty three. Their trek fills one long strand of the book. Los Angeles then was still a small, plain town. School days and the start of Pomona College close the tale.
75150-x-ray-violet-ray-and-other-rays:
X-Ray, Violet Ray and Other Rays is a small health guide by Maynard Shipley. The book stands as Little Blue Book number 1050 in its set. Haldeman-Julius edited the set and printed it at Girard, Kansas, in 1926. The title adds the use of rays in modern medicine as its field. Five chapters run from everyday uses to martyrs of the ray art.

X-rays find flaws in iron and steel for bridges and buildings. They test the cylinders of airplane engines and so avert crashes. One petrol tank showed rivet heads outside and none inside at all. Bad railway axles, drilled wrong and filled over, got a whole lot scrapped. Later chapters weigh the curative claims made for X-rays in sickness. Whooping cough and malaria stand named among those bold claims. The martyrs who died by the rays get their own sad chapter.
75231-a-girl-and-her-ways:
Girl and Her Ways is a girls novel by Amy Le Feuvre, from Ward Lock of London. A gentian frontispiece fronts the story of a young guest and a waiting house. Contents open with an invasion, the young guest, and the house that was waiting. Jim Paget, an unpleasant experience, and a fresh proposition follow in the heads.

A private chauffeur and a day in the New Forest lighten the middle chapters. Dark clouds, left alone, a visit to Cornwall, and Thorold secret deepen the tale. A new friend and a golden time close the contents of the romance. Le Feuvre wrote shelf upon shelf of wholesome tales for girls.
75332-christina-and-the-boys:
Christina and the Boys is a story for young readers by Amy Le Feuvre. Hodder and Stoughton published the book at London in 1906, with pictures by Gordon Browne. Le Feuvre was known for tales such as Two Tramps and Probable Sons. The contents promise highwaymen, a ghost, a winter picnic, and a trip to London.

The heroine is Christina, a small pale child in a short frock and frilled apron. Her mother died at her birth, and her father has been abroad ever since. An old nurse raised her in two nursery rooms of a great house, Bracken Towers. Her one delight is her father's library, a dim room lined with books from floor to ceiling. The first chapter finds her before its fire, wide eyed at a tale she has heard. From that quiet start the story moves into the wider world of the boys.
7554-quotes-and-images-from-the-diary-of:
Samuel Pepys kept his diary through the 1660s, the decade of plague, fire, and Restoration London, and this volume gathers its quotations and images. The reader can copy any short segment, open the diary eBook below, and find the full context. It is a finder and a browser, not a substitute for the diary itself.

The entries catch Pepys in mid-life. There are money and wine needed for a burying, and a good handsome wench kissed. There is a fair salute on horseback in Rochester streets, and a most conceited fellow with not over much in him. A play not very good though much commended, a cat that will be a cat still, and a most tedious sermon all appear. The collection gives Pepys at his frankest, in sentences that still sound alive.
76393-english-ways-and-by-ways:
Scribner printed this travel book in letters in October 1920. English Ways and By-Ways gives the letters of John and Ruth Dobson, written from England to their friend Leighton Parks. A Burns tag heads it: for me, an aim I never fash — I rhyme for fun.

The book is given to one who knows the Dobsons as well as the writer does, and can bear witness to the truth of the tale. The Legacy opens the trip, then a school of instruction and a fool-proof car. The car arrives, and the Great North Road runs. The England of Fielding and the end of the north road follow. A by-election, sheep-dogs, brigands and bootblacks, and Falstaff fill the letters' England.
76453-through-unknown-ways:
Lucy Ellen Guernsey wrote an old world story in the Stanton Corbet Chronicles, printed at London in a new edition. The danger is over, a picture says, look up and see your fallen adversary. Book one opens on December 10, 1684. Perhaps I may as well begin by telling how I came to write it at all, the narrator says.

Lady Corbet, my mistress, with whom I live as waiting gentlewoman and companion, gave me the use of this cabinet, she tells. She speaks her mind in these pages if nowhere else. See there, child, said Lady Corbet of a dead lady's finery: the poor bedizened thing had to leave all her finery behind her in the grave. Book two moves to August 1685, and book three to Studley Hall in 1687.
76744-round-the-world-in-any-number-of-d:
Maurice Baring wrote Round the World in Any Number of Days, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1914. The book is a travel diary in dated entries, light in tone. Its frontispiece jokes that his ticket is for New Zealand, though the trip circles the globe.

Baring sails from Tilbury on June 21, through the Bay of Biscay to Gibraltar, Naples, and Port Said. He crosses the Red Sea in July heat, rides the monsoon to Ceylon, and goes on to Fremantle, Adelaide, Melbourne, and Sydney. New Zealand follows, then Rarotonga and Tahiti, and the Pacific crossing to San Francisco. He reaches New York in October. The entries mix shipboard humor, food, booksellers, and sharp small portraits of places seen in passing.
76829-how-to-write-photoplays:
How to Write Photoplays is a craft guide by Embrie Zuver in its third print. The leaf shows a copyright of nineteen fifteen from a New York scene firm. Its front words swear no pad fills the book past need. Read with care and heed its steps, and stage craft skill can be won. Trade words of the film shops fill the first of its short drills.

Drills run through plot build, synopsis, cast lists, and scene links in turn. What the lens can take, sub heads, and mail props each get a drill. High point build, feel, and script form hold the mid drills of the set. Where to sell plays and what sums are paid close the craft side. Rule boards and rights close the book in short last drills.
77336-hecuba-and-other-plays:
Euripides wrote Hecuba and Other Plays, here in English verse by Michael Wodhull. Routledge put it out at London in 1888, in Morley's Universal Library. Henry Morley, who taught English letters at University College, London, wrote the opening essay. The series put great books in cheap form for all readers. Its list runs from Sheridan and Moliere to Dante, Don Quixote, and Candide.

Hecuba is the famed queen of Troy, brought low when her town fell to the Greeks. Her grief and wrath drive the chief play of the book. Greek plays turn on fate, grief, and the pride of kings and gods. Wodhull keeps the verse form of the Greek stage in English dress. Readers get an old master in a plain, low-cost book, made to sit on any shelf.
77723-jungle-days:
Jungle Days is a nature book by William Beebe, published in New York and London in nineteen twenty five. A picture of an Indian hut on the Mazaruni River fronts the volume. Chapters first ran in magazines, as layered copyright pages for nineteen twenty three and twenty five show. A chain of jungle life opens the contents.

My jungle table, midnight beach combing, and falling leaves follow as chapter heads. The jungle sluggard, mangrove mystery, and the life of death promise close watching of tropical creatures. Beebe ran a research station in Guiana and wrote its life for lay readers with a poet's eye. Feeding, hunting, and rotting in the forest are his themes.
7805-first-plays:
A. A. Milne's First Plays gathers five pieces written in 1916 and 1917, in the order given: Wurzel-Flummery, The Lucky One, The Boy Comes Home, Belinda, and The Red Feathers. Milne says only one touches the war, though the war made the book possible, since soldiering gave a journalist time for a costly gamble.

Playwriting, he jokes, is a luxury like golf, only dearer: articles pay for certain, novels at least get printed, but a play may bring nothing but disillusion. Dedicated to his mother, the volume shows the future Pooh author trying comic stagecraft with wit, warmth, and a soldier's spare hours.
78433-northcliffe-boys:
Northcliffe Boys is a moral tale by Charlotte O Brien, from the Religious Tract Society. Rider and Son printed the London tract society book for working class readers. Contents run from George home and George at work to good news and temptation. Good for evil, in the hospital, and in the new home close the short tale.

Chapter one sets autumn winds blowing through Northcliffe streets strewn with fallen leaves. A cold, damp, dull afternoon finds one exception, a boy of about twelve. Tract fiction taught honesty, industry, and kindness through one lad trials. O Brien had written Basil, or Honesty and Industry, in the same improving line.
79202-alley-ways:
Alley Ways is a short story by Helen Hull, author of The Fire, printed in the Century Magazine in February 1918. It opens at closing time in a department store. Cynthia, a clerk, hurries between the sheeted counters toward the door. She has lingered so long that the other clerks have gone. Bell, the manager, unlatches the door for her himself.

Cynthia slips out with a grave good night, secretly proud of Bell's smooth manner and of her own small place in his store. Outside waits Queenie, a girl she was meant to shake off, with a sick, sly look in her wide blue eyes. Queenie falls into step beside her. Cynthia cannot strike at her as her mother demanded, and the walk home turns on what both girls are thinking.
79292-rest-days:
Rest Days: A Study in Early Law and Morality is an anthropological treatise by Hutton Webster, professor of social anthropology in the University of Nebraska. Macmillan printed it at New York in 1916. Webster also wrote Primitive Secret Societies. His epigraph, from Marsden's History of Sumatra, states his method: the science of mankind cannot be improved by abstract speculation; only a regular series of authenticated facts can raise us toward knowledge.

The first chapter treats tabooed days at critical epochs. Four regular tabu periods marked the Hawaiian month, strikingly like a Sabbath. The Society Islands, the Marquesas and New Zealand kept their own tabooed days. Fiji adds its instances. The book is comparative anthropology in the service of one institution's deep history.
79499-the-angel-that-troubled-the-waters:
The Angel That Troubled the Waters and Other Plays, by Thornton Wilder, was published in New York in 1928 by Coward-McCann. Wilder was already known for The Bridge of San Luis Rey and The Cabala. The contents list sixteen short plays, most on Bible themes or figures from the past.

Titles include Proserpina and the Devil, Brother Fire, Leviathan, and Hast Thou Considered My Servant Job? A foreword looks back at the hard start of writing at age sixteen, full of hope and thin proof. Wilder notes that all rights are held and no staging is allowed without leave. The plays are brief, spare, and built for voice and moral choice.
79552-the-castaways:
James Otis wrote The Castaways, or On the Florida Reefs, issued in New York by A L Burt with copyright in eighteen eighty eight. Otis had earlier written Toby Tyler. Twenty eight chapters fill the tale. Chapter one is On Board the Sea Queen. A plate shows Ben holding the oars while Jake poised the spear for a cast. A noisy little tug boat opens the story.

A Consultation, A Quack Doctor, and An Ill Timed Excursion follow the sailing. The Drifting Hulk, On the Simoon, and The Reef bring the wreck. On the Key, A Midnight Visitor, and The Island Specter follow. Catching the Ghost and After the Norther fill the middle. The Fate of the Sea Queen and Adieu to Content Key close the island stay. Boys get a Florida reefs adventure of wreckers and salvage.
79594-dark-days:
Dark Days, a novel by Hugh Conway, comes here in a cheap Chicago pocket edition. Donohue published it for the vest pocket trade in small format. Conway won fame with Called Back, the great sensation tale of his day. Advertisements for pocket dictionaries crowd the front pages of this little book.

Such editions sold full novels at tiny prices for train and coat pocket reading. Dark Days belongs to the same line of mystery and sensation as his hit. A blind hero and a hidden crime drive the plot, in the Conway manner. Cheap reprints kept his name alive long after the first boom of the tale. Sensation fiction of the 1880s filled many such vest pocket volumes.
8108-literary-and-social-essays:
George William Curtis collected these literary and social essays, many written for magazines between 1853 and 1891. His subjects include Emerson and Hawthorne from Homes of American Authors, a North American Review study of Hawthorne's works, Rachel the actress. Thackeray in America, Sir Philip Sidney, Longfellow, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and Washington Irving, read at Ashfield and printed by the Grolier Club. The Emerson essay opens with Concord, an hour's ride from Boston.

Curtis writes as a cultivated American man of letters, introducing English and American authors to a general audience. The essays preserve mid-nineteenth-century taste and friendship, since Curtis knew many of his subjects. For readers of American literary history, the volume is a warm, well-informed companion to the age of Emerson and Hawthorne.
8532-andivius-hedulio-adventures-of-a-ro:
Edward Lucas White wrote Andivius Hedulio, adventures of a Roman nobleman in the days of the empire. Maps show the Roman Empire in the second century and the city of Rome under the empire, tracing Hedulio's wanderings. The book, dedicated to the memory of a friend, follows its hero through the empire at its height.

White, a classicist and novelist, writes historical adventure with scholarly care for Roman life, from the city to the provinces. Readers get a tale of travel, intrigue, and Roman manners, grounded in research. The novel suits lovers of Roman fiction who want a hero's travels in a well-built ancient world.
8932-lessons-in-life-a-series-of-familia:
Timothy Titcomb, the pen name of Josiah Gilbert Holland, wrote these familiar essays after his Letters to the Young and Gold Foil won a wide readership. Titcomb states his aim plainly: he does not try to be brilliant or deep. He treats, in a friendly way, the questions that face thoughtful men and women each day.

The essays deal with work, character, money, home, and the conduct of life, in the voice of a wise neighbor rather than a preacher. They sum up the common sense of their age in short, readable pieces. For modern readers they offer a clear window on nineteenth-century American ideals of a good life.
9162-becket-and-other-plays:
Alfred, Lord Tennyson, Poet Laureate, gathered four plays in this volume: Becket, The Cup, The Falcon, and The Promise of May. Becket, dedicated to the Lord Chancellor, Earl of Selborne, recalls his great predecessor Thomas Becket. Henry the Second, Becket, and bishops such as Foliot and Roger fill its cast.

Tennyson admits the play was not shaped for the modern stage, yet Selborne praised it. The other plays offer shorter trials of love and honor. The volume shows Tennyson's late turn to drama, grave, stately, and rich in historic color.
9255-the-gorgon-s-head-from-a-wonder-boo:
Hawthorne retold the myth of the Gorgon's head for children in A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys, framed by talks on the Tanglewood porch. He held that classical myths could make capital reading for the young, if shaped with freedom. A great freedom was needed, he admits, yet myths stay themselves through change, unlike almost anything else.

So he shaped the old forms anew as fancy dictated, without guilt of sacrilege. Perseus, Medusa, and the winged horse come alive for young readers. The tale remains a beloved gateway to Greek myth, told in Hawthorne's clear, warm voice.
9258-the-miraculous-pitcher-from-a-wonde:
Hawthorne's Miraculous Pitcher, from A Wonder-Book, finds the children in merry May, halfway up a monstrous hill. No longer in the Tanglewood playroom, they climb toward the bald tiptop, a height below Chimborazo or Mont Blanc, yet higher than a thousand ant-hillocks to short childish strides. The hillside frames the tale.

Then comes Baucis and Philemon, whose pitcher never empties for kind guests, and whose humble cottage becomes a temple. Hawthorne retells the myth with warmth for young ears. The story remains a beloved lesson in hospitality, told in his clearest style.
9329-the-widow-o-callaghan-s-boys:
Gulielma Zollinger wrote this children's novel in 1904, in its tenth edition, about the Widow O'Callaghan's boys. Can't I depind on ye, b'ys? asks the frontispiece, as Pat and Mike, Barney, Tommie, and little Jim take on work, geese, roofs, and kitchens. The General makes gravy, Pat markets, and Mike sits on a roof with a knife.

Through mishaps and cheers, the boys learn pluck, loyalty, and care for their mother. Zollinger writes with warm humor and Irish flavor. The book remains a charming family story of a household holding together by grit and love.
9334-the-spectator-volume-1-eighteenth-c:
Henry Morley, professor of English at University College, London, edited this new edition of The Spectator in 1891. It reproduces the original text both as first issued and as corrected by its authors, with introduction, notes, and index. This first of three volumes opens the great eighteenth-century periodical to Victorian readers.

Addison and Steele's essays, on manners, letters, and society, shaped English prose for a century. Morley's notes gloss old customs and allusions. The volume remains a standard scholarly edition, and a fine entry to the Spectator's witty, humane world.
9792-redemption-and-two-other-plays:
Leo Tolstoy wrote Redemption and Two Other Plays, a volume of drama on faith, guilt, and society. Fruits of Culture and Redemption head the contents, with full casts of Russian gentry, gypsies, and servants. Redemption's people include Fedya Protosov, his wife Lisa, and Victor Karenin, with Masha the gypsy girl beside. Officers, doctors, and musicians crowd the stage.

The plays stage moral crisis in drawing rooms and low restaurants, where love, drink, and conscience collide. Tolstoy's drama favors plain truth over stage tricks. A reader gets late Tolstoy on stage, earnest and searching, with Russian life laid bare in speech and act.
a-defence-of-poetry-and-other-essays:
Percy Bysshe Shelley's A Defence of Poetry and Other Essays gathers his prose in one volume. On Love opens the collection by asking what love is, and calling it the bond that connects man with everything that exists. On Life, On a Future State, and On the Punishment of Death follow. Speculations on Metaphysics and on Morals pursue his philosophy.

An essay on Athenian literature, arts, and manners, and his preface to Plato's Symposium, show Shelley the classical scholar. The Defence of Poetry closes the volume, answering Peacock's claim that poetry was obsolete. Poets, Shelley concludes, are the unacknowledged legislators of the world. Written in white heat in 1821, the Defence remained unpublished until 1840. These essays are the prose twin of the lyrics: the same mind arguing that imagination, not reason alone, remakes human life.
a-flock-of-girls-and-boys: Nora Perry gathers a flock of girls and boys in stories for young readers. Its tales include that little Smith girl, the egg boy, Major Molly's Christmas promise, Polly's valentine, and Sibyl's slipper. A boarding school Samaritan, Becky, Ally, and a Thanksgiving guest complete the flock. Perry writes warm stories of school, holiday, and friendship.
across-the-plains-with-other-memories-an:
Robert Louis Stevenson's collection of memories and essays is headed by Across the Plains, his notebook of an emigrant train journey from New York to San Francisco. The contents list twelve pieces. Sidney Colvin's letter at the front explains he chose and arranged papers written before Stevenson left for the South Seas, and notes the last of them were written in gloom and sickness.

After the title essay come The Old Pacific Capital, on Monterey, and Fontainebleau, on the artists' colony in the French forest. An epilogue to An Inland Voyage and two sets of random memories follow. Essays including The Lantern-Bearers, A Chapter on Dreams, Beggars, and A Christmas Sermon round out the volume. Stevenson turns travel notes, boyhood recollection, and moral reflection into one volume, unified by his voice rather than by subject.
andivius-hedulio-adventures-of-a-roman-n: Edward Lucas White tells the adventures of Andivius Hedulio, a Roman nobleman in the days of the empire, dedicated to the memory of Robert Louis Stevenson. The novel follows its hero through Roman streets, courts, and dangers, loving adventure and peril. White's learned romance brings ancient Rome to life with vigour.
angels-and-ministers-and-other-victorian: Laurence Housman gathers angels and ministers and other Victorian plays, opening with the Queen, God bless her, and his favourite flower. The plays revisit Victorian figures and scenes with Housman's gentle irony and pageant style. They offer a playwright's affectionate look back at an age just past. The plays charm most when read aloud.
bar-20-days:
Clarence E. Mulford's Bar-20 Days sends Hopalong Cassidy and Johnny Nelson on a holiday errand. Two tired but happy punchers ride into a coast town and dismount at the best hotel. The marshal makes them hang up their guns with the clerk: this is fence country now. He warns them, smiling, to leave their cash too.

Buck Peters has delegated the mission that brought them from the Bar-20 ranch. Freed of business, the boys sample the town's pleasures as only cowpunchers can. The marshal predicts empty pockets and aching heads within twenty-four hours. Mulford writes the West in dialect, with affection for men smarter than they look. Bar-20 Days is an episodic spree among his Hopalong novels, lighter than the gunfight books and full of bar-room comedy.
becket-and-other-plays:
Alfred Tennyson gathered four plays in this volume, headed by Becket. The laureate dedicated the Becket drama to the Earl of Selborne, the Lord Chancellor of his own day, as a memorial of Selborne's great predecessor. Thomas Becket moves from Chancellor of England to Archbishop of Canterbury in the dramatis personae, with Henry II, Gilbert Foliot, and John of Salisbury ranged around the quarrel of crown and church.

Three shorter plays follow. The Cup sets Roman officers plotting in a conquered province: Antonius signs an order to seize Sinnatus on any trace of treason, hating the Senate's filthy tools even as he obeys. The Falcon turns on a falcon and a vow, and The Promise of May brings the drama home to an English village. Tennyson's late theatre favours verse, conscience, and fate.
biographical-essays:
Biographical Essays, by Thomas De Quincey, gathers the magazine portraits of the author of the Confessions of an English Opium-Eater. De Quincey's volume opens with Shakspeare. He calls the playwright modern poetry's presiding genius. The glory of the human intellect is his other title for him. The essay begins by worrying a small fact with great care. Shakespeare was baptized on the twenty fifth of April, 1564. Tradition makes his birthday the twenty third, the day he also died.

De Quincey builds lives from such grains. His essays treat writers as minds to be entered, not records to be summarized. Digression is the method and the pleasure. This collection belongs to the De Quincey writings series, alongside the Confessions and Suspiria de Profundis.
britannica-1911-bank-holidays:
Bank holidays, in the United Kingdom, are days kept as close holidays in all banks under the Bank Holidays Act of 1871. Before 1834 the Bank of England closed on saints' days and anniversaries some thirty-three days a year. In 1834 those closures were cut to four: Good Friday, 1 May, 1 November, and Christmas Day.

The 1871 act, carried through the Commons by Sir John Lubbock, set Easter Monday, Whit Monday, the first Monday of August, and 26 December as bank holidays in England and Ireland. Ireland added 17 March in 1903. Scotland kept its own list, led by New Year's Day and Christmas Day. The 1911 Britannica entry adds the legal effect: no one must pay or act on such a day, and acting the next day counts as acting in time.
britannica-1911-chelys:
Chelys is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the common lyre of the ancient Greeks. The Greek word means tortoise, and the Latin name is testudo. The instrument had a convex back made of tortoise shell, or of wood shaped like the shell. Tradition tied it to the oldest Greek lyre, said to have been invented by Hermes. Walking by the Nile, he heard music from a tortoise shell. Tendons stretched across it had been set humming by the wind.

Since classic times the name has been applied loosely to various stringed instruments, bowed and twanged, probably for their vaulted backs. Greek vases often show the chelys lyre with the true tortoise shell drawn in. Propertius calls it the lyra testudinea. The entry, signed by Kathleen Schlesinger, also notes that Scaliger first drew attention to the difference between the chelys and the cithara.
britannica-1911-hendiadys:
Hendiadys is a rhetorical figure from the Greek hen dia dyoin. The phrase means one by means of two. Two words joined by a conjunction express a single idea. Usually two substantives replace a substantive and adjective. Virgil's Georgics gives the classical example. Pateris libamus et auro means cups and gold. The sense is simply cups of gold. The whole entry is this single short paragraph.

No history, examples list or authorities follow it. The figure's form is its entire content. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hendiadys entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hundred-days: Hundred Days, or Cent Jours in French, names the span from the twentieth of March 1815 to the twenty-eighth of June that year, as the short 1911 Britannica entry explains. Napoleon reached Paris on the first of those dates, back from exile on Elba. Louis the Eighteenth was restored to the throne on the last of them. The prefect of Paris first used the French phrase in a speech of welcome to the returning king.
britannica-1911-knollys:
Knollys is the name of an English family traced from Sir Thomas Knollys (d. 1435), a lord mayor of London. Its first great figure was Sir Francis Knollys (c. 1514–1596), whose father Robert had served Henry VII and Henry VIII. Francis entered parliament in 1542. He was knighted in 1547 while serving in Scotland. As a firm supporter of the reformed faith, he fled abroad when Mary came to the throne.

Under Elizabeth, his kinswoman by marriage, he became a privy councillor and vice-chamberlain. In 1568 he took charge of Mary Queen of Scots at Carlisle. He later held her at Bolton and Tutbury castles, and argued religion with his prisoner. He was treasurer of the household from 1572 to his death on the 19th of July 1596. His son William, made Baron Knollys in 1603 and Viscount Wallingford in 1616, lost his offices through his wife's kinship to the countess of Somerset.
britannica-1911-petau-denys:
Denys Petau lived from 1583 to 1652 and was a Jesuit scholar of France. The 1911 Britannica life notes his Latin name, Dionysius Petavius, as well. He was born at Orleans in August 1583 and schooled at Paris. Isaac Scaliger swayed him toward the dimmer Fathers of the church. In 1603 he took a lectureship at the university of Bourges.

Two years later he resigned to enter the Society of Jesus in full. For many years he taught divinity at the College de Clermont in Paris. That college was the chief Jesuit house in the capital then. In 1627 he published a great work on the reckoning of time. It built on and improved the labours of Scaliger in that field.
britannica-1911-railways: Railways is a large entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica, and the hosted opening is its list of parts. Those parts cover general statistics, economics and law, British and American railway law, and accident statistics. Further parts deal with finance, construction, locomotive power, rolling stock, city railways, and light railways. The list alone shows the scale of the full treatment.
britannica-1911-rogation-days:
Rogation Days is a church article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about three days of prayer in the Christian year. They are the Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday before Ascension Day. The name comes from a Latin word for beseeching, since the days were long marked by litanies sung in procession. The week that holds them is called Rogation Week.

In 511 the first Council of Orleans ordered that the three days be kept with fasting and processions. All work was to stop so that all could join in. Pope Leo the Third later set the days up at Rome, but without the fasting. Saint Augustine had brought the custom to England earlier, learning it on his way through Gaul. The Council of Clovesho in 747 confirmed the rule. The place name Gospel Oak is a relic of these walks.
buried-alive-a-tale-of-these-days:
Arnold Bennett wrote a comic tale of these days, fronted by twelve chapter heads. A puce dressing-gown opens the list. A pail, a photograph, and a scoop by the press come next. Alice on hotels gives the landlady her say.

A Putney morning, a confession, and an invasion fill the mid-run. A glossy male and a hid truth raise the stakes. Escape and Alice's turns close the list. Night in Selwood Terrace, South Kensington, opens the tale in mock grand style. Two lights burn in one house while the globe spins its best face from the sun. John Frederick Farrar, a doctor, gets the book as Bennett's helpmate in this and many books.
camping-for-boys:
H. W. Gibson wrote a camp guide for boys, with notes in this copy that date its core advice to 1913. A front poem sets the tone: wood smoke at dusk, birch logs, and night sounds read by ear. Proved camps of joy call young feet, the verse holds. A photo by Joseph Legg shows the heart of the camp.

Notes at the front warn in plain words. Health tips from 1913 may now mislead, and some stuff named is now banned or unsafe. Cash sums want a rate of twenty to one to read in 2004 terms, the note adds. Character, not mere fun, is camp's true aim here: good men formed, and chiefs picked or dropped by their own worth. Safe sleep, sound food, and clean sport fill the plan.
castilian-days:
John Hay's Castilian Days sketches Spain in a holiday edition illustrated after a special visit to Castile by Mr. Pennell. The publishers omitted a few chapters of the original edition, judging them less descriptive and less rich in picturesque material for the illustrator.

Otherwise the text stands unchanged, with contents on Madrid al fresco, Spanish living and dying, tradition in Spanish life, bullfighting, red-letter days, and an hour with the painters. A castle in the air, the city of the Visigoths, the Escorial, a miracle play, and the cradle and grave of Cervantes follow. Readers who love Spain will find Hay's sketches vivid, witty and observant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aliturgical-d:
Aliturgical days are days on which the liturgy, the Eucharistic sacrifice, may not be celebrated. The term, not in any English dictionary, is a convenience label from the modern Greek aleitourgetikos. The idea is far more familiar in the East than in the West. In the Roman Rite only one day is generally recognized as aliturgical: Good Friday. That day the Holy Sacrifice is not offered, and the Mass of the Presanctified contains no prayer of consecration.

In the early centuries, aliturgical days were numerous in both East and West. At first Mass seems to have been offered only on Sundays, the few festivals then recognized, and martyrs' anniversaries, with the bishop officiating. Days of stations, which coincided with the Wednesday and Friday fast, may have gone without the liturgy. Writers such as Tertullian show an opinion that offering the Holy Sacrifice sat ill with a serious fast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-of-da:
Ancient of Days is a name the prophet Daniel gives to God, in chapters seven, verses nine, thirteen, and twenty-two. Daniel sets God's eternal power against the frail life of the empires of the world, and the title carries that contrast in a single phrase.

Christian art drew from these passages its general way of picturing the first person of the Holy Trinity. The name runs in Aramaic as Atiq yomin, in the Greek Septuagint as palaios hemeron, and in the Latin Vulgate as Antiquus dierum, three tongues carrying one image of age without end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bothrys:
Bothrys, now Batroun on the Lebanese coast, was founded by Ithobaal of Tyre, father of Jezebel, near Cape Lithoprosopon. Ancient geographers from Strabo to Hierocles name it, and it served as suffragan of Tyre in Antioch's patriarchate. An earthquake in 551 cracked the cape and opened a large harbor, and Theophanes calls the city Bostrys.

Known Greek bishops number three: Porphyrius in 451, Elias about 512, and Stephen in 553. A tenth-century list still names the see as Petrounion. Today Batroun holds 2,500 people, half Maronite and half Greek, and centers a caza in the Lebanon district. Its Maronite diocese counts 60,000 Catholics, 50 churches, 30 priests, one seminary, 64 schools, and 12 monasteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-augusti:
A biographical entry presents David-Augustine de Brueys, a French theologian and playwright born at Aix in 1640 and dead at Montpellier in 1723. Raised a Calvinist in a Protestant family, he studied law, then theology with such success that he joined Montpellier's consistory. In 1681 he answered Bossuet's Exposition of Catholic Doctrine.

Soon converted by Bossuet himself, he gave up Protestantism in 1682, becoming a priest after his wife's death. His later works explain his conversion, defend the Mass, outward worship, the Church, and the Eucharist, and treat fanaticism and obedience to rulers. With Palaprat he also wrote comic plays and tragedies, staged with great success and published in 1712, with later editions following.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denys:
A life of Denys van Leeuwen, called the Carthusian, born at Ryckel in 1402 and dead in 1471. A shepherd boy in youth, he studied at Saint-Trond and Zwolle, where rector John Cele shaped his religious leanings. At eighteen he aimed at Saint Bruno's order, but Roermond first refused him as under age, so he studied three years at Cologne.

Admitted in 1423, he lived a hard Carthusian round of Mass, Office, and prayer, often sleeping only three hours a night. Reading filled his cell, from every summa and chronicle to Greek and Arab philosophers and both canon and civil law. Writing filled it too: commentaries on the Psalms from 1434, then the whole Bible and the Fathers, enough to fill twenty-five folio volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ember-days:
Ember Days, from the Latin Quatuor Tempora, or four times, are fast days at the start of each season. Pope Gregory VII fixed them for the whole Church as the Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday after 13 December, after Ash Wednesday, after Whitsunday, and after 14 September. Their aims were to thank God for nature's gifts, to teach moderate use of them, and to help the needy.

Their occasion lay in Rome's farm rites, when pagans sought their gods at seeding in December, harvest in June, and vintage in September. The Church, converting pagan peoples, sought to sanctify customs that could serve a good end. Rome at first kept fasts in June, September, and December only, and Gelasius speaks of all four seasons. Saturdays of ember weeks also became days for ordaining priests and deacons. The Eastern Church never adopted them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-druys:
Jean Druys, thirtieth abbot of Parc near Louvain, was born at Cumptich and died in 1635. Schooled at Saint-Trond, Liège, Namur, and Louvain, he joined Parc's Norbertine abbey in 1587, took his licentiate in 1595. He rose through sub-prior and theology teacher to succeed Abbot Loots.

Druys served as vicar-general to Prémontré's abbot-general and sat on Archduke Albert's council and the States of Brabant. He reformed Louvain university as visitor, a task finished in 1617, visited Douai and Héverlé. He rebuilt his own abbey after soldiers' damage, and in 1628 was charged with reshaping his order's statutes to Trent's decrees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laurence-hump:
Laurence Humphreys (1571-1591) was an English layman and martyr, born in Hampshire to Protestant parents. A bookish youth, well read in the Bible and religious works, he sought religious debate at eighteen and met Father Stanney, who soon converted him.

Virtuous and kind-hearted, he loved visiting prisoners and the sick, teaching the ignorant, and practising works of mercy, corporal and spiritual. In 1591, seriously ill, in delirium he named Queen Elizabeth harlot and heretic. Overheard by Protestants, he was jailed at Winchester before full recovery. At trial he could not recall the words, yet would not dispute the witnesses and accepted suffering for them. For those words alone he was condemned and executed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moralities-mo:
Moralities, also called morality plays, grew out of the miracle plays. Together with them they made up most of medieval drama, flourishing in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries across Europe, especially in France. Where a miracle play staged Bible stories, saints' lives and pious legends to teach the faith, a morality staged allegory to shape character.

Its figures were personified abstractions, vices and virtues, qualities of mind and general conceptions, speaking and acting out a moral lesson. Dr. Ward's classic definition puts it that way. Performed outdoors on movable scaffolds with the usual properties, much like miracle plays at first, moralities reached their best-known English form in Everyman. The entry follows their authors, staging and slow decline before the Renaissance stage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orkneys:
The Orkneys, islands north of Scotland across the Pentland Firth, hold a Norse-descended, Calvinist, English-speaking people of 30,000 on 375 square miles. Level, rocky, treeless, and partly swampy, they grow barley, oats, potatoes, and beets, and raise 30,000 cattle, 40,000 sheep, and sturdy small horses yearly.

Herring, cod, lobster, seals, whales, and trout feed islanders besides, and down and woven shawls bring export income. Kirkwall, a trading town of 5,000 with a good harbor, serves as capital, and the entry follows Norse earls, Scottish annexation, and the islands' churches. Mining for iron, tin, and silver also goes on successfully across the islands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passion-plays:
Passion plays grew from medieval religious drama, itself born of church liturgy, not from ancient theatre. Worship was thoroughly dramatic, above all Mass, with its forward action, dialogue of priest, ministers, and choir, and the people's part. Feast Gospels at Christmas, Epiphany, and Easter called for many roles, and poetry and music pressed the great events home to layfolk.

Tenth-century Benedictines of Saint Gall wrote sequences, hymns, litanies, and tropes, musical elaborations of the liturgy, above all the introit, sung antiphonally by choirs. Church drama starts with the Easter introit trope, kept in a Saint Gall manuscript from Tutilo's time, where singers trade the risen Lord's greeting. Later pages trace the plays from church to marketplace, their growth, suppression, and survival at Oberammergau and elsewhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-power-of-the-:
The phrase power of the keys comes from Christ's words to Peter in Matthew 16:19. Its sense opens out in Isaiah 22, where the key of the house of David goes to Eliacim son of Helcias as the mark of full rule in the Kingdom of Juda. By using the phrase, Christ plainly meant to give Peter supreme rule over His Church. Its sole aim is a short history of what church writers have meant by the phrase.

In the Fathers the words crop up often, almost always showing the Church's power to forgive sins. The power to grant or hold back pardon well fits the opening and shutting of heaven's gates. Yet that reading narrows the sense too far, for pardon is but one way church rule is wielded. Augustine's De Doctrina Christi gives a sample of the use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quentin-massy:
Quentin Massys was a painter born at Louvain in 1466 who died at Antwerp in 1530. This encyclopedia entry corrects his epitaph, which gives 1529, since he lived past 13 July and died before 16 September 1530. His life is adorned, or obscured, with legends. He was certainly the son of a smith. Nothing proves he first plied his father's trade, but he worked as a bronzier and medalist, and Erasmus wrote in 1528 that Massys had engraved his medallion.

That medal, perhaps the one dated 1519, survives in a copy at Basle. Molanus in 1575 credited Massys with the standard of the baptismal fonts at Saint Pierre, Louvain, though his account is full of errors. His Saint Anne at Brussels, the entry judges, is the most gracious, tender, and sweet work in all northern painting. It shows a spiritual conversation of holy persons in earthly dress within a serene, paradisal court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rogation-days:
Rogation Days are days of prayer, once also of fasting, set by the Church to turn away God's anger, seek protection in calamity, and win a good harvest. In England they were called Gang Days. They stood high in English esteem: King Alfred's laws counted theft on these days equal to theft on Sunday or a high holy day. Their observance lasted until 1571.

The Major Rogation falls on 25 April and the Minor on the three days before Ascension. The Major seems old, introduced to counter the heathen Robigalia processions, and was regulated by Gregory the Great. The Minor came from Mamertus, Bishop of Vienne, and was ordered by the Fifth Council of Orleans in 511 and approved by Leo III. The liturgy joins procession and Rogation Mass. For 25 April the Missal orders that if St Mark's feast moves, the procession does not.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-station-days:
Station days, in the early Church, were fast days ending earlier than strict fasts. On a station day the fast ran until None, between twelve and three, later until Sext, nine to twelve. A proper fast day ran until Vespers, three to six. Ancient liturgical writers commonly called fast days stationes, but the entry insists on distinguishing statio from jejunium.

Pamelius refused the distinction, while Cardinal Bona allowed that statio sometimes equalled jejunium but not as an absolute rule. Tertullian described a less rigorous fast, a semi-jejunium, broken sooner, and for him ending a station meant the same as ending a fast. Gregory the Great named certain Roman churches as stations for solemn festivals until Sext. The entry traces a term from fasting discipline to Roman processional worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-sand: John Wainewright's Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows John Sandys, an English martyr from the diocese of Chester. He reached Reims on 4 June 1583. There he was ordained in the Holy Cross Chapel of Reims Cathedral by Cardinal Archbishop Louis de Guise, and he left for the mission on 2 October 1584. Executed at Gloucester on 11 August 1586, he was cut down still conscious. He struggled with an executioner who had blackened his face and used a rusty knife, and died praying for his persecutors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wurzburg-abbe:
Wurzburg Abbeys describes four Benedictine houses: Holy Redeemer or Saint Kilian's, Saint Andrew's later Saint Burchard's, Saint Stephen's, and Scotch Saint James's. Burchard, Bishop of Würzburg, founded Holy Redeemer about 745, and its monks ran the cathedral and school until Bishop Bernwelf in 786 replaced them with canons called Brothers of Saint Kilian. The expelled monks, over fifty strong, found refuge at Neustadt under resigned Bishop Megingaud.

Saint Andrew's, founded by Burchard after 748, won fame for its school, sank in the tenth century, and rose under Hugo's 988 reform, gaining Burchard's body in 984 and his name. Fire about 1030 led Abbot Wilemuth to rebuild church and house from 1033 to 1042, dedicated by Bruno before Henry III and six bishops. Saint Stephen's, founded in 1013, turned Benedictine in 1057, joined Bursfeld reform in 1459, and lasted until secularization in 1803. Saint James's, a Scotch house from 1134 under Macarius, honoured 24 January, kept Irish and Scots monks.
ceres-runaway-and-other-essays:
Alice Meynell's Ceres' Runaway and Other Essays, from the 1909 Constable edition, opens with a fancy: a Roman municipality chasing a wild crop of poppies it cannot overtake. The contents list twenty short essays, among them Laughter, The Little Language, The Sea Wall, The Tow Path, and two pieces on children of tumult. Meynell's subjects hide inside small occasions.

She writes on daffodils, plaid, audiences, and tethered constellations with a poet's compression and a critic's judgment. A passage on a thousand London people made fast in their own mediocrity shows her moral edge. Meynell, once mooted as poet laureate, perfected the short literary essay in England, and this volume shows her range.
characters-of-shakespeare-s-plays:
William Hazlitt's Characters of Shakespeare's Plays first appeared in 1817, and this World's Classics edition adds an introduction by Arthur Quiller-Couch. Hazlitt treats one play at a time in a separate essay. Cymbeline opens the contents, followed by Macbeth, Julius Caesar, and Othello. Hamlet, Lear, and Romeo and Juliet stand among the tragedies.

Histories run from Richard II through Henry VIII and King John. The comedies close the volume, from Twelfth Night to the Comedy of Errors. Doubtful plays and the poems and sonnets receive a final essay. Hazlitt writes as a lover, not a professor, judging characters as living people. His Macbeth and Hamlet essays helped invent the modern way of reading Shakespeare. The prose is familiar, fervent, and quotable, criticism as literature in its own right.
chopin-and-other-musical-essays:
Henry T. Finck published six musical essays with Scribner's Sons, copyrighted in 1889 and reissued in 1894. The title essay calls Chopin the greatest genius of the pianoforte. Finck notes that a New York dealer sold three times as much Chopin as any other romantic or classical composer. Yet the deepest late works, he complains, went unplayed in parlours and halls alike.

How composers work follows, gathering habits of creation. Schumann is mirrored in his letters in the third essay. Music and morals argues an old question, with Pythagoras prescribing melodies against passions. Italian and German vocal styles are compared. German opera in New York closes the volume, a report from the critic's own beat. The tone is learned, combative, and fond.
cowley-s-essays:
Abraham Cowley wrote the essays gathered here near the end of his life, and this Cassell edition of 1893 adds a long introduction on the poet. Cowley had been a Royalist secretary, a fellow of the Royal Society, and a celebrated poet. His father, a London stationer, died before Abraham was born in 1618. Spenser's poems, found in his mother's parlor, first woke his love of verse.

The essays themselves praise a quiet, retired life. Cowley writes on liberty, solitude, obscurity, and agriculture. He weighs greatness and avarice and finds both costly. A discourse warns of the dangers of an honest man in much company. Of Myself closes the set with calm self-examination. Readers get seventeenth-century prose at its most graceful, from a courtier who concluded that gardens beat courts and contentment beats ambition.
curly-and-floppy-twistytail-the-funny-pi: Howard Roger Garis's bedtime stories follow Curly and Floppy Twistytail, two piggie boys living in a little house at the edge of a wood. Each short tale gives them a small adventure: getting named, helping mother, going to school, meeting an elephant, a turtle and Santa Claus. Written for reading aloud, the stories mix animal mischief with homely lessons.
dangerous-days:
Mary Roberts Rinehart opens Dangerous Days at a dinner given by Natalie Spencer, a futile hostess absorbed by menu details while her steel-manufacturer husband Clayton faces graver matters. The novel, written during the First World War, plays out in an American industrial city pulled toward war production. German sympathizers and labor agitators work the shadows.

A radical admiring jewel shop windows calculates what honest workmen's wages buy for Wall Street's women, and vows America shall not pull England's chestnuts from the fire. Anna, the Spencers' German maid, and a suspicious watch draw Clayton toward the plot at home. Rinehart, famous for mysteries, here wrote a wartime domestic novel about loyalty, marriage, and sabotage.
discourses-biological-geological-essays:
Eleven lectures and addresses by Thomas Henry Huxley fill this 1894 set of biological and geological essays. A list at the front gives each piece its year and place. On a Piece of Chalk, from 1868, opens the book; Huxley gave it to the working men of Norwich.

The problems of the deep sea and results from the Challenger expedition follow. Yeast, the formation of coal, and the border land between the animal and vegetable kingdoms fill the middle. A study of Peronospora spores, freeing oxygen in sunlight, shows the scale of his eye. A lobster serves for the study of zoology. Biogenesis and abiogenesis, his 1870 presidential address, and talks on fossils and evolution close the set.
doe-osti-17119311-radiation-effects-of-h:
Kyle Holloway, Philip Petersen, Michael Heighes, and Jason Schulthess report on neutron damage in high entropy alloys. Their August 2025 report comes from Idaho National Laboratory. High entropy alloys mix several metals in near equal shares. They are candidates for Generation IV reactors, which run hotter and harsher than current plants. Thirteen alloy systems were made and irradiated in the Advanced Test Reactor.

Samples were formed by spark plasma sintering of cryogenically milled powder. They were then cut into small tensile bars. After irradiation, every alloy sample behaved in a brittle way. Each broke before yielding, with low strain at fracture. The authors link the brittleness to missing post processing after sintering. Only the refractory based alloys were fully analyzed so far. Fracture and hardness studies come next.
doe-osti-2589262-computed-tomography-sca:
National Energy Technology Laboratory report DOE/NETL-2025/4949, dated 24 September 2025, documents detailed scans of rock core from the Clinton Formation in eastern Ohio. Thomas Paronish, Andrew Holleran, Mathias Pohl, and eight co-authors report the work. Core came from twelve Ohio wells held by the state's Division of Geological Survey, and the report runs to 68 pages.

Core samples were imaged with computed tomography, which uses X-rays to map pores, fractures, and dense minerals inside the rock. Multi-sensor core logging added physical measurements along each core. One cover image shows a fracture in core from the C. Poling #2 well at 2,747 feet, imaged at very fine scale. Well histories and depth records fill much of the report. The data give engineers a public record of how this formation stores and moves fluids.
doe-osti-2998403-study-and-improvement-o:
Fermilab internship report FERMILAB-TM-2872-STUDENT, by Giovanni Chiello under Angela Fava and Donatella Torretta, from the 2023 Italian student program, studies the trigger system of the ICARUS neutrino detector. ICARUS is the far detector of the Short-Baseline Neutrino program, hunting signs of a fourth, sterile neutrino. Its liquid argon chamber sees every passing particle, so a trigger must decide in microseconds what is worth recording.

Background rates drive the design. Cosmic ray events arrive about once every seven beam spills, argon-39 decays and stray muon products add roughly 0.03 hertz, and the combined minimum-bias rate lands near one event per six spills, about 0.12 hertz. A trigger primitive demands at least nine light-detector signals in coincidence. Improvements weighed in the report aim to keep rare neutrino events while shedding that steady background.
doe-osti-3002145-rapid-oxidation-of-uran:
Zach Brubaker, Jordan Roach, and Avery Wood test a fast way to rust uranium-bearing steel in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4171, dated October 2025. Their method is combustion synthesis, a reaction that feeds its own heat once lit. Standard lab methods heat slowly, so they miss what happens to particles formed in sudden, extreme heat.

The team burned a uranium alloy, U2NiCrFe4, in reactions fueled by uranyl nitrate and glycine. Peak temperatures passed 1,200 degrees Celsius. Microscope images, element maps, and Raman spectra showed iron oxides forming first and fastest. Uranium oxide appeared only in small amounts, since the fast cooling limited its growth. The result supports combustion synthesis as a stand-in for real high-temperature events.
doe-osti-3004999-oklo-sponsored-testing-:
Darius Lisowski, Alex Grannan, Taeil Kim, and colleagues at Argonne report sponsored testing in final CRADA report ANL/NSE-25/75. The sponsor is Oklo, an advanced reactor company. Its fuel assembly design, jointly built by Oklo and Argonne, was installed in PELICAN, a pressure-drop test loop for core assemblies. The tests validate the simulation software used to predict coolant flow behavior.

Thirteen tests, numbered 050 through 062, swept flow rates across laminar, transition, and turbulent regimes. Five pressure transmitters yielded 65 pressure-drop data points, 41 of them unique. Pressure rose quadratically with flow, as theory expects. The SAS system code, run with two correlation sets, matched the measured drops strongly across the range. Reactor licensing leans on exactly this kind of code-versus-data check.
doe-osti-3013193-updates-to-anaerobic-di:
Argonne report ANL-25/68, by Branden Leonhardt, Jacob Englander, Longwen Ou, and co-authors, dated December 2025, updates the anaerobic digestion pathways for animal manure in the R&D GREET 2025 model. GREET is Argonne's life-cycle tool for counting the greenhouse gas cost of fuels and vehicles. Manure handling is a major methane source, releasing 2,312 kilotons in the United States in 2022.

The update revises how the model treats business-as-usual manure management for each livestock sector, replacing earlier national-average assumptions with refined practice data. It also reworks digester modeling across four technologies, from covered lagoons to mixed plug flow units. Well-to-wheel results are shown through a heavy-duty compressed natural gas transit bus example. The authors close by flagging where the model should improve next.
doe-osti-3021396-advanced-reactor-design:
INL report INL/RPT-25-89556, Revision 0, dated September 2025 and led by Christopher Paul Chwasz with authors from several schools and labs, assesses the physical security of advanced reactor designs. New reactor types move radioactive material into new configurations, and each design's structures, systems, and components differ in weight and exposure to attack or theft. The report ranks those elements for select advanced reactor designs.

For each design, the team scored components by defense line, weight, and exposure, covering heat removal, reactivity control, radionuclide retention, support power, and instrumentation. In one assessment, resin tanks and drums carried medium weight as the main radionuclide retention system, while a radwaste building scored low in weight but very high in exposure. The rankings point designers to built-in mitigations. Protection should be part of the plant, not bolted on afterward.
doe-osti-3028241-plasma-assisted-pre-cha:
William Northrop of Carnegie Mellon University, with Satbir Singh and Ales Srna and Sandia National Laboratory as partner, reports award DE-EE0009877 on ignition for heavy-duty natural gas engines. The engines must run stoichiometric and highly dilute while meeting ultra-low nitrogen oxide limits expected under 2027 EPA and California rules. The project set hard targets: at least 2 percent better brake thermal efficiency and 4 percent lower total cost of ownership than a typical multi-cylinder engine with three-way catalyst.

The team built a plasma-assisted pre-chamber ignition system around nanosecond pulsed discharges. Testing moved through an optically accessible rapid-compression machine, a constant-volume chamber, and an optical single-cylinder engine, with simulations alongside. One modeling fix added crevice volume equal to nearly 22 percent of the clearance volume, which brought computed and measured peak motoring pressures into good agreement.
doe-osti-3365558-precision-spectroscopy-:
Yale University's final report for DOE award DE-SC0023672, led by David C. Moore from February 2023 to January 2026, demonstrates a new way to watch single nuclear decays. Instead of catching the energy a decay deposits, the team measures the tiny mechanical recoil of the whole microscopic particle holding the nucleus. Momentum conservation makes the method sensitive even to neutrinos, which slip through ordinary detectors untouched.

The group reported the first mechanical detection of individual decays, from radon-220 daughters implanted in levitated spheres. Smaller nanoparticles, about 100 nanometers, reached impulse resolution within a factor of five of the Standard Quantum Limit, fine enough in principle to feel one neutrino's kick. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory partners developed squeezed-light readout theory to push below that limit. Uses run from neutrino physics to nuclear forensics.
doe-osti-3366075-integration-of-solid-ox:
National Energy Technology Laboratory report DOE/NETL-2026/5339, by Alex Noring, Josh Kuffour, Arun Iyengar, and Gregory Hackett, studies powering artificial intelligence data centers with solid oxide fuel cells. These fuel cells convert natural gas to electricity electrochemically at high efficiency, and they scale in modules. AI campuses need firm power faster than grids can deliver it, making on-site generation attractive.

Scoping analysis compares grid-connected and islanded designs. In the fully on-site cases, the fuel cell plant carries the whole load at 99.999 percent availability, and transformers and backup diesel generators drop out of the design. Inverters feed 480-volt power straight to the computing halls, though a UPS-like buffer is still included. Cases contrast current and advanced fuel cell technology. The work gives developers a template for fuel-cell-powered campuses.
dorothy-dale-s-camping-days:
Margaret Penrose takes Dorothy Dale out of school and into the woods in Dorothy Dale's Camping Days, issued by Cupples and Leon in New York in 1911. Dorothy and her chum Tavia are the heart of the series, and the camping trip gives them freedom, fresh air, and trouble in equal shares. The frontispiece shows Dorothy sliding into a frail bark canoe.

Early chapters start with a hayrick, a disastrous drag ride, and a camp pitched too soon. Strange meetings and a night scare follow; at one point Dorothy wakes to find the door of her shelter bolted from outside and the windows fastened. Penrose gives her girls real nerve: they scout, paddle, and solve their own scrapes. The book sells outdoor life to town girls as health, pluck, and the joy of a campfire with friends.
dorothy-dale-s-queer-holidays:
Margaret Penrose sends Dorothy Dale home for a holiday full of small mysteries in Dorothy Dale's Queer Holidays, from Cupples and Leon in 1910. Tavia, her wild chum, leads off as usual: the first chapters are hers, from what happened to Tavia to the tangled web she wove. A light in a window starts the girls guessing.

Shoplifters in a store, a stolen ring, and haunted woods keep the holiday busy. One chapter is built around a magazine ghost, and a frontispiece shows a ghost brought out of a closet. A little woman in black, a holly wreath with thorns, and a scream from a castle fill out the list. College boys from Glenwood join the fun near the end. Penrose mixes schoolgirl talk with detective play, and Dorothy's steady head untangles what Tavia's rash hands knot up.
dream-days:
Kenneth Grahame wrote Dream Days, published in 1898, a companion to his earlier book The Golden Age. Like that book, it looks back at childhood in a country house, where five children live under the care of aunts and uncles they call Olympians. The grown narrator recalls their games, quarrels, and small adventures, and the way children build whole worlds out of a garden, a road, or a rainy day.

One tale in the set outgrew the book. In The Reluctant Dragon, a boy finds a gentle, poetry-loving dragon in a cave, and must stage a fake fight between the beast and St. George to satisfy the village. Grahame later wrote The Wind in the Willows, and the same warm humor runs through these pages.
emerson-and-other-essays:
John Jay Chapman leads with Emerson in Emerson and Other Essays, first printed in 1899 and reprinted in this AMS edition of 1969. Six more essays follow: Walt Whitman, a study of Romeo, Michael Angelo's sonnets, the fourth canto of the Inferno, Robert Browning, and Robert Louis Stevenson. Chapman opens with a fierce extract from The Conduct of Life against flattering the masses.

Emerson, in the quoted passage, wishes the masses tamed, drilled, divided, and broken up, so that honest individuals may be drawn out of them. Chapman takes that warfare between the individual and society as the leading thought of Emerson's life. Each generation, he writes, fields a poet or two who exalt the single soul. The essays are brilliant, combative, and personal, the work of a critic who wrote like a duelist and read like a poet.
escape-and-other-essays:
Arthur Christopher Benson's Escape, and Other Essays was published in New York in 1915. Essays from the Century Magazine and the Cornhill appear here by permission. An introduction walks the reader beside the slow river Cam. Fen Ditton, Horningsea, and the bishops' retreat at Ely colour the opening pages.

Fifteen essays follow the title piece on escape, the wish to slip life's harness. Literature and life, the new poets, and Walt Whitman treat reading. Charm, sunset, and villages give the book its contemplative middle. Dreams, schooldays, and authorship turn the gaze inward. Herb moly and heartsease, plants of healing and rest, close the volume in figure. Benson's gift is for the familiar essay at its most civilized: unhurried, observant, and quietly glad to be alive.
essays:
Alice Meynell's Essays, in the 1914 Burns and Oates gathering, sorts her short prose under headings: Winds and Waters, In a Book Room, Commentaries, Wayfaring, and Arts. Ceres' Runaway reappears among wells, rain, tow paths, and tethered constellations. The book-room section treats pathos, composure, the honours of mortality, and the little language of children.

Commentaries consider laughter, the rhythm of life, solitude, and the hours of sleep, while the arts essays reach Tithonus, the plaid, and Victorian caricature. A passage rebuking our lack of respect for successors' wisdom shows her moral temper. This larger collection lets readers follow Meynell's essay art whole: brief, exact, and quietly Catholic in outlook.
evolution-and-ethics-and-other-essays:
Thomas Henry Huxley delivered the title essay of this volume at Oxford as the Romanes Lecture, and his preface mourns Romanes himself, dead young. The discourse fills the first half of the book; other essays on science, morals, and politics make up the rest. Huxley chose his subject deliberately: the bearing of modern scientific thought on morals and politics.

The lecture's argument became his most quoted. The cosmic process, nature's struggle for existence, is no guide for human conduct; the ethical process exists precisely to combat it. A garden kept against weeds supplies his governing image of society maintained against nature. Written near the end of his life, the lecture is the old controversialist's considered answer to those who would read morality straight off evolution.
first-plays:
Milne tries the stage in First Plays, a set of five early plays. A. A. Milne wrote them in 1916 and 1917, and says so in a droll introduction. They were, he writes, the pastime of a temporary soldier, not the work of a professional playwright. Only one of the five, he notes, deals with the war that made them possible.

The plays are Wurzel-Flummery, The Lucky One, The Boy Comes Home, Belinda, and The Red Feathers. The sampled pages come from the homecoming play. Philip, back from France, lights his pipe at the breakfast table, two hours late. His Uncle James asks if he smokes now. Philip cries out in wonder: what did his uncle think they did in France? Milne's light touch, later famed in the nursery, is already at work here.
five-little-plays:
Sutro gathers five one-act plays in Five Little Plays, printed at New York in 1922. Alfred Sutro wrote them for the small stage. The set holds The Man in the Stalls, A Marriage Has Been Arranged, The Man on the Kerb, The Open Door, and The Bracelet. The first was produced at the Palace Theatre on October 6, 1911.

The sampled scene is a poor home. Joe weighs a found purse in his hand, heavy with money his wife Mary cannot bring herself to open. She had hoped, she says, that someone with a heart might have come in with him that night and set them on their legs again. Joe coughs through the night, and the dispensary's medicine does no good. Sutro builds his small plays on such turns of hope, want, and kindness.
football-days:
Edwards looked back on the rough early decades of American college football, and on the men behind the ball. A Princeton man of 1900, he fills the book with players' own memories, introduced by Walter Camp of Yale. The frontispiece shows three victorious Princeton captains: Hillebrand, Cochran, and Edwards himself. The dedication honors John P. Poe Jr., killed on a battlefield in France.

One story has Bill Hotchkiss of Williams playing a savage game in mud and snow three inches deep. Afterward he stood planted like a bull at bay, unable to walk on ruined ankles. William H. Edwards carried him off the field on a boy's sled. The book came out in 1916.
four-short-plays:
John Galsworthy wrote these four short plays, which the hosted volume heads Hall-Marked and Others and draws from his Six Short Plays. Hall-Marked, billed as a satiric trifle, opens the set on a bungalow verandah, where two ladies' dogs have been fighting in a pond. The Squire, the Rector, the Doctor, and the Cabman complete a cast named mostly by their stations.

Defeat, The Sun, and Punch and Go follow. Galsworthy worked in miniature the same themes as his novels: class polish, wartime loss, and the theatre's own machinery, which Punch and Go turns into a play about putting on a play. The pieces are curtain-raisers in length, built for an evening's bill. Readers of the Forsyte books will find the same cool irony, compressed into single scenes.
gala-days:
Gail Hamilton, the pen name of Mary Abigail Dodge, published Gala-Days in 1863 and filled it with comic essays in her own brisk voice. Hamilton opens by dragging a trunk down from the garret herself rather than ask her husband Halicarnassus, who would have debated the errand for three days. The marriage becomes a running joke and a partnership of equals in print, if not in trunk-hauling.

Essays follow on a call to her countrywomen, success in life, Harvard class day, a concert, and the happiest days. Dodge wrote during the Civil War years for a wide magazine audience, arguing women's competence while making readers laugh. Her tone, tart, funny, and unsentimental, made her one of the best-known American women essayists of her time.
gems-of-poetry-for-girls-and-boys:
Dated 1850, this slim book of verse was made for girls and boys, with pictures of scenes such as a view of Cincinnati and a cotton plant. A May-Day song opens the book, praising flowers, brooks, lambs, and bees. The poems are short, rhymed, and easy to learn by heart.

Later pieces include The Old Oaken Bucket, a song of longing for a farm well, and The Good-Natured Girls, about two sisters who never fight. A winter piece toasts the apple tree. The tone stays sweet and moral, in the manner of its time. At about a few dozen pages of verse, it is a small window on what adults chose for children to recite.
greek-studies-a-series-of-essays:
Walter Pater's Greek Studies collects his essays on the art and religion of ancient Greece, printed here in Macmillan's 1910 Library Edition. Sculpture stands first in the volume's concerns: the beginnings of Greek carving, the marbles of Aegina, and the age of the athletic prizemen. Pater reads statues as records of feeling, each generation of artists solving the body's form a little further. Myth follows art, with Dionysus studied at length as god of wine, theater, and ecstatic suffering.

Inside, Demeter and Persephone carry the essays into the grain mysteries and the Greek idea of death and return. Hippolytus, veiled and doomed, closes the mythic sequence in Pater's most delicate register. The prose moves slowly on purpose: sensation first, then the idea the sensation leaves behind. Readers who know Pater as the Renaissance critic will find his Greece here, a younger, stranger country of marble athletes and suffering gods.
healthful-sports-for-boys: Alfred Rochefort Calhoun's guide arranges boys' sports by season, beginning with spring marbles, whip tops, kites, hoops and fishing. Summer brings boating, canoeing, small sail boats and swimming, with styles, diving and water games explained step by step. Tag, leap frog, duck on the rock and counting-out rhymes complete a practical book on how games are played and sides chosen.
hello-boys:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox's Hello, Boys! is a book of war verses written largely in France, where Wilcox spent seven months among American soldiers. She wrote the poems for entertainments in camps and hospitals, deliberately using the simplest language so that soldiers themselves could take them to heart.

The contents run from Thanksgiving and tributes to Highland lads through camp songs and farewells. Wilcox notes that soldiers asked her to autograph scores of copies, one poem to the extent of 350. The London edition of 1919 gathers verses first tried out before audiences of thousands. Readers who want the war as ordinary soldiers heard it sung and spoken will find Wilcox plain, sentimental and close to her audience.
hilda-lessways:
Arnold Bennett published this novel in 1911, as a mate to his Clayhanger books. Hilda Lessways lives with her widowed mother in the Five Towns. She hates house work and longs for a larger life. A post as editorial secretary, won through shorthand skill, opens her way to London.

The six books trace her start, fall, burden, and hard-won release. Edwin Clayhanger crosses her path, but Hilda stays the center. Bennett fills the tale with shops, chapels, printers, and trains. Readers follow a proud young woman learning, at real cost, what freedom demands.
historical-lectures-and-essays:
Charles Kingsley's Historical Lectures and Essays, in the 1902 Macmillan edition, begins with the first discovery of America, told through Bjarne Grimolfson's ship sinking under sea-worms in the Irish Ocean. Kingsley delights in the detail of the boat payed with seal blubber, which worms will not hurt, and in Bjarne's lot-drawing when the boat holds only half the crew.

Lectures follow on Cyrus as servant of the Lord, ancient civilisation, and the naturalists Rondelet, Vesalius, and Paracelsus, heroes to the clergyman-scientist Kingsley. The Buchanan essay carries him into Reformation France, where Diana of Poitiers hunts heretics. Kingsley lectures as he preached: vividly, morally, and with a naturalist's eye for concrete fact.
how-to-tell-a-story-and-other-essays:
Mark Twain's title essay in this little collection is his ars poetica of the platform. The humorous story, he says, is American; the comic story is English, the witty story French. The humorous story depends on the manner of the telling, may wander and arrive nowhere, and must be told gravely by a man concealing that he sees the joke.

The Golden Arm, printed here as The Wounded Soldier's companion piece, is his working example, a ghost tale whose snapper must be dropped carelessly and caught late. Mental Telegraphy Again argues for thought transference from his own coincidences. The Invalid's Story, the closing piece, is the famous tale of a corpse, a box of limburger cheese, and a railway journey. Four short pieces and one long lesson in the art he practised nightly.
in-the-hands-of-the-malays:
G. A. Henty collected In the Hands of the Malays and Other Stories, published by Blackie in 1905. The title tale opens on May 1, 1669, on a rocky island off Sumatra. A man of unclear nation, with an Arab cast of face, stands at the shore. Other tales are On the Track and A Frontier Girl.

On the Track follows a son who vows to clear his father's name. A lawyer offers him a post at six dollars a week while he hunts a clue. Capture, frontier life, and loyalty drive the tales. Henty writes for boys in his usual brisk style.
in-the-name-of-the-bodleian-and-other-es:
Augustine Birrell gathered essays in In the Name of the Bodleian, published in London in 1906. The title paper celebrates Oxford's great library. Other pieces treat bookworms, confirmed readers, first editions, and gossip in a library. Lawyers at play, old booksellers, and copyright follow.

Later essays turn to Johnson, Boswell, Paine, Bradlaugh, and Disraeli. Epitaphs amuse him, including one for a sincere and contented man named Smith. Birrell shelters a love of odd passages behind Carlyle's example. The book is a bookman's miscellany, light in tone, wide in range, and full of quotable passages for keen readers.
italian-journeys:
William Dean Howells wrote Italian Journeys from travel in 1864 and after, first issued in 1867. The road to Rome from Venice opens the book. Padua, Ferrara, Bologna, and Genoa lead to a sea trip to Naples. Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Capri get full days.

Ecelino, the thirteenth-century lord of Vicenza and Verona, is recalled on the Ferrara road. Fearless, abstemious, and hard, he was hurt to death seeking Milan, Howells notes.
